title: A first script, a line at a time
intro: Four small steps that end in a script with a variable, a loop and a function of your own. Each step adds to what you wrote in the one before, so nothing is thrown away.

steps.title: Say something
steps.task: Replace pass with a line that prints Good morning. Watch the output pane beside the editor: it runs a moment after you stop typing.

tests.label: prints Good morning

hints: Text goes in double quotes inside print(), and the line keeps the one tab of indent that pass had.
steps.explain: _ready() is called by Godot once, when the node joins the running game. Everything indented under it is its body; the indent is not decoration, it is how GDScript knows where the function ends.

steps.title: Keep a value
steps.task: Above _ready(), add a variable: var day := 1. Then add a second print that uses it to print Day 1. print takes several things separated by commas and writes them one after another.
steps.solution:
extends Node

var day := 1

func _ready() -> void:
	print("Good morning")
	print("Day ", day)

tests.label: there is a variable day, and it is 1
prints Day 1
the print uses the variable, not a typed 1
tests.why: Print the variable: print("Day ", day)

hints: The variable goes at the left edge, outside any function – that makes it belong to the whole script.
print("Day ", day) – mind the space inside the quotes.
steps.explain: := means "make a variable and work out its type from the value" – here an int. Change the 1 to 12 and the output follows, which is the whole point of a variable. Chapter D is about them.

steps.title: Do it for each
steps.task:
Add a list of chores and print each on its own line, after the two lines you already print:

var chores := ["water the beans", "feed the dog", "check the post"]

Use a for loop, not three prints.
steps.solution:
extends Node

var day := 1
var chores := ["water the beans", "feed the dog", "check the post"]

func _ready() -> void:
	print("Good morning")
	print("Day ", day)
	for chore in chores:
		print(chore)

tests.label: prints the greeting, the day, then the three chores in order
uses a for loop
tests.why: A loop is the point of this step.

hints: The shape is for chore in chores: and, one tab further in, print(chore).
The loop goes inside _ready(), so for has one tab and print(chore) has two.
steps.explain: Add a fourth chore to the list and the loop prints it without being told. Code that reads a list is the beginning of data-driven design, which is how Little Hours holds its 50 rooms.

steps.title: Name the job
steps.task: Write a function of your own, greeting(who: String) -> String, that returns "Good morning, " followed by the name and a full stop – so greeting("Wren") gives Good morning, Wren. Then change the first print to use it, with any name you like.

tests.label: _ready() prints what greeting() returns
tests.why: Call it inside print: print(greeting("Wren"))

hints: A function starts at the left edge: func greeting(who: String) -> String:. Its body is one line, return and the text.
Strings join with +: "Good morning, " + who + "."
steps.explain: A variable, a loop and a function: most scripts in most games are made of these three. The next chapters take each of them slowly.

title: The Inspector, written as code
intro: The script below is one Node2D that draws a signpost. It starts in the middle of a 320 by 180 screen. In six steps you will place it, turn it, size it and tint it from _ready() – then do two things the Inspector cannot: keep changing a value while the game runs, and change one from the keyboard. Leave _draw() as it is.
starter:
extends Node2D

func _ready() -> void:
	pass

# A signpost, drawn around the node's own origin: the pink dot at (0, 0).
func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(-2, 10, 4, 20), Color("#7a5230"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(-22, -10, 44, 20), Color("#f2c14e"))
	draw_line(Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(14, 0), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, 6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 2, Color("#e0566f"))

steps.title: Position
steps.task: In the Inspector you would open Transform and type 80 and 120 into Position. Do the same from _ready(): replace pass with a line that puts the node at x 80, y 120. Watch the sign move to the lower left of the view.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2(80, 120)

# A signpost, drawn around the node's own origin: the pink dot at (0, 0).
func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(-2, 10, 4, 20), Color("#7a5230"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(-22, -10, 44, 20), Color("#f2c14e"))
	draw_line(Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(14, 0), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, 6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 2, Color("#e0566f"))

tests.label: position is (80, 120)

hints: A position is two numbers kept together as a Vector2: Vector2(x, y).
position = Vector2(80, 120), indented one tab where pass was.
steps.explain: The pink dot is the node's origin, and position says where that dot goes. 120 is lower than the 90 it started at, because y grows downwards. Nothing in _draw() changed: the drawing is made around the origin, and moving the node moves the drawing with it. Try Vector2(0, 0) to see where a new node starts in Godot.

steps.title: Rotation
steps.task: Next field down: Rotation, which the Inspector shows in degrees. Add a line to _ready() that turns the sign 30 degrees clockwise, so that its arrow points down a slope.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2(80, 120)
	rotation_degrees = 30

# A signpost, drawn around the node's own origin: the pink dot at (0, 0).
func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(-2, 10, 4, 20), Color("#7a5230"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(-22, -10, 44, 20), Color("#f2c14e"))
	draw_line(Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(14, 0), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, 6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 2, Color("#e0566f"))

tests.label: the node is turned 30 degrees clockwise
and is still at (80, 120)

hints: There are two properties for this. The one that counts in degrees has degrees in its name.
rotation_degrees = 30. A positive number turns clockwise.
steps.explain: The sign turned about the pink dot: rotation is always about the origin. If you wrote rotation = 30 first and got a strange angle, you have met the trap – plain rotation is in radians, and 30 radians is nearly five full turns. Try -30: negative is anticlockwise.

steps.title: Scale
steps.task: Scale is the last of the Transform group. Make the sign twice as wide and twice as tall.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2(80, 120)
	rotation_degrees = 30
	scale = Vector2(2, 2)

# A signpost, drawn around the node's own origin: the pink dot at (0, 0).
func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(-2, 10, 4, 20), Color("#7a5230"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(-22, -10, 44, 20), Color("#f2c14e"))
	draw_line(Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(14, 0), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, 6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 2, Color("#e0566f"))

tests.label: scale is (2, 2)
still turned 30 degrees

hints: Scale has a number for each direction, so it is a Vector2 too – even when both numbers are the same.
scale = Vector2(2, 2)
steps.explain: Like rotation, scaling happens about the origin: the pink dot stayed where it was and everything grew away from it. The two numbers need not match – Vector2(3, 1) stretches it sideways, and Vector2(-2, 2) flips it to point the other way, which is how many games turn a character round.

steps.title: Modulate
steps.task: Further down the Inspector, under Visibility, is Modulate: a colour that every pixel of the node is multiplied by. Give the sign a warm pink cast – a colour with all of its red, and 0.7 of its green and blue.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2(80, 120)
	rotation_degrees = 30
	scale = Vector2(2, 2)
	modulate = Color(1.0, 0.7, 0.7)

# A signpost, drawn around the node's own origin: the pink dot at (0, 0).
func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(-2, 10, 4, 20), Color("#7a5230"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(-22, -10, 44, 20), Color("#f2c14e"))
	draw_line(Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(14, 0), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, 6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 2, Color("#e0566f"))

tests.label: modulate keeps all of the red
0.7 of the green
0.7 of the blue
and the scale is untouched

hints: A colour is made with Color(red, green, blue), each from 0.0 to 1.0.
modulate = Color(1.0, 0.7, 0.7)
steps.explain: Modulate multiplies, it does not paint: the yellow board lost some of its green and blue and went towards orange, and the dark arrow hardly changed, because a small number times 0.7 is still small. White, Color(1, 1, 1), leaves everything alone, which is why it is the default. A fourth number is transparency – try Color(1, 1, 1, 0.4) for a ghost of a sign.

steps.title: Keep turning
steps.task: Everything so far the Inspector could have done. Now something it cannot: change a value while the game runs. Add a _process(delta) function that turns the sign a little every frame, at a steady 90 degrees a second. It starts from the 30 degrees set in _ready().
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2(80, 120)
	rotation_degrees = 30
	scale = Vector2(2, 2)
	modulate = Color(1.0, 0.7, 0.7)

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	rotation_degrees += 90 * delta

# A signpost, drawn around the node's own origin: the pink dot at (0, 0).
func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(-2, 10, 4, 20), Color("#7a5230"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(-22, -10, 44, 20), Color("#f2c14e"))
	draw_line(Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(14, 0), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, 6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 2, Color("#e0566f"))

tests.label: it starts at 30 degrees
one second later it has turned 90 degrees more: 120
after four seconds, a full turn: 390

hints: The function is func _process(delta: float) -> void:, at the left edge like _ready(). Godot calls it once every frame; delta is how many seconds the last frame took.
Add a small amount each frame: rotation_degrees += 90 * delta. Ninety a second, times the fraction of a second that has passed.
steps.explain: _ready() ran once and set where things start – that is the Inspector's job, done in code. _process() runs every frame and is where a game lives. Multiplying by delta is what makes the speed "per second" and not "per frame", so it turns at the same rate on a fast computer and a slow one; Chapter I is about that. Notice that _draw() still runs only once: turning a node does not redraw it.

steps.title: Hide and show
steps.task: Last: the Visible tick box, worked from the keyboard. In _process(), each time the ui_accept action is pressed – Space, or the A button under the view – flip visible: hide the sign if it is showing, show it if it is hidden. One press is one flip, however long the key is held.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2(80, 120)
	rotation_degrees = 30
	scale = Vector2(2, 2)
	modulate = Color(1.0, 0.7, 0.7)

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	rotation_degrees += 90 * delta
	if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):
		visible = not visible

# A signpost, drawn around the node's own origin: the pink dot at (0, 0).
func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(-2, 10, 4, 20), Color("#7a5230"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(-22, -10, 44, 20), Color("#f2c14e"))
	draw_line(Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(14, 0), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_line(Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, 6), Color("#3a2b30"), 2)
	draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 2, Color("#e0566f"))

tests.label: it starts visible
one press hides it
the next press shows it again
holding the key down is one press, not one per frame
and it stays hidden when nothing is pressed

hints: Ask the Input object whether the action was pressed on this frame: Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept").
Inside that if, flip the value: visible = not visible.
steps.explain: Click the view and press Space. You have now set all five of the Inspector's everyday fields from code, and two of them while the game was running. That is the division of labour in every Godot project: the Inspector for how things start, scripts for how they change. is_action_just_pressed is true for one frame only; its cousin is_action_pressed is true for as long as the key is down, and would make the sign flicker. Chapter K sorts those out.

title: A scene tree of your own
intro: You will give MiniNode its methods one at a time – add a child, find a child, follow a path down, climb with .. – and finish by printing the whole tree. Methods go inside the class, so they are indented one tab, with their bodies at two.

steps.title: Adopt a child
steps.task:
Inside the class, under _init, write a method add_child(child: MiniNode). It must do two things: put child at the end of this node's children, and tell the child that this node (self) is now its parent.

Then, in _ready(), make two nodes named World and HUD, add them to root in that order, and print Main has 2 children – using root.name and the size of root.children, not typed-in words.

tests.label: Main has two children
the first child is World
the second child is HUD
each child knows Main is its parent
prints Main has 2 children

hints: The method has two lines in its body: children.append(child) and child.parent = self. It sits inside the class, so func has one tab and the body two.
In _ready(): var world := MiniNode.new("World"), then root.add_child(world). The print is print(root.name, " has ", root.children.size(), " children").
steps.explain: The link is written twice – once in the parent's list, once in the child's parent – and keeping those two in step is the whole job of add_child. Forget the second line and the tree can be walked down but not up. self means "the node this method was called on": in root.add_child(world), that is root.

steps.title: Find a child by name
steps.task:
Give the class a method child_named(n: String) -> MiniNode that looks through this node's own children and returns the one whose name is n, or null if none has that name. It does not look at grandchildren.

In _ready(), add a node named Player under World, and print the name of what root.child_named("HUD") finds.

tests.label: child_named("World") finds World
a name nobody has gives null
Player is a child of World
Main does not find Player: she is a grandchild
prints HUD

hints: Loop over children; inside the loop, if child.name == n: then return child.
return null goes after the loop, level with for – it is reached only when the loop found nothing.
steps.explain: This is one step of a path. get_node("HUD") on a real node does this: look at my own children, compare names. It never searches the whole tree, which is why root.child_named("Player") finds nothing even though a Player exists.

steps.title: Follow a path down
steps.task:
Now the real thing. Write get_node_or_null(path: String) -> MiniNode: split the path at each /, start here, and take one child_named step for each part. If any step finds nothing, the answer is null; otherwise it is wherever you end up.

In _ready(), add a Sprite under Player, then print the name of the node at "World/Player/Sprite", asked from root.

tests.label: Sprite is under Player
a one-step path works
asked from World, the path is Player/Sprite
a path with a wrong step gives null, not an error
prints Sprite

hints: Keep a variable for where you are: var here: MiniNode = self. Then for part in path.split("/"): and move: here = here.child_named(part).
Straight after moving, check: if here == null: return null. Without it the next turn of the loop calls child_named on nothing. After the loop, return here.
steps.explain: A path is a loop of single steps – that is all there ever was to it. The fourth check is the one to think about: the same Sprite is World/Player/Sprite from Main and Player/Sprite from World, because a path starts from whoever asks. Try "World//Player" or "" in your print and see what your version makes of them.

steps.title: Climb with ..
steps.task:
Teach get_node_or_null one more word. When a part of the path is .., the step goes to the parent and not to a child. Going up from the top of the tree finds nothing, so the answer is null.

In _ready(), print the name of the node at "../../../HUD", asked from sprite.

tests.label: from Sprite, .. is Player
from Sprite, ../.. is World
from Player, ../../HUD goes up twice and down once
.. works in the middle of a path too
above the top of the tree there is nothing: null, not an error
paths that only go down still work

hints: Inside the loop, choose which way to step: if part == "..": then here = here.parent, else: the child_named line you already have.
Leave the if here == null: return null check after both branches. The top node's parent is null, so the same check catches climbing too far.
steps.explain: Up is one line because a node has one parent; down needed a search because it has many children. Notice that the null check you wrote for misspelt names also handles climbing off the top, for free. And look at what "../../../HUD" assumes: that Sprite is exactly three levels below a node with a HUD child. Move the Sprite and it breaks – which is why the advice is to reach down, not up.

steps.title: See the whole tree
steps.task:
Last, make the tree show itself. Write tree_lines(depth := 0) -> Array: it returns a list of lines, this node's name first – indented by two spaces for each level of depth – followed by the lines of each child in order, one level deeper.

At the end of _ready(), print each line of root.tree_lines().

tests.label: tree_lines() lists the tree top to bottom, two spaces per level
asked from World, the branch starts at no indent
a node with no children is one line, at the depth it was given
prints the tree

hints: Start the list with this node's own line: var lines := [" ".repeat(depth) + name]. " ".repeat(2) is four spaces.
Then, for each child, add all of its lines to yours: lines.append_array(child.tree_lines(depth + 1)). Return lines after the loop.
steps.explain: That printout is the Scene dock. The order it comes out in – a node, then everything under it, then the next sibling – is tree order, the order Godot draws in. You now have every piece of the real thing in about thirty lines: add_child, a path lookup that goes down and up, and a walk over the whole tree. Add a Clock under HUD and a Shadow under Player, and watch where they land in the list.

title: A room, described in data
intro: By the end the output pane shows a card for a kitchen: its name, its size, how much of it is wall, its paint and its lamp. The measurements are Little Hours's own – a 96-pixel tile and a room 8 tiles by 14. Everything is a variable at the top of the script, so each step adds a line or two up there and one print in _ready().

steps.title: Name the room
steps.task: Above _ready(), make a String variable called room_name holding Kitchen. Then replace pass with a line that uses the variable to print Room: Kitchen.
steps.solution:
extends Node

var room_name := "Kitchen"

func _ready() -> void:
	print("Room: ", room_name)

tests.label: room_name is the String "Kitchen"
prints Room: Kitchen
the print uses the variable
tests.why: Print the variable rather than typing Kitchen a second time.

hints: Text needs its quotes: var room_name := "Kitchen", at the left edge of the script.
print("Room: ", room_name) – one tab in, where pass was. The space after the colon is inside the quotes.
steps.explain: := saw the quotes and made room_name a String. Change Kitchen to Bathroom and the card follows, because the print reads the variable. Put it back before you go on.

steps.title: Measure it in tiles
steps.task: A room is laid out on a grid. Add a constant TILE of 96 (pixels), and two int variables, cols of 8 and rows of 14. Then work out two more variables from them, width and height, in pixels, and print a second line: 768 by 1344 pixels.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const TILE := 96

var room_name := "Kitchen"
var cols := 8
var rows := 14
var width := cols * TILE
var height := rows * TILE

func _ready() -> void:
	print("Room: ", room_name)
	print(width, " by ", height, " pixels")

tests.label: TILE is a constant
tests.why: The tile size never changes while the game runs: make it a const.

tests.label: TILE is 96
width is 768, an int
height is 1344, an int
width is worked out from TILE
tests.why: Multiply cols by TILE instead of typing 768.

tests.label: prints 768 by 1344 pixels

hints: Three lines for what you decide – const TILE := 96, var cols := 8, var rows := 14 – then two for what follows from it.
var width := cols * TILE and var height := rows * TILE. The line to print is print(width, " by ", height, " pixels").
steps.explain: Int times int is an int, so width is a whole number of pixels. Change TILE to 48 and both sizes halve: one edit, in one place. Notice too that width is worked out once, when the script starts. A variable holds a value, not a formula, so changing cols later would not change width. Put TILE back to 96.

steps.title: One value for the size
steps.task: Width and height always travel together, so keep them together too. Add a variable size that is a Vector2i made from width and height, and print a third line: Size: (768, 1344).
steps.solution:
extends Node

const TILE := 96

var room_name := "Kitchen"
var cols := 8
var rows := 14
var width := cols * TILE
var height := rows * TILE
var size := Vector2i(width, height)

func _ready() -> void:
	print("Room: ", room_name)
	print(width, " by ", height, " pixels")
	print("Size: ", size)

tests.label: size is Vector2i(768, 1344)
prints Size: (768, 1344)

hints: A Vector2i is made from two ints: Vector2i(width, height).
var size := Vector2i(width, height), then print("Size: ", size).
steps.explain: Vector2i rather than Vector2, because pixels are counted: the output has no .0 in it. Try Vector2 and look at the difference, then change it back. From here on size.x and size.y are the width and the height.

steps.title: How much is wall?
steps.task:
The top 384 pixels of the room are wall, and the rest is floor. Add an int variable wall_h of 384, and a float variable wall_share: the wall's height as a share of the room's height, a number between 0 and 1. Print it as a whole percentage: Wall: 29 percent.

Try the obvious division first and look at what you get.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const TILE := 96

var room_name := "Kitchen"
var cols := 8
var rows := 14
var width := cols * TILE
var height := rows * TILE
var size := Vector2i(width, height)
var wall_h := 384
var wall_share := float(wall_h) / height

func _ready() -> void:
	print("Room: ", room_name)
	print(width, " by ", height, " pixels")
	print("Size: ", size)
	print("Wall: ", roundi(wall_share * 100), " percent")

tests.label: wall_h is 384
wall_share is about 0.286, not 0
prints Wall: 29 percent

hints: wall_h / height is an int divided by an int, so it is 0. One side has to be a float before the division happens.
var wall_share := float(wall_h) / height. For the percentage, multiply by 100 and round to a whole number with roundi(): print("Wall: ", roundi(wall_share * 100), " percent").
steps.explain: That was the trap, on purpose. 384 / 1344 as ints is 0, and the card would have said the room had no wall. With float() on one side the share is 0.2857…, and roundi() turns 28.57 into the 29 a person wants to read. Swap roundi for int and it says 28: cutting off is not rounding.

steps.title: Paint the walls
steps.task: Give the room a colour. Add wall_colour, a Color made from the hex code #e8c9a0, and shade, the same colour darkened by 0.3, for the corners. Print both as hex: Paint: e8c9a0, shade: a28d70.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const TILE := 96

var room_name := "Kitchen"
var cols := 8
var rows := 14
var width := cols * TILE
var height := rows * TILE
var size := Vector2i(width, height)
var wall_h := 384
var wall_share := float(wall_h) / height
var wall_colour := Color("#e8c9a0")
var shade := wall_colour.darkened(0.3)

func _ready() -> void:
	print("Room: ", room_name)
	print(width, " by ", height, " pixels")
	print("Size: ", size)
	print("Wall: ", roundi(wall_share * 100), " percent")
	print("Paint: ", wall_colour.to_html(false), ", shade: ", shade.to_html(false))

tests.label: wall_colour is #e8c9a0
shade is wall_colour darkened by 0.3
prints Paint: e8c9a0, shade: a28d70

hints: A colour from a hex code is Color("#e8c9a0"), with the quotes. The darker one comes from a method on the first: wall_colour.darkened(0.3).
.to_html(false) turns a colour into its hex text: print("Paint: ", wall_colour.to_html(false), ", shade: ", shade.to_html(false)).
steps.explain: shade is not a second colour somebody chose, it is worked out from the first. Change the hex code to #a0c9e8 and the shade follows it. That is how a game keeps a palette consistent: pick a few colours, and derive the rest.

steps.title: Switch the lamp on
steps.task: The lamp has three settings. Make an enum Lamp with OFF, LOW and FULL, in that order, and a variable lamp set to Lamp.LOW. Add a bool lit that is true whenever the lamp is not off – worked out from lamp, not typed in. Print the last line of the card: Lamp: LOW, lit: true.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const TILE := 96

enum Lamp { OFF, LOW, FULL }

var room_name := "Kitchen"
var cols := 8
var rows := 14
var width := cols * TILE
var height := rows * TILE
var size := Vector2i(width, height)
var wall_h := 384
var wall_share := float(wall_h) / height
var wall_colour := Color("#e8c9a0")
var shade := wall_colour.darkened(0.3)
var lamp := Lamp.LOW
var lit := lamp != Lamp.OFF

func _ready() -> void:
	print("Room: ", room_name)
	print(width, " by ", height, " pixels")
	print("Size: ", size)
	print("Wall: ", roundi(wall_share * 100), " percent")
	print("Paint: ", wall_colour.to_html(false), ", shade: ", shade.to_html(false))
	print("Lamp: ", Lamp.keys()[lamp], ", lit: ", lit)

tests.label: Lamp.OFF comes first
Lamp.FULL comes last
lamp is Lamp.LOW
lit is the bool true
lit is worked out from lamp
tests.why: Compare lamp with Lamp.OFF instead of typing true.

tests.label: prints Lamp: LOW, lit: true

hints: enum Lamp { OFF, LOW, FULL } goes near the top, outside any function. "Not equal" is written !=.
var lit := lamp != Lamp.OFF. Printing lamp itself gives the number 1; the name is Lamp.keys()[lamp].
steps.explain: Six lines of output from a script with no decisions and no loops in it – only data, each piece in the type that suits it: a String for the name, ints for what is counted, a float for a share, a Vector2i and a Color for values with parts, an enum for a choice and a bool for a yes or no. Set lamp to Lamp.OFF and read the last line again.

title: An almanac that decides
intro: You will write four small functions and a loop. At the end the output is ten days of almanac – Day 6: Summer, Rainy – and a forecast of when it next rains. The functions are already named for you where a step needs one; Chapter F is about writing them, and here you only fill in the bodies.

steps.title: Count the seasons
steps.task: Seasons are numbered 0, 1, 2, 3 and last DAYS_PER_SEASON days each. Days 1 to 5 are season 0, days 6 to 10 are season 1, and so on; after season 3 the year starts again, so day 21 is season 0. Make season_index(day) return the right number for any day, using only arithmetic – no if.

tests.label: season_index(5)  →  0: day 5 is still the first season
season_index(21)  →  0: the year starts again

hints: Integer division counts how many whole seasons have gone by – but days start at 1, so take one off first. Then % wraps the count back to 0 after 3.
return (day - 1) / DAYS_PER_SEASON % 4
steps.explain: The output line now reads 0 1 0. / sorted the days into boxes of five and % wrapped the boxes round in fours – the two halves of division, each doing its job. Without the - 1, day 5 would land in summer. Little Hours works its seasons out the same way.

steps.title: Decide the sky
steps.task:
Add a function sky(day: int) -> String under season_index. The rules, in order of importance:

  • in winter (season 3), every even-numbered day is "Snowy";
  • otherwise, every third day (3, 6, 9 …) is "Rainy";
  • otherwise it is "Clear".

Then add a print to _ready() to try it on a few days.

tests.label: sky(12)  →  "Rainy": an even day, but not in winter
sky(18)  →  "Snowy": a winter day that is even and a third day – snow wins

hints: A ladder with three rungs: if, elif, else, each ending in a return. "Even" is day % 2 == 0.
The first rung needs two things to be true at once: if season_index(day) == 3 and day % 2 == 0:. It has to come before the rain rung.
steps.explain: Day 18 is the one that tests the order: it is even, in winter, and divisible by three. The snow rung is asked first, so snow wins. Swap the first two rungs and the check for day 18 fails – the order of a ladder is part of its meaning.

steps.title: Name the season
steps.task: Numbers are for the program; people want names. Add season_name(day: int) -> String, which returns "Spring", "Summer", "Autumn" or "Winter" for seasons 0 to 3. One value choosing between four fixed answers is a job for match.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5

func season_index(day: int) -> int:
	return (day - 1) / DAYS_PER_SEASON % 4

func sky(day: int) -> String:
	if season_index(day) == 3 and day % 2 == 0:
		return "Snowy"
	elif day % 3 == 0:
		return "Rainy"
	else:
		return "Clear"

func season_name(day: int) -> String:
	match season_index(day):
		0:
			return "Spring"
		1:
			return "Summer"
		2:
			return "Autumn"
		_:
			return "Winter"

func _ready() -> void:
	print(season_index(1), " ", season_index(6), " ", season_index(21))
	print(sky(3), " ", sky(16), " ", sky(17))
	print(season_name(1), " ", season_name(16))

tests.label: uses match
tests.why: An if ladder works too, but this step is for trying match.

hints: Match on the number, not the day: match season_index(day):, then a pattern and a return for each season.
Each branch is two lines – 0: and, one tab deeper, return "Spring". Finish with _: for winter, so every path through the function returns something.
steps.explain: The expression after match is worked out once and compared with each pattern. Ending on _ rather than 3 is deliberate: a function that promises a String must return one whatever happens, and Godot checks that every path does.

steps.title: Print ten days
steps.task:
Now the almanac itself. Replace the trial prints in _ready() with a loop that prints one line for each of days 1 to 10, in exactly this form:

Day 1: Spring, Clear

tests.label: prints lines like Day 1: Spring, Clear – for days 1, 3, 6 and 10 among them
uses a for loop
tests.why: Ten prints would do it, but a loop is the point.

hints: To go from 1 to 10 the range has to end at 11: for day in range(1, 11):.
Inside the loop: print("Day ", day, ": ", season_name(day), ", ", sky(day)).
steps.explain: Ten lines from two. Change the range to range(1, 41) and read two whole years: the seasons come round again at day 21, and the snow only ever falls in the last five days of each twenty. Put it back to 11 before the last step.

steps.title: When does it next rain?
steps.task: Add next_rain(day: int) -> int: the first day after day whose sky is "Rainy". You cannot know how far ahead that is, so this is a job for while. Then, after the loop in _ready(), print Next rain after day 10: day 12, using the function for the 12.

tests.label: next_rain(3)  →  6: after day 3, not day 3 itself
next_rain(15)  →  21: it does not rain all winter
uses a while loop
prints Next rain after day 10: day 12

hints: Start a variable at the day after: var d := day + 1. Keep adding one to it while the sky that day is not rainy, then return it.
while sky(d) != "Rainy": with d += 1 inside, and return d after the loop, back at the function's own indent.
steps.explain: From day 15 the loop walks through five days of winter – snowy, clear, snowy, clear, snowy – before it finds rain on day 21. A for could not have been told how far to go. The line that saves it from running for ever is d += 1; delete it and watch the page give up. An almanac in forty lines, and every one of them is an operator, a decision or a loop.

title: A day, told by small functions
intro: You will write functions that each do one job and have a type on everything. By the end you can ask for any moment of the day and get its time, its phase and its season, and you will have passed a lambda to say how a list of moments should be shown.

steps.title: Minutes from a share
steps.task: The day is a share from 0.0 (sunrise) to 1.0 (nightfall), and the clock runs from 06:00 to 22:00 – that is minute 360 to minute 1320 since midnight. Write minutes_of(f: float) -> int that returns the whole minutes for a share. In _ready(), print the minutes at 0.5.

tests.label: minutes_of(0.0) is 360, an int
minutes_of(1.0) is 1320
halfway is minute 840
_ready() prints 840

hints: lerpf(a, b, t) slides from a to b as t goes from 0 to 1. It returns a float, so it needs int() before it can be returned as an int.
return int(lerpf(360.0, 1320.0, f))
steps.explain: One parameter, one return, and a type on each. Notice that nothing here knows about a "game" or a "clock": the function is a plain sum, which is why you can test it with any number. Try minutes_of(0.25) in _ready(): 600, or ten o'clock.

steps.title: Minutes to text
steps.task: Write clock_text(mins: int) -> String that turns minutes since midnight into HH:MM with two digits each: 545 becomes 09:05. Use the split from Chapter E – / for hours, % for what is left – and wrap the hour so that it never reads 24 or more. Change _ready() to print the clock for halfway through the day.

tests.label: 545 minutes is 09:05
past midnight wraps: 1500 is 01:00
the two functions work together: sunrise is 06:00
_ready() prints 14:00

hints: The format "%02d:%02d" takes an array of two ints: hours first, then minutes.
return "%02d:%02d" % [(mins / 60) % 24, mins % 60]
steps.explain: A function that calls another is the whole idea: clock_text(minutes_of(0.5)) reads from the inside out, share to minutes to text. minutes_of returns an int and clock_text asks for an int, so Godot is happy; if either had been a float you would have been told.

steps.title: Name the phase
steps.task: Write phase(f: float) -> String: "Morning" before 0.2, "Daytime" before 0.55, "Evening" before 0.75, otherwise "Night". Write it as a ladder of ifs that each return, with no elif or else, and have _ready() print the phase at 0.6.

tests.label: 0.2 itself is already Daytime
0.75 is Night
_ready() prints Evening

hints: Each rung is one line: if f < 0.2: return "Morning". Ask the smallest question first.
The fourth line is not an if at all: after the three rungs, return "Night".
steps.explain: Every road through phase ends in a return, so the -> String promise holds; the last line is what keeps it. Take it out and Godot, in the editor, will tell you that not all code paths return a value.

steps.title: The season, with a default
steps.task: Write season_index(day: int, days_per_season: int = 5) -> int: days 1 to 5 are season 0, days 6 to 10 are season 1, and after season 3 it starts again at 0. Subtract 1 from the day first, since days start at 1. The default means that most callers do not have to say how long a season is.

tests.label: day 5 is still season 0
day 6 starts season 1
day 21 wraps back to season 0
with 3-day seasons, day 4 starts season 1
_ready() prints season_index(7), which is 1

hints: Whole days since the start are day - 1. Dividing that by the length of a season, as ints, counts whole seasons; % 4 wraps them.
return ((day - 1) / days_per_season) % 4
steps.explain: Integer division is doing exactly what Chapter D warned about, on purpose: it throws away the part-way through a season and keeps the count of whole ones. And season_index(7) in _ready() gets the default, while season_index(4, 3) in the tests overrides it.

steps.title: Say it your way
steps.task: Write report(moments: Array, say: Callable) -> Array. It goes through the moments, calls say on each one, and returns the array of answers. Then in _ready() call it for the moments [0.0, 0.5, 0.9] with a lambda that returns the clock and the phase together, like 06:00 Morning, and print each line.

tests.label: report applies the lambda to every moment
and works with any lambda
an empty list gives an empty list
prints three lines like 06:00 Morning

hints: Start with var lines := [], loop with for m in moments:, and lines.append(say.call(m)). Return the array after the loop, not inside it.
In _ready(): report([0.0, 0.5, 0.9], func(f): return clock_text(minutes_of(f)) + " " + phase(f)), then a for that prints each line.
steps.explain: report knows nothing about clocks: it applies whatever it is given. Swap the lambda for func(f): return season_index(int(f * 20) + 1) and the same function reports seasons. That is the point of a function as a value: the loop is written once, and the part that changes is passed in. Godot's own Array.map is this function, written for you.

title: A bag you can fill, count, empty and sell from
intro: Five steps: put things in, count them, take them out, sell them, and list what is left. The bag is a dictionary from the name of a thing to how many you have, and by the end it can never hold a wrong number.

steps.title: Put things in
steps.task: Write a function add_item(key: String, n: int = 1) that adds n to the count kept under key in bag. A thing that is not in the bag yet counts as 0, so adding to it must not be an error. Then, in _ready(), use it to put in 3 of "carrot" and 1 of "tomato", and print the bag.

tests.label: after _ready() the bag holds 3 carrots
and 1 tomato
add_item("carrot", 2) adds to what is there: 5 carrots
add_item("pumpkin") starts a new key at 1
prints { "carrot": 3, "tomato": 1 }

hints: Reading bag[key] for a key that is not there is an error. bag.get(key, 0) gives you 0 instead.
The body is one line: bag[key] = int(bag.get(key, 0)) + n. The default = 1 in the signature is what lets you write add_item("tomato").
steps.explain: Read with get, write with []: that one line works whether the key was there or not, which is why nothing has to check first. The int() is a habit you will see all through the game's code. Its bag is read back from a JSON save, and JSON hands every number back as a float (Chapter S).

steps.title: Count them
steps.task: Write count_of(key: String) -> int: how many of a thing are in the bag, and 0 for something that has never been in it. Asking must not change the bag. Then add a line to _ready() that uses it to print Carrots: 3.

tests.label: count_of("koi") is 0, not an error
asking about koi does not put a koi key in the bag
prints Carrots: 3

hints: It is get with a fallback again, this time returned and not stored.
return int(bag.get(key, 0)), and in _ready(): print("Carrots: ", count_of("carrot")).
steps.explain: From now on nothing outside these functions needs to touch bag directly. The rest of the script asks count_of(), and the question of what a missing key means is answered in exactly one place.

steps.title: Take things out
steps.task: Write remove_item(key: String, n: int = 1) -> bool. If the bag holds fewer than n, it changes nothing and returns false. Otherwise it takes n away and returns true – and when that leaves none, it erases the key, so the bag never lists a thing you have 0 of. In _ready(), remove the tomato and print the bag again.

tests.label: after the tomato goes, prints { "carrot": 3 }
remove_item("carrot", 2) returns true
and leaves 1 carrot
remove_item("carrot", 5) returns false: there are not 5
and the bag is unchanged
remove_item("koi") returns false
removing the last carrot erases the key

hints: Start by asking count_of(key) and keeping the answer. If it is less than n, return false before touching anything.
Then two cases: exactly n left means bag.erase(key); more than that means bag[key] = have - n. Either way, return true.
steps.explain: The second line of output shows why the key is erased: { "carrot": 3 }, not { "carrot": 3, "tomato": 0 }. A bag that can hold zeros has two ways of saying "none", and one day a loop over its keys will offer to sell you nothing.

steps.title: Sell one
steps.task: Add a price list above the functions: const PRICES := {"carrot": 6, "tomato": 8, "pumpkin": 20}. Then write sell_one(key: String) -> bool, which sells one unit: it takes one out of the bag and adds its price to coins. A thing with no price is not sold and stays in the bag; a thing you have none of pays nothing. It returns whether a sale happened. In _ready(), sell one carrot and print Coins: 6.

tests.label: prints Coins: 6
sell_one("carrot") returns true
and coins is now 12
with 1 carrot left
sell_one("tomato") returns false: there is no tomato
and no coins appear from nowhere
a shell has no price, so it is not sold
and it is still in the bag

hints: Two things can stop a sale, and each is an early return false: there is no price for it, or remove_item(key) said no.
Check the price first. If you remove first and then find there is no price, the shell is gone and nobody was paid.
if not PRICES.has(key): return false, then if not remove_item(key): return false, then coins += int(PRICES[key]) and return true.
steps.explain: The coins are added on the one path where a unit has really left the bag, and nowhere else. The game's sell_one() is built the same way, and its comment gives the reason: a rapid double tap on Sell must never mint free money.

steps.title: Read it back
steps.task: Finish with the shopkeeper's view. Write worth() -> int: walk every key in the bag and add up count × price, counting nothing for a thing that has no price. Then, at the end of _ready(), print one line for each thing in the bag in the form carrot x2, and after them Worth: 12.

tests.label: prints carrot x2 and Worth: 12
two pumpkins more and worth() is 52
nine shells change nothing: a shell has no price
walks the bag with for
tests.why: for key in bag: gives you each key in turn.

hints: for key in bag: gives you each key. Inside the loop, the count is count_of(key) and the price is PRICES.get(key, 0).
In worth(): start var total := 0, add count_of(key) * int(PRICES.get(key, 0)) each time round, and return it after the loop.
steps.explain: That is a working inventory in under forty lines: a dictionary, a table of prices and five functions, each of which does one thing and trusts the others. Add "shell": 1 to PRICES, or put a pumpkin in the bag in _ready(), and watch the listing and the total follow.

title: A pet roster, a class at a time
intro: Six steps that end with a dog and a cat who each speak in their own way, a count of how many pets exist, and a collar that one of them has and the other does not. The classes are inner classes, written above _ready().
starter:
extends Node

var pets: Array = []

func _ready() -> void:
	pass

steps.title: A class and an object
steps.task: Between var pets and _ready(), write an inner class Pet with one variable, pet_name, a String, and an _init that takes the name and stores it. In _ready(), make a Pet called "Pup", append it to pets, and print its pet_name.

tests.label: Pet.new("Mog").pet_name is "Mog"
_ready() puts a pet in pets
and the first one is called Pup
prints Pup

hints: An inner class starts at the left edge with class Pet:; its variables and functions are indented one tab under it.
Inside the class: var pet_name: String, then func _init(n: String) -> void: with the one line pet_name = n. In _ready(): pets.append(Pet.new("Pup")).
steps.explain: Pet is the description; Pet.new("Pup") is one pet made from it. The argument travels from new() to _init, and from there into the object's own variable.

steps.title: Give it behaviour
steps.task: Add two functions to Pet. sound() -> String returns "...", the noise of a pet nobody has heard yet. speak() -> String returns the pet's name, then says , then whatever sound() returns. Change the print so it prints what Pup's speak() returns.

tests.label: a plain Pet's sound() is "..."
Pet.new("Mog").speak() is "Mog says ..."
prints what Pup says
speak() asks sound() for the noise
tests.why: Build the sentence from sound(), not from a typed "...": the next step depends on it.

hints: Both functions go inside the class, indented like _init.
speak() is one line: return pet_name + " says " + sound().
steps.explain: speak() does not know what the noise is. It asks sound(), and that small indirection is about to pay off.

steps.title: A kind of pet
steps.task: Below Pet, write a class Dog that extends Pet. Give it an _init that takes the name and hands it up with super, and its own sound() that returns "Woof". Do not write a speak() for it. Then make Pup a Dog in _ready().

tests.label: Dog.new("Rex").speak() is "Rex says Woof"
a Dog is a Pet
a plain Pet still says ...
Pup is a Dog now
prints Pup says Woof

hints: The first line is class Dog extends Pet:. Inside it, _init(n: String) has one line, super(n), which runs Pet's _init with the name.
Then func sound() -> String: returning "Woof", and in _ready() change Pet.new("Pup") to Dog.new("Pup").
steps.explain: The output changed and speak() did not. It was written once, in Pet; called on a dog, its sound() reaches the dog's. And the dog has a pet_name it never declared, set by a constructor it only passed along to.

steps.title: Build on the original
steps.task: Add a class Cat that extends Pet the same way, with a sound() of "Meow". A cat also speaks differently: its speak() returns what Pet's speak() returns, followed by , then naps. Use super to get the original; do not rebuild the sentence. In _ready(), append a Cat called "Mog" after Pup, and replace the print with a loop that prints speak() for every pet.

tests.label: Cat.new("Tib").speak() is "Tib says Meow, then naps"
pets holds two pets
and the second is a Cat
prints Pup says Woof and Mog says Meow, then naps
Cat's speak() builds on Pet's with super.speak()
tests.why: Call super.speak() and add to what it returns.

hints: Cat starts as a copy of Dog with "Meow" in it.
Its extra function: func speak() -> String: returning super.speak() + ", then naps".
The loop: for pet in pets: and, inside it, print(pet.speak()).
steps.explain: Follow one call through. pet.speak() on Mog runs Cat's speak(), which calls Pet's through super, which calls sound() and gets Cat's again, because the object is still a cat. The loop itself knows nothing about dogs or cats. It asks each pet to speak, and each answers as what it is.

steps.title: Count them on the class
steps.task: Keep a count of every pet ever made. Give Pet a static var count := 0 and add one to it in Pet's _init. Add a static func census() -> String to Pet that returns Pets: followed by the count. At the end of _ready(), print the census; call it on the class, not on a pet.

tests.label: after _ready(), Pet.count is 2
Pet.census() is "Pets: 2"
making another Dog makes it 3
prints Pets: 2

hints: static var count := 0 goes inside Pet, beside pet_name. In _init, add count += 1.
A number does not join to a string with +: return "Pets: " + str(count). In _ready(): print(Pet.census()).
steps.explain: Neither Dog nor Cat mentions the count, and both are counted, because both constructors call super(n) and the counting is in Pet's. count is not any one pet's: there is a single number, kept by the class.

steps.title: Has a collar
steps.task: Some pets wear a collar. Write a small class Collar with a String variable tag, set by its _init. Give Pet a variable collar that starts as null, and a function id() -> String that returns the collar's tag, or "no collar" for a pet without one. At the end of _ready(), give Pup a collar tagged "4 Mill Lane", then print a line for every pet in the form Pup wears: 4 Mill Lane.

tests.label: Collar.new("x").tag is "x"
Pup's id() is "4 Mill Lane"
Mog's id() is "no collar"
Pup's collar is a Collar object
prints what each pet wears

hints: Collar is a class of four lines, the same shape as Pet was in step one.
In Pet: var collar: Collar = null, and an id() that checks if collar == null: before it reads collar.tag.
In _ready(): pets[0].collar = Collar.new("4 Mill Lane"), then a second loop printing pet.pet_name, " wears: ", pet.id().
steps.explain: A dog is a pet, so Dog extends Pet. A pet has a collar, so Pet holds one in a variable, and it can be missing, swapped, or one day shared with a class that is not a pet at all. Try giving Mog a collar, then try making a CollaredDog class instead, and see which you would rather maintain.

title: A walker that keeps its speed
intro: The script is one Node2D in a small game view that restarts whenever you stop typing. The square is drawn for you; you will give it a start, a movement, a wrap-around, a clock and a pause. Press Space or the round button in the last step to use it.

steps.title: Start at the left edge
steps.task: _ready() runs once, before the first frame: the place for a starting state. Make the square begin just off the left side of the view: position should be Vector2(-16, 90). Nothing moves yet, and the square is out of sight – that is right.

tests.label: the square starts at (-16, 90)
and with no movement written, it stays there

hints: A Vector2 is made with two numbers: Vector2(x, y).
position = Vector2(-16, 90), in place of pass in _ready().
steps.explain: _ready() ran once when the view started, and never again until you changed the code and the view restarted. That is the line between the two kinds of function: one happens once, at the start; the other happens all the time.

steps.title: Walk at a speed
steps.task: In _process(delta), move the square right at SPEED pixels a second. Multiply by delta, or it will cross the view in a flash.

tests.label: sixteen frames of a sixteenth of a second (one second) move it 64 pixels
one more second at half the frame rate moves it another 64

hints: position.x += SPEED * delta
Without * delta the square moves 64 pixels every frame, and the second test fails because eight frames moves it 512.
steps.explain: The tests ran a second of play twice, once as sixteen short frames and once as eight long ones, and the square covered the same ground. That is what delta buys. Try deleting * delta to see it vanish off the right in a blink, then put it back.

steps.title: Come round again
steps.task: The square walks off the right and is gone for ever. When position.x is greater than 336, put it back at -16 on the left, so it loops. Do that in _process after the move.

tests.label: it still walks
after a hundred frames it has gone round once and is on its way again
it never stays past the right edge

hints: An if on position.x > 336.0 that sets position.x = -16.0.
It goes after position.x += SPEED * delta, inside _process, one more indent.
steps.explain: Walk-and-check in one place: every frame it moves, then looks to see if it has gone too far. Watch it come round, over and over. Make the width 336 smaller, say 200, and the loop gets shorter.

steps.title: Count the time
steps.task: Add two variables, var frames := 0 and var elapsed := 0.0. Each frame add one to frames and add delta to elapsed. Then show them: in _draw(), after the square, write them at the top of the view with draw_string, and call queue_redraw() in _process so that the text keeps up.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const SPEED := 64.0   # pixels a second

var frames := 0
var elapsed := 0.0

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2(-16, 90)

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	frames += 1
	elapsed += delta
	position.x += SPEED * delta
	if position.x > 336.0:
		position.x = -16.0
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(-8, -8, 16, 16), Color("#f2a65a"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(-position.x + 8, -position.y + 20), "frames %d   seconds %.1f" % [frames, elapsed], 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: 16 frames counted
and 1.0 seconds
8 slower frames add another second, not another 0.5
while the frame count only goes up by 8
asks for a new drawing with queue_redraw()
tests.why: _draw() runs once, and again only after queue_redraw().

tests.label: shows the numbers with draw_string

hints: In _process: frames += 1 and elapsed += delta, then queue_redraw() at the end.

The text is drawn in the square's own coordinates, so give it an offset that cancels the position: Vector2(-position.x + 8, -position.y + 20). Format it with "frames %d seconds %.1f" % [frames, elapsed].
steps.explain: Two numbers, one honest and one not. elapsed counts real seconds, however fast the frames come; frames is how many times the loop ran, and on your screen means nothing about time. The test above fed both a different frame rate and only one of them agreed. That is the whole case for delta.

steps.title: Hold still
steps.task: Make ui_accept (Space, or the round button) stop the walker for one second. When it is pressed, switch processing off with set_process(false) and start a timer: get_tree().create_timer(1.0).timeout.connect(...) with a lambda that calls set_process(true). Put the check at the top of _process.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const SPEED := 64.0   # pixels a second

var frames := 0
var elapsed := 0.0

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2(-16, 90)

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):
		set_process(false)
		get_tree().create_timer(1.0).timeout.connect(func() -> void: set_process(true))
		return
	frames += 1
	elapsed += delta
	position.x += SPEED * delta
	if position.x > 336.0:
		position.x = -16.0
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(-8, -8, 16, 16), Color("#f2a65a"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(-position.x + 8, -position.y + 20), "frames %d   seconds %.1f" % [frames, elapsed], 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: after a tap on ui_accept, processing is off
and no frame has been counted
a second later the timer has switched it back on
uses set_process(false)
tests.why: That is what stops _process being called.

tests.label: wakes it again with a timer
tests.why: A node that is not processing cannot wake itself from _process.

hints: At the top of _process: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):, and under it set_process(false), the timer, and a return.
get_tree().create_timer(1.0).timeout.connect(func() -> void: set_process(true))
steps.explain: Press Space and the square freezes, the counters stop, and a second later everything resumes where it was. While it is off, _process is not called at all, which is why the timer – something outside it – has to be the one to turn it back on. The same trick, with a node that waits to be woken by something it cares about, is how idle nodes cost nothing.

title: A coin run, joined up with signals
intro: You start with a Player class that picks up coins and tells nobody. By the end, three other things react to each coin, and Player has gained two lines and still knows about none of them.

steps.title: Announce it
steps.task: Give Player a signal called coin_collected that carries one int, the coin's value. Then make collect() emit it, passing value, after it has counted the coin.

tests.label: Player has a signal called coin_collected
collect() emits it with the coin's value
tests.why: Inside collect(): coin_collected.emit(value)

tests.label: still prints Coins in the bag: 2

hints: The declaration goes inside the class, at the same indent as var coins: signal coin_collected(value: int).
The last line of collect(): coin_collected.emit(value).
steps.explain: The output has not changed, and that is the point of this step. The player now announces every coin to an empty room. Emitting with nobody connected is not an error and costs almost nothing, so an emitter never has to check whether anyone is there.

steps.title: Listen to it
steps.task: Now the score. Write a function _on_coin_collected(value: int) in the main script (not in Player) that adds value to score and prints the new total as Score: 6. In _ready(), connect it to the player's signal before the first coin is collected.
steps.solution:
extends Node

class Player:
	signal coin_collected(value: int)
	var coins := 0

	func collect(value: int) -> void:
		coins += 1
		coin_collected.emit(value)

var player := Player.new()
var score := 0

func _ready() -> void:
	player.coin_collected.connect(_on_coin_collected)
	player.collect(1)
	player.collect(5)
	print("Coins in the bag: ", player.coins)

func _on_coin_collected(value: int) -> void:
	score += value
	print("Score: ", score)

tests.label: prints Score: 1 and then Score: 6
score ends at 6

hints: The function goes at the left edge, like _ready(). Two lines: score += value, then a print.
The connection is the first line of _ready(): player.coin_collected.connect(_on_coin_collected) – the function's name, no brackets.
steps.explain: Look at where the Score: lines fall in the output: before Coins in the bag, because each emit called your function at once, in the middle of collect(). Move the connect line below the first collect and the first coin goes unheard – a connection only hears what is emitted after it is made.

steps.title: A badge, with bind
steps.task: Add var badges: Array = [] and a function _unlock(_value: int, badge: String) that appends badge to badges and prints Unlocked: followed by it. Connect it to coin_collected as a second listener, using bind to fill in the badge name "First coin".
steps.solution:
extends Node

class Player:
	signal coin_collected(value: int)
	var coins := 0

	func collect(value: int) -> void:
		coins += 1
		coin_collected.emit(value)

var player := Player.new()
var score := 0
var badges: Array = []

func _ready() -> void:
	player.coin_collected.connect(_on_coin_collected)
	player.coin_collected.connect(_unlock.bind("First coin"))
	player.collect(1)
	player.collect(5)
	print("Coins in the bag: ", player.coins)

func _on_coin_collected(value: int) -> void:
	score += value
	print("Score: ", score)

func _unlock(_value: int, badge: String) -> void:
	badges.append(badge)
	print("Unlocked: ", badge)

tests.label: badges contains "First coin"
prints Unlocked: First coin
the badge name is given with bind
tests.why: Connect _unlock.bind("First coin") – the signal sends the value, bind adds the name.

tests.label: the score still ends at 6

hints: The signal sends one value, the function takes two. bind supplies the second: bound values arrive after the signal's own.
player.coin_collected.connect(_unlock.bind("First coin"))
steps.explain: _unlock knows nothing about coins: it takes a name and unlocks it. The underscore on _value tells Godot the parameter is unused on purpose. But read the output – the "first coin" badge unlocked twice, once per coin. Print badges at the end of _ready() if you want to see it. The next step fixes that.

steps.title: Only the first time
steps.task: A first-coin badge should unlock once. Change the badge's connection so that it is removed after the first time it is called, without adding any variable or if.
steps.solution:
extends Node

class Player:
	signal coin_collected(value: int)
	var coins := 0

	func collect(value: int) -> void:
		coins += 1
		coin_collected.emit(value)

var player := Player.new()
var score := 0
var badges: Array = []

func _ready() -> void:
	player.coin_collected.connect(_on_coin_collected)
	player.coin_collected.connect(_unlock.bind("First coin"), CONNECT_ONE_SHOT)
	player.collect(1)
	player.collect(5)
	print("Coins in the bag: ", player.coins)

func _on_coin_collected(value: int) -> void:
	score += value
	print("Score: ", score)

func _unlock(_value: int, badge: String) -> void:
	badges.append(badge)
	print("Unlocked: ", badge)

tests.label: badges is exactly ["First coin"] – unlocked once, however many coins follow
uses a one-shot connection
tests.why: connect() takes a second argument: CONNECT_ONE_SHOT.

tests.label: the score listener still hears both coins

hints: connect takes a second argument after the Callable.
player.coin_collected.connect(_unlock.bind("First coin"), CONNECT_ONE_SHOT)
steps.explain: One signal, two listeners, two lifetimes: the score hears every coin, the badge heard one and let go. Neither knows about the other, and Player has not been touched since step one.

steps.title: Wait for the goal
steps.task:
Finish the level. In the main script, declare signal goal_reached and const GOAL := 10, and have _on_coin_collected emit goal_reached whenever the score is at least GOAL.

Then write run_level(): it prints Level started, waits for goal_reached, and prints Level complete: with the score. Call it in _ready() after the two connections, and collect a third coin worth 10 after the other two.
steps.solution:
extends Node

signal goal_reached

const GOAL := 10

class Player:
	signal coin_collected(value: int)
	var coins := 0

	func collect(value: int) -> void:
		coins += 1
		coin_collected.emit(value)

var player := Player.new()
var score := 0
var badges: Array = []

func _ready() -> void:
	player.coin_collected.connect(_on_coin_collected)
	player.coin_collected.connect(_unlock.bind("First coin"), CONNECT_ONE_SHOT)
	run_level()
	player.collect(1)
	player.collect(5)
	player.collect(10)
	print("Coins in the bag: ", player.coins)

func run_level() -> void:
	print("Level started")
	await goal_reached
	print("Level complete: ", score)

func _on_coin_collected(value: int) -> void:
	score += value
	print("Score: ", score)
	if score >= GOAL:
		goal_reached.emit()

func _unlock(_value: int, badge: String) -> void:
	badges.append(badge)
	print("Unlocked: ", badge)

tests.label: the script has a signal called goal_reached
prints Level started, then later Score: 16 and Level complete: 16
run_level() waits with await goal_reached
tests.why: The middle line of run_level() is: await goal_reached

tests.label: score ends at 16
and there is still one badge

hints: Three lines in run_level(): a print, await goal_reached, a print.
At the end of _on_coin_collected: if score >= GOAL: and, under it, goal_reached.emit().
In _ready() the order is: two connections, run_level(), then three collect calls. Call run_level() plainly, with no await in front.
steps.explain: Read the output top to bottom. Level started comes first and Level complete five lines later: run_level() sat paused at its await while _ready() collected three coins. It woke in the middle of the third collect(), the moment goal_reached was emitted, which is why Level complete is printed before Coins in the bag. Change the third coin to be worth 1 and the level never completes – quietly, as awaits do. That is a whole small game's worth of joining up: an emitter, a listener, a one-shot, a bound argument and a coroutine.

title: A walker with a dash
intro: Your script is one Node2D in a small game view that restarts each time you stop typing. Click the view, then use the arrow keys or W A S D; on a phone, use the buttons under it. This page's Input Map has four actions bound to those keys – move_left, move_right, move_up, move_down – and the built-in ui_accept on Space and the round button.

steps.title: Walk sideways
steps.task: Make the square walk left and right at SPEED pixels a second while move_left or move_right is held. Ask for both actions with one call to Input.get_axis, and remember delta.

tests.label: holding move_right for one second moves it 80 pixels right
holding move_left for two seconds moves it 160 pixels back
holding both, it stands still
with nothing held, it stays where it is

hints: Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right") gives -1, 0 or 1. The negative action goes first.
Replace pass with: position.x += Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right") * SPEED * delta
steps.explain: Click the game and try it. There is no if anywhere: with nothing held the axis is 0, and adding zero is standing still. Hold left and right together and they cancel. Without the * delta the square would move 80 pixels every frame and leave the screen at once (Chapter I).

steps.title: All four ways
steps.task: Add up and down. Read a second axis from move_up and move_down, put the two numbers in a Vector2, and move position by that vector times SPEED and delta.

tests.label: holding move_up for one second moves it 80 pixels up the screen
holding move_down for two seconds moves it 160 pixels down
and it still walks sideways

hints: Up the screen is smaller y, so move_up is the negative action: Input.get_axis("move_up", "move_down").
position += Vector2(x, y) * SPEED * delta
steps.explain: Eight directions from two lines. Now do an experiment before the next step: walk from the left edge to the right edge and count the seconds. Then go corner to corner, holding two keys. The diagonal is a longer trip and it does not take longer. Something is wrong.

steps.title: Fix the diagonal
steps.task: Held together, right and down make the vector (1, 1), which is 1.41 long – so the square walks 113 pixels a second diagonally. Make every direction the same speed. Input.get_vector takes all four actions and never gives a vector longer than 1.

tests.label: straight: one second covers 80 pixels
diagonal: one second also covers 80 pixels, not 113
and the diagonal went up and to the left

hints: The four names go in this order: left, right, up, down – negative x, positive x, negative y, positive y.
Two lines become one: var dir := Input.get_vector("move_left", "move_right", "move_up", "move_down"), then position += dir * SPEED * delta.
steps.explain: Walk corner to corner again: it now takes as long as it should. Building the vector yourself and calling .normalized() on it passes too, and is what you would do with a direction that did not come from Input. This one line is, word for word apart from the variable's type, how Little Hours reads its keys.

steps.title: Face the way you went
steps.task: A dash needs a direction even when no key is held, so remember one. Add var facing := Vector2.RIGHT, and whenever the direction from the keys is not zero, store it in facing. Show it: in _draw(), draw a line from the centre to facing * 14, and ask for a new drawing whenever facing changes.

tests.label: facing starts as Vector2.RIGHT
after walking up, facing is Vector2.UP
and it still is when the keys are let go
after walking left, facing is Vector2.LEFT
_draw() draws the nose with draw_line
tests.why: In _draw(): draw_line(Vector2.ZERO, facing * 14, Color.WHITE, 2)

tests.label: asks for a new drawing with queue_redraw()
tests.why: Without it _draw() runs once and the nose never turns.

hints: After moving: if dir != Vector2.ZERO: and under it facing = dir. With no key held, dir is zero and facing keeps its last value.
Moving a node does not redraw it, and does not need to. Changing what the drawing looks like does: call queue_redraw() in the same if.
In _draw(): draw_line(Vector2.ZERO, facing * 14, Color.WHITE, 2)
steps.explain: The white nose turns as you steer and stays put when you stop. This is polling's weak spot and the usual patch for it: Input can only tell you about now, so anything about a moment ago is a variable you keep yourself.

steps.title: Dash
steps.task: Add const DASH := 40.0. Each time ui_accept is pressed, jump the square DASH pixels in the direction it is facing. One press, one dash – holding the key down must not dash again.

tests.label: a tap of ui_accept dashes 40 pixels the way it faces
holding ui_accept for 30 frames is still only one dash
walking up still works
and the next dash goes up

hints: There are two questions you could ask about ui_accept. One is true on every frame the key is down; the other only on the frame it went down.
if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"): and under it position += facing * DASH.
steps.explain: Press Space, then hold it: one dash each time. Now change just_pressed to pressed and hold it again – 40 pixels every frame, and the square is gone before you can let go. Put it back. Notice that a diagonal dash is the same length as a straight one: facing came from get_vector, so its length is 1.

steps.title: Stay in the room
steps.task: The view is 320 × 180 and the square is 16 across. As the last thing in _process, keep the centre of the square between (8, 8) and (312, 172) so that neither walking nor dashing can take it off the screen.

tests.label: walking left for five seconds stops at the left wall
walking up stops at the top
a dash into the wall stops at the wall
and the far corner is (312, 172)

hints: A Vector2 has a clamp(min, max) that keeps each of x and y between the matching parts of two other vectors.
The last line of _process: position = position.clamp(Vector2(8, 8), Vector2(312, 172))
steps.explain: That is a complete little controller: an axis pair for what is held, a remembered direction, a just-pressed for the one-off, and a clamp so nothing the player does can break it. Every line reads an action, never a key – so it already works with the arrows, with WASD and with the buttons under the view, and you did nothing to make it so.

title: A garden you can walk around
intro: Your script is one Node2D that draws a whole garden with _draw() (Chapter O explains the drawing calls; here they are written for you). Everything it draws is in the node's local space, so the node's own position decides where the garden's corner lands on the screen. Click the view and use the arrow keys.
starter:
extends Node2D

const VIEW := Vector2(320, 180)    # what the screen shows
const ROOM := Vector2(640, 360)    # the whole garden: twice the view each way
const SPEED := 96.0                # pixels a second

var you := Vector2(160, 110)       # where your feet are, in garden pixels
var trees := [Vector2(110, 96), Vector2(210, 130), Vector2(330, 80), Vector2(450, 150), Vector2(260, 250), Vector2(540, 300), Vector2(90, 300)]

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO         # the garden's corner on the screen's corner

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	you = you.clamp(Vector2.ZERO, ROOM)   # nobody walks off the grass
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, ROOM), Color("#7aa35a"))
	for x in range(0, 641, 64):
		draw_line(Vector2(x, 0), Vector2(x, 360), Color("#6f9651"))
	for tree in trees:
		draw_tree(tree)
	draw_you()
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(8, 16), "Day 1", HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

func draw_tree(feet: Vector2) -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(feet.x - 3, feet.y - 16, 6, 16), Color("#6b4a2f"))
	draw_circle(feet + Vector2(0, -28), 16, Color("#2f6b3f"))

func draw_you() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(you.x - 5, you.y - 18, 10, 18), Color("#c9556e"))
	draw_circle(you + Vector2(0, -23), 6, Color("#f1c39b"))

steps.title: Walk
steps.task: Make the arrow keys move you at SPEED pixels a second: the actions are ui_left, ui_right, ui_up and ui_down. Up the screen is less y, and walking diagonally must be no faster than walking straight. Put your lines above the clamp that is already in _process.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const VIEW := Vector2(320, 180)    # what the screen shows
const ROOM := Vector2(640, 360)    # the whole garden: twice the view each way
const SPEED := 96.0                # pixels a second

var you := Vector2(160, 110)       # where your feet are, in garden pixels
var trees := [Vector2(110, 96), Vector2(210, 130), Vector2(330, 80), Vector2(450, 150), Vector2(260, 250), Vector2(540, 300), Vector2(90, 300)]

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO         # the garden's corner on the screen's corner

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	var dir := Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down")
	you += dir * SPEED * delta
	you = you.clamp(Vector2.ZERO, ROOM)   # nobody walks off the grass
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, ROOM), Color("#7aa35a"))
	for x in range(0, 641, 64):
		draw_line(Vector2(x, 0), Vector2(x, 360), Color("#6f9651"))
	for tree in trees:
		draw_tree(tree)
	draw_you()
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(8, 16), "Day 1", HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

func draw_tree(feet: Vector2) -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(feet.x - 3, feet.y - 16, 6, 16), Color("#6b4a2f"))
	draw_circle(feet + Vector2(0, -28), 16, Color("#2f6b3f"))

func draw_you() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(you.x - 5, you.y - 18, 10, 18), Color("#c9556e"))
	draw_circle(you + Vector2(0, -23), 6, Color("#f1c39b"))

tests.label: one second of holding right moves you 96 px right, to (256, 110)
one second of up takes 96 off your y: (256, 14)
one second of left and down together is still 96 px of travel

hints: You need a direction, as a Vector2 no longer than 1. Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down") gives exactly that, already pointing up for the up key.
Then one line of movement: you += dir * SPEED * delta.
steps.explain: Direction times speed times time: the whole of movement in one line. If you build the direction yourself from two get_axis() calls it needs .normalized(), or the diagonal check fails at 135.8 px. Now walk up to the tree on the left and stand above its trunk. You are drawn on top of its leaves, which is wrong, and is the next step.

steps.title: Behind and in front
steps.task: The trees are all painted first and you last, so you are always in front. Write draw_order() -> Array: every pair of feet in the garden – the trees' and yours – as one list of Vector2s, sorted so the smallest y comes first. It must not change trees. Then make _draw() go through that list instead, calling draw_you() when it reaches you and draw_tree() for the rest.

tests.label: draw_order() lists all eight pairs of feet, smallest y first
at the start you are third: behind five trees, in front of two
walk down for a second and you are fifth
trees still holds seven trees
_draw() paints in the order draw_order() gives
tests.why: Loop over draw_order() in _draw(), in place of the loop over trees.

hints: Start from a copy of the list, trees.duplicate(), and append(you) to it. Appending to trees itself would plant a tree on your feet every frame (Chapter G).
Sort it with feet.sort_custom(func(a, b): return a.y < b.y), and return it.
In _draw(): for feet in draw_order(): then if feet == you: draw_you(), else: draw_tree(feet).
steps.explain: Walk round a tree: behind its leaves when you are above its base, in front of its trunk when you are below. This is everything y_sort_enabled does. It works here because you and every tree are measured at the feet – the positions are the bottoms of the drawings, not their middles.

steps.title: A camera that follows
steps.task: Walk right and you leave the screen: the garden is bigger than the view. Add var cam := Vector2(160, 110) – the point of the garden that should be at the centre of the screen – and each frame, after the clamp, set it to where you are. Then move the garden so that point lands on the middle of the view: the node's position must be VIEW / 2 - cam.

tests.label: walk right for a second, to x = 256
then stand still: cam is where you are
the garden is placed at VIEW / 2 - cam
so you are drawn in the middle of the screen

hints: Two lines, after the clamp and before queue_redraw(). The first is cam = you.
The second is position = VIEW / 2 - cam.
steps.explain: You are now pinned to the middle of the view and the garden slides under you. That is all a camera is: nothing in the garden changed its own numbers; their parent moved the opposite way, and you + position – your local position plus the parent's – is your place on the screen. Two things have gone wrong, though. Walk to an edge and the view shows grey beyond the grass. And the "Day 1" sign, which was meant to sit in the corner of the screen, has been left behind in the corner of the garden.

steps.title: Limits
steps.task: Stop the view at the garden's edges. The camera's point may be you, but never nearer than half a view to any side of ROOM: clamp it between VIEW / 2 and ROOM - VIEW / 2.

tests.label: walk left for a second, to x = 64
the view has stopped at the left edge: position.x is 0
walk all the way to the far corner
the view shows the last 320 x 180 of the garden: position is (-320, -180)
walk back towards the middle
away from the edges you are in the middle of the screen again

hints: Vector2 has a clamp(min, max) that clamps x and y at once – the line above yours uses it.
cam = you.clamp(VIEW / 2, ROOM - VIEW / 2)
steps.explain: Walk into a corner: the view stops and you carry on to the fence, off-centre for the first time. These four numbers are limit_left, limit_top, limit_right and limit_bottom on a Camera2D, which does this clamp for you.

steps.title: Glide
steps.task: The camera is nailed to you: start walking and the whole garden starts with a jolt. Make it glide. Add const GLIDE := 5.0, and each frame move cam only part of the way to the clamped point it wants, with lerp: a share of GLIDE * delta, never more than 1.

tests.label: a second into a walk the camera is on its way but still behind you
stand still and it settles on you
walk to the left fence
the limits still hold: cam.x settles at 160, not 0

hints: Keep the clamped point in a variable instead of assigning it straight to cam: var want := you.clamp(VIEW / 2, ROOM - VIEW / 2).
cam = cam.lerp(want, minf(1.0, GLIDE * delta))
steps.explain: Set off and the camera lags, then catches up as you stop: the garden feels heavier and calmer. This is position_smoothing_enabled, and GLIDE is position_smoothing_speed. Try 2 and 12. Multiplying by delta keeps the glide the same on a fast screen and a slow one; the minf stops a very long frame from throwing the camera past its target.

steps.title: A sign that stays put
steps.task: Last, the sign. It is drawn at (8, 16) in the garden, and it should be at (8, 16) on the screen. Write to_garden(screen_point: Vector2) -> Vector2, which turns a place on the screen into the place in the garden that is under it right now, and draw the sign at to_garden(Vector2(8, 16)).

tests.label: walk down and to the right for two seconds
the middle of the screen is over the camera's point
to_garden(Vector2(8, 16)), drawn by this node, lands on the screen at (8, 16)
the sign is drawn at to_garden(...)
tests.why: Give draw_string() the point to_garden(Vector2(8, 16)) in place of Vector2(8, 16).

hints: A garden point p is drawn on the screen at p + position. You want the opposite: which p gives a chosen screen point?
return screen_point - position – then use to_garden(Vector2(8, 16)) as the second argument of draw_string().
steps.explain: The sign holds still while the garden moves under it. to_garden() is Godot's to_local() for a node that is not turned or scaled, and undoing the camera for everything on the interface is the whole job of a CanvasLayer. One finishing touch from Little Hours: write position = (VIEW / 2 - cam).round(), so the garden never sits between two pixels. You have built y-sorting, a camera with limits and smoothing, and a UI layer – each of them one or two lines of Vector2 arithmetic.

title: A walker and a box
intro: One Node2D draws a floor, one solid box, a white cross for the target and a walker. Click anywhere in the view to send the walker there: the click already calls walk_to(). At the moment nothing listens.
starter:
extends Node2D

const SPEED := 80.0       # pixels a second
