const RADIUS := 8.0       # the walker is a disc this big, at their feet

var pos := Vector2(40, 60)           # where the walker is
var target := Vector2(280, 150)      # where they are going
var solids: Array[Rect2] = [Rect2(130, 50, 60, 80)]

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO           # draw in screen pixels

## Send the walker somewhere. A click on the view calls this.
func walk_to(p: Vector2) -> void:
	target = p

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if Input.is_mouse_button_pressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT):
		walk_to(get_global_mouse_position())
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#d9c7a3"))
	for r in solids:
		draw_rect(r, Color("#7a5a45"))
	draw_line(target + Vector2(-4, -4), target + Vector2(4, 4), Color.WHITE, 2.0)
	draw_line(target + Vector2(-4, 4), target + Vector2(4, -4), Color.WHITE, 2.0)
	draw_circle(pos, RADIUS, Color("#c9556e"))

steps.title: Walk to the target
steps.task: In _process, move pos towards target at SPEED pixels a second. They must land exactly on the target and stay there – no overshoot, no shivering.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const SPEED := 80.0       # pixels a second
const RADIUS := 8.0       # the walker is a disc this big, at their feet

var pos := Vector2(40, 60)           # where the walker is
var target := Vector2(280, 150)      # where they are going
var solids: Array[Rect2] = [Rect2(130, 50, 60, 80)]

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO           # draw in screen pixels

## Send the walker somewhere. A click on the view calls this.
func walk_to(p: Vector2) -> void:
	target = p

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if Input.is_mouse_button_pressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT):
		walk_to(get_global_mouse_position())
	pos = pos.move_toward(target, SPEED * delta)
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#d9c7a3"))
	for r in solids:
		draw_rect(r, Color("#7a5a45"))
	draw_line(target + Vector2(-4, -4), target + Vector2(4, 4), Color.WHITE, 2.0)
	draw_line(target + Vector2(-4, 4), target + Vector2(4, -4), Color.WHITE, 2.0)
	draw_circle(pos, RADIUS, Color("#c9556e"))

tests.label: one second of walking covers 80 px
then they are sent to (40, 150)…
…and arrive exactly on it
…and stay there, without shivering

hints: Vector2 has a move_toward(to, step) that never passes to. The step for one frame is SPEED * delta.
pos = pos.move_toward(target, SPEED * delta)
steps.explain: Click around: wherever the cross goes, they follow and stop dead on it. They also stroll straight through the box, as its first walk showed. Before they can stop at it, the script has to be able to say what "in the box" means.

steps.title: What is solid
steps.task:
Two functions, and a colour so you can see them work.

  • to_box(p: Vector2, r: Rect2) -> float – how far the point p is from the rectangle r, and 0 if it is inside. The nearest point of a rectangle is p with its x and y clamped to the rectangle's edges.
  • blocked(p: Vector2) -> bool – true when a disc of RADIUS centred on p overlaps any rectangle in solids: when p is nearer than RADIUS to one.

Then, in _draw(), paint the walker Color.RED whenever blocked(pos).

tests.label: to_box: 10 px to the left of the box is 10 away
to_box: inside the box is 0
to_box: off a corner, it is the distance to the corner (3 across, 4 up: 5)
blocked: the middle of the box
blocked: 5 px from its left face, because the disc is 8 wide
not blocked: 10 px from its left face
not blocked: 8.5 px from its corner – a disc, not a square
not blocked: out on the open floor
the walker is painted red while blocked(pos)
tests.why: In _draw(), choose the colour with: Color.RED if blocked(pos) else Color("#c9556e")

hints: The nearest point: Vector2(clampf(p.x, r.position.x, r.end.x), clampf(p.y, r.position.y, r.end.y)). Return p.distance_to() it.
blocked() is a loop: for r in solids:, and inside it if to_box(p, r) < RADIUS: return true. After the loop, return false.
The colour is a one-line choice: Color.RED if blocked(pos) else Color("#c9556e").
steps.explain: Send them across the box and they flush red the moment their edge touches it, not their centre – and a little later at the corners than a square would. Nothing stops them yet: blocked() only answers a question. But notice what it asks about: any point you like, not only where they are. That is what makes the next step one line.

steps.title: Stop at the wall
steps.task: Ask before you step. Work out where this frame's step would put them, and take it only if that place is not blocked.

tests.label: sent to the middle of the box…
…they never end up inside it
they are standing at its left face

hints: Keep the result of move_toward in a variable instead of assigning it straight to pos.
var next := pos.move_toward(target, SPEED * delta), then if not blocked(next): pos = next.
steps.explain: They cannot turn red any more. But run the first walk again – press Show me this step's neighbour, or retype a space – and watch them cross to the box and stick to its face like a fridge magnet, though the cross is only a little way down and round the corner. The step they keep being refused is mostly "right" and a little "down", and the "down" part was never the problem.

steps.title: Slide along it
steps.task: Take the step one axis at a time. First try moving only x to where the step would put it, keeping the old y; if that place is clear, take it. Then try only y, from wherever that left them.

tests.expr: not blocked(pos) and pos.x <= 122.0 and pos.y > 95.0
tests.label: two and a half seconds in, they are sliding down the box's left face
they round the corner and arrive at (280, 150)

hints: The place to test for the first half is Vector2(next.x, pos.y): the new x with the old y.
if not blocked(Vector2(next.x, pos.y)): pos.x = next.x – then the same for y, testing Vector2(pos.x, next.y).
steps.explain: Now they reach the box, slide down its face, roll round the corner and walk on. The wall refuses the x half of each step and the y half still happens. Assigning pos.x = next.x, and not adding a step, keeps the exact landing from step 1. Click just the other side of the box, level with them, to find the limit of sliding: with no "down" in the step there is nothing to slide with, and they push at the wall for ever. The last two steps deal with that.

steps.title: Say when you are there
steps.task:
Other code will want to know when the walk is over – that is the moment to open the door or pick the apple. Add:

  • signal arrived, and var walking := true
  • walk_to() sets walking to true; _process moves nobody while it is false
  • when pos reaches target: walking becomes false and arrived is emitted – once, not every frame after
  • var arrivals := 0, and a function _on_arrived(), connected to the signal in _ready(), that adds one to it and prints arrived

tests.label: sent to (40, 150)…
…arrived is emitted when they get there
walking is false once they have arrived
standing there for a second does not emit it again
sent back to (40, 60)…
…a second walk, a second arrival
_on_arrived() prints arrived

hints: The signal goes at the top with the variables: signal arrived. In _ready(): arrived.connect(_on_arrived).
In _process, after queue_redraw(): if not walking: return. Move queue_redraw() up so it still runs.
After the two axis moves: if pos == target: then walking = false and arrived.emit().
steps.explain: Each click that can be reached ends in one line in the output. The walking flag is what makes it once: without it pos == target stays true and the signal fires sixty times a second. The walker does not know or care who is listening (Chapter J) – in Little Hours the listener is whatever you tapped: the walk ends and the fridge opens.

steps.title: Give up gracefully
steps.task:
Click in the middle of the box. They walk to its face and push at it for ever: arrived never comes, and anything waiting for it waits for ever too. Teach them to give up.

  • Add const STALL_TIME := 0.25, const CRAWL := 2.0 and var stall := 0.0.
  • Each frame, measure how far they actually moved. If it was less than CRAWL * delta – slower than 2 pixels a second – add delta to stall; otherwise set stall back to 0.
  • When stall reaches STALL_TIME, the walk is over where they stand: make that spot the target, so that the arrival you wrote in the last step does the rest.
  • A new walk_to() starts with stall at 0.

tests.label: sent to the middle of the box…
…they give up: walking is false
arrived was still emitted, once
the target is now the spot where they stand, outside the box
sent back to the start…
…a clear walk still arrives exactly
sent the long way round the corner…
…sliding slowly is not being stuck: they get there

hints: Remember where they were before the two axis moves: var before := pos. Afterwards, pos.distance_to(before) is how far they really got.
if pos.distance_to(before) < CRAWL * delta: stall += delta, else: stall = 0.0.
Then, before the arrival check: if stall >= STALL_TIME: target = pos. And stall = 0.0 in walk_to().
steps.explain: Click inside the box: they walk up, lean on it for a quarter of a second, and settle, and the output says arrived. Giving up is one line because of how you wrote arriving: move the target to where they are, and they are there. Little Hours has this timer with nearly the same number – STALL_TIME := 0.28 – and for the same reason: its comment says that without it, walking to a piece whose standing spot is partly blocked "would leave them shoving at it forever and the interaction would never run". A walker, a solid, a slide, a signal and a way out: that is the skeleton of the real thing.

title: A walker with a hop
intro: Your script is one Node2D that draws a small figure with draw_rect (Chapter O is about drawing). It stands at its feet: the node's origin is on the floor and everything is drawn upwards from there. By the end it walks with ← and →, steps and bobs as it goes, and hops on Space.

steps.title: A frame from time
steps.task: Nothing moves yet. Start with the clock. Add a variable walk_t that starts at 0.0 and counts seconds in _process. Then write frame() -> int, which turns walk_t into the number of the walk frame showing now: there are 4 frames, played at FPS a second, looping.

tests.label: a quarter of a second in (with → held), walk_t is 0.25
and frame() is 2
an eighth of a second later, frame() is 3
and then it wraps round to 0

hints: In _process, replace pass with walk_t += delta.
The frame is the expression from the first section: int(walk_t * FPS) % 4.
steps.explain: The figure has not moved, but it now knows what time it is in animation terms: eight frames a second, round and round through 0, 1, 2, 3. The checks hold → because in two steps' time the clock will only run while walking.

steps.title: Legs that step
steps.task:
Use the frame. Write lift(side: int) -> float: how many pixels a foot is off the floor. side is -1 for the left leg and 1 for the right. On frame 1 the left foot is up by 5.0; on frame 3 the right foot is; otherwise the answer is 0.0.

Then make each leg in _draw() shorter by its lift, and ask for a new drawing every frame – a drawing is kept until you do.

tests.label: on frame 1 the left foot is 5 pixels up
and the right foot is down
on frame 2 both feet are down
on frame 3 the right foot is up
_draw() uses lift(-1) and lift(1) for the legs
tests.why: A leg is a rectangle 26 tall; make its height 26 - lift(-1).

tests.label: asks for a new drawing with queue_redraw()
tests.why: Without it _draw() runs once and the legs never change.

hints: lift is two ifs and a final return 0.0. The first: if frame() == 1 and side == -1: return 5.0.
In _draw(), the left leg becomes Rect2(-7, -26, 6, 26 - lift(-1)). The top of the leg stays put and the bottom rises.
If the legs do not move, add queue_redraw() to _process.
steps.explain: It marches on the spot: left, both, right, both. Nothing about the drawing is stored – each time _draw() runs it asks lift(), which asks frame(), which reads the clock. Change FPS to 3.0 to watch the four frames one at a time.

steps.title: Only while walking
steps.task: Now let the keys decide. Add const SPEED := 40.0. In _process, read left and right into one number with Input.get_axis("ui_left", "ui_right"). While it is not zero, move position.x by that direction at SPEED pixels a second and let walk_t count. When it is zero, set walk_t back to 0.0, so the figure stands on frame 0 with both feet down.

tests.label: standing still, walk_t stays at 0
and the figure has not moved
holding → for 0.875 s moves it 35 pixels right
and it is on walk frame 3
let go, and walk_t goes back to 0
holding ← for a second moves it 40 pixels left

hints: var dir := Input.get_axis("ui_left", "ui_right") is −1, 0 or 1.
if dir != 0.0: then two lines – walk_t += delta and position.x += dir * SPEED * delta – and under else:, walk_t = 0.0.
steps.explain: Click the game and walk about. Two different kinds of change are happening. Moving position slides the finished drawing across the screen and needs no new drawing at all; changing the frame does, which is why queue_redraw() is there. Resetting the clock on stopping is what the game's own character does too, so nobody is left standing with one foot in the air.

steps.title: A bob
steps.task:
A walk that keeps the head dead level looks like sliding. Write bob() -> float: a sine wave of walk_t, 2 pixels high, that swings twice in each cycle of four frames. A cycle lasts 4 / FPS seconds, so the angle to give sin is walk_t * FPS * PI.

In _draw(), shift the body and the head down by bob(), rounded to a whole pixel. Leave the legs where they are.

tests.label: standing still, bob() is 0
half-way through frame 0 the body is 2 pixels down
half-way through frame 1, with a foot lifted, it is 2 pixels up
_draw() uses bob()
tests.why: Add the rounded bob to the y of the body and the head.

hints: func bob() -> float: and one line: return sin(walk_t * FPS * PI) * 2.0.
At the top of _draw(): var b := roundf(bob()). Then the body is Rect2(-8, -44 + b, 16, 20) and the head Rect2(-7, -60 + b, 14, 14).
steps.explain: The body dips while both feet are down and rises as a foot comes up, the way a real walk does. Because the bob is worked out from walk_t and added to fixed numbers, it can never drift, and it is zero the instant the figure stops. The legs were drawn two pixels up inside the body from the start so that no gap opens when the body rises.

steps.title: An eased hop
steps.task:
Give it a hop on Space. Add const HOP := 24.0 (pixels) and const HOP_TIME := 0.5 (seconds), and three things:

  • ease_out(x: float) -> float – the one-line curve from the tweens section.
  • hop_height(p: float) -> float – the height for a hop that is a share p done. 1.0 - absf(2.0 * p - 1.0) climbs from 0 to 1 and back down as p goes from 0 to 1; pass that through ease_out and multiply by HOP.
  • var hop_t := 1.0 – how much of the hop is done; 1 means "not hopping". When ui_accept is pressed and no hop is under way, set it to 0.0. While it is below 1, add delta / HOP_TIME, stopping at 1.0. Every frame, set position.y to FLOOR - hop_height(hop_t).

tests.label: ease_out(0.5) is 0.75
a hop starts and ends on the floor
half-way through it is HOP pixels up
a quarter of the way through it is already three quarters of the way up
without a press, the figure stays on the floor
a quarter of a second after Space it is at the top of the hop
and half a second after Space it has landed

hints: ease_out returns 1.0 - (1.0 - x) * (1.0 - x).
hop_height returns HOP * ease_out(1.0 - absf(2.0 * p - 1.0)).

In _process: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") and hop_t >= 1.0: sets hop_t = 0.0. Then if hop_t < 1.0: does hop_t = minf(hop_t + delta / HOP_TIME, 1.0). Last, position.y = FLOOR - hop_height(hop_t).
steps.explain: Press Space. The figure leaves the floor fast, hangs near the top and comes down faster and faster – the ease is what makes that feel like weight instead of a lift going up and down. This is a tween written by hand: a share of the time, bent by a curve, turned into a value. In a real project create_tween() would do the same job; here you can see every part of it. Try HOP_TIME := 1.5 for the moon.

steps.title: Squash on landing
steps.task: The landing has no weight yet. On the frame the hop finishes – when hop_t reaches 1.0 – set scale to Vector2(1.3, 0.7): wide and short. And on every frame, bring scale back towards Vector2.ONE with move_toward, at a rate of delta.

tests.label: before any hop, scale is (1, 1)
just after landing it is wider and shorter
two seconds later scale is exactly (1, 1) again
and it is standing on the floor

hints: The landing is the moment hop_t becomes 1. Inside if hop_t < 1.0:, after the line that advances it, add if hop_t >= 1.0: and set the scale there.
The recovery is one line, outside any if: scale = scale.move_toward(Vector2.ONE, delta).
steps.explain: Hop again and watch the feet. The squash happens around the node's origin, and the origin is on the floor, so the figure spreads where it stands. move_toward was the right chaser here because it arrives: the last check asks for a scale of exactly (1, 1), and a lerp would still be creeping towards it. You now have a frame cycle, a sine bob, an eased hop and a squash – the same four ingredients the next section finds in the real game.

title: A stamina bar from nothing
intro: A bar that drains while you hold Space and refills when you let go, with a colour that warns you, an outline and a number – and that redraws itself only when it has something new to show.

steps.title: The track
steps.task: Start at the back. In _draw(), paint the empty bar: the rectangle BAR in the colour TRACK. Keep the draws += 1 line; it is counting for later.

tests.label: _draw() paints BAR in the TRACK colour
tests.why: draw_rect takes a Rect2 and a Color.

tests.label: _draw() runs without an error, and only once

hints: draw_rect(BAR, TRACK), indented under _draw().
steps.explain: A dark slot in the middle of the view. BAR starts at (−60, −6) and is 120 wide and 12 tall, so the node's origin is its centre. And draws is 1: nothing has asked for a second drawing.

steps.title: The fill
steps.task:
Now the geometry. Write fill_rect(v: float) -> Rect2: the part of BAR that is full when the value is v out of MAX. It starts where BAR starts and is as tall; only its width is a share of the bar's. Values below 0 or above MAX must not draw outside the bar.

Then paint fill_rect(value) in FILL, over the track.

tests.label: at 50 the fill is the left half of the bar
at 100 it is the whole bar
at 0 it has no width
at 150 it is still only the whole bar
and below 0 it has no width
_draw() paints fill_rect(value)
tests.why: After the track: draw_rect(fill_rect(value), FILL)

hints: The share is v / MAX, kept between 0 and 1 with clampf.
A Rect2 from a position and a size: Rect2(BAR.position, Vector2(BAR.size.x * share, BAR.size.y)).
In _draw(), after the track: draw_rect(fill_rect(value), FILL).
steps.explain: Seventy per cent of the slot is green. fill_rect draws nothing – it answers a question – which is why the checks could ask it about 150 and −20 without those ever being on screen. Change value at the top to 20.0 and watch the view restart with a shorter bar.

steps.title: Spend it
steps.task: Make the value move. Add _process(delta): while ui_accept is held, value falls by 40 a second; otherwise it rises by 20 a second. Keep it between 0 and MAX. And remember what a changed value needs before the screen will show it.

tests.label: holding Space for a second takes value from 70 to 30
a second of rest brings it back to 50
and the bar was redrawn as the value changed
it cannot fall below 0
or rise above MAX

hints: if Input.is_action_pressed("ui_accept"): then value -= 40.0 * delta; under else:, value += 20.0 * delta.
After the if: value = clampf(value, 0.0, MAX).
If the number moves and the bar does not, end _process with queue_redraw().
steps.explain: Click the game and hold Space. The widget is alive, and _draw() did not change at all in this step: it already painted whatever value said. State changes in _process, the picture is made in _draw(), and queue_redraw() is the only thing that passes between them.

steps.title: Colour and an outline
steps.task:
A bar should say how worried to be. Write bar_color(v: float) -> Color: Color("#8fd36a") (green) when v is above 50, Color("#e8c94f") (amber) when it is above 25, and Color("#d64545") (red) otherwise. Use it for the fill in place of FILL.

Then give the bar an outline in Color("#f4ead8"): an unfilled rectangle one pixel bigger than BAR all round. Think about where in _draw() it has to go.

tests.label: above 50 it is green
at exactly 50 it is amber
at 26 it is still amber
at 25 and below it is red
the fill is painted in bar_color(value)
tests.why: draw_rect(fill_rect(value), bar_color(value))

tests.label: an unfilled rectangle is drawn after the fill
tests.why: The third argument of draw_rect is `filled`: draw_rect(BAR.grow(1), colour, false, 1.0) – and it goes last.

hints: bar_color is a ladder: if v > 50.0: return …, then if v > 25.0: return …, then a plain return for red.
BAR.grow(1) is BAR made one pixel bigger on every side.
Last line of _draw(): draw_rect(BAR.grow(1), Color("#f4ead8"), false, 1.0). The false means "outline only" and the 1.0 is its thickness.
steps.explain: Hold Space and watch it pass through amber into red. The outline goes last so that nothing paints over it; try moving that line to the top of _draw() and it is still there, only because it lies outside the bar – shrink it to BAR itself and the track and fill would cover half its thickness.

steps.title: Say the number
steps.task: Write label_text(v: float) -> String, which gives "70 / 100" for 70: the value rounded to a whole number, then MAX. Draw it under the bar with draw_string, in white, at size 12, starting at the bar's left edge.

tests.label: label_text(29.6) rounds to "30 / 100"
_draw() writes label_text(value) with draw_string
tests.why: draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, position, label_text(value), HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: _draw() runs without an error

hints: "%d / %d" % [roundi(v), roundi(MAX)] – %d wants whole numbers, and roundi rounds to one.
The position is the text's baseline. Vector2(BAR.position.x, BAR.end.y + 16) puts it a little below the bar.
The whole call: draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(BAR.position.x, BAR.end.y + 16), label_text(value), HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)
steps.explain: The widget now needs no Label node beside it: the number is part of the drawing and can never disagree with the bar, because both come from value in the same _draw(). Change the 16 to 0 to see what "the position is the baseline" means – the text sits on the bottom edge of the bar, not under it.

steps.title: Only when it changes
steps.task: Leave the bar alone until it is full and it is still being redrawn sixty times a second, to paint the same picture. Make it ask only when there is something new: in _process, remember value before you change it, and call queue_redraw() only if it is different afterwards.

tests.label: left alone for ten seconds, the bar is full
and _draw() stopped running once it was full
holding Space starts the redrawing again
and value has fallen to 60

hints: First line of _process: var before := value.
Replace the bare queue_redraw() with if value != before: and the call indented under it.
steps.explain: Nothing looks different, and that is the point: the bar is now free whenever it is still. For one bar it hardly matters. For a screen of forty widgets, or on a phone whose battery you are spending, "draw when it changed" is the habit that keeps a game cool. The exception is the thing that changes every frame anyway – and the next tutorial has one.

title: A stopwatch face
intro: A round dial with twelve marks, a fast red hand that goes round every ten seconds, a slow hand that counts the laps, and a readout. Space starts and stops it. Everything round on it comes from one small function.

steps.title: The face
steps.task: Paint the dial around the origin: a filled circle of radius R in FACE, then a rim on top of it – an arc all the way round, from angle 0.0 to TAU, in INK, 3 pixels thick. Give the arc 48 points so that it looks round.

tests.label: the face is a draw_circle
tests.why: draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, R, FACE)

tests.label: the rim is a draw_arc, drawn after the face
tests.why: draw_arc(centre, radius, start angle, end angle, point count, colour, width) – after the circle, so it sits on top.

tests.label: _draw() runs without an error

hints: draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, R, FACE) replaces pass.
Then draw_arc(Vector2.ZERO, R, 0.0, TAU, 48, INK, 3.0).
steps.explain: A plate with a dark edge. Change the 48 to 6 and the rim becomes a hexagon: an arc is straight pieces between points, and "round" is only "enough of them". Change TAU to PI and only the lower half is drawn – angles start on the right and turn clockwise.

steps.title: Round the edge
steps.task:
Write on_face(turn: float, radius: float) -> Vector2: the point radius pixels from the centre, turn of the way round the dial, measured the way a clock is read. A turn of 0.0 is twelve o'clock, 0.25 is three o'clock, 0.5 is six. The angle for a turn is turn * TAU - PI / 2.0.

Use it to draw twelve tick marks with a loop: each a line from on_face(i / 12.0, R - 8.0) to the same turn at R - 3.0, in INK, 2 thick.

tests.label: a turn of 0 is straight up: y is −50…
…and x is 0
a quarter turn is three o'clock: x is 50
half a turn is six o'clock: y is 50
three quarters is nine o'clock, and the radius is respected
a loop draws the ticks with draw_line and on_face
tests.why: for i in 12: then draw_line(on_face(i / 12.0, R - 8.0), on_face(i / 12.0, R - 3.0), INK, 2.0)

hints: Two lines: var angle := turn * TAU - PI / 2.0, then return Vector2(cos(angle), sin(angle)) * radius.
In _draw(), after the rim: for i in 12: and, indented, draw_line(on_face(i / 12.0, R - 8.0), on_face(i / 12.0, R - 3.0), INK, 2.0).
steps.explain: Twelve marks, none of them placed by hand. on_face hides the two awkward facts about angles – that they start at three o'clock and are measured in radians – behind a number anyone can read: how far round. Change the 12 to 60 (in both places) for a mark every second.

steps.title: A hand that moves
steps.task: Add var seconds := 0.0 and count time into it in _process. Write fast_turn() -> float: how far round the fast hand is, which is seconds as a share of LAP. Draw the hand as a line from the centre to on_face(fast_turn(), R - 12.0) in RED, 2 thick. This picture is different every frame, so ask for it every frame.

tests.label: 2.5 seconds after it is started, seconds is 2.5
and the fast hand is a quarter of the way round
_draw() draws a hand to on_face(fast_turn(), …)
tests.why: draw_line(Vector2.ZERO, on_face(fast_turn(), R - 12.0), RED, 2.0)

tests.label: asks for a new drawing with queue_redraw()
tests.why: Without it the hand is drawn once, at twelve, and never again.

hints: _process is two lines: seconds += delta and queue_redraw().
fast_turn() returns seconds / LAP. It may go past 1 – a turn of 1.25 points the same way as 0.25.
Last in _draw(): draw_line(Vector2.ZERO, on_face(fast_turn(), R - 12.0), RED, 2.0).
steps.explain: The hand sweeps, and the whole dial – plate, rim, twelve ticks – is being repainted every frame to move one line. That is fine: fifteen calls are nothing. If the face were costly to draw you would split it into two nodes, a face that draws once and a hand that redraws, which is exactly what Little Hours does with its floors and its water. (The checks press Space at the start, which does nothing yet. It will.)

steps.title: Start and stop
steps.task: A stopwatch starts stopped. Add var running := false. When ui_accept is pressed – once for each press, not for as long as it is held – flip running. Count time only while it is running.

tests.label: before Space is pressed, no time passes
press Space, and a second later seconds is 1
and running is true
press Space again and it stops
and the time holds at 1

hints: Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") is true for one frame for each press. running = not running flips a bool.
Put seconds += delta under if running:.
steps.explain: Click the game and press Space. In the answer shown here queue_redraw() moved under if running: as well, so a stopped watch is not repainted – the habit from the stamina bar. Yours passes either way.

steps.title: A slow hand and a cap
steps.task: Add the lap counter: slow_turn() -> float, which goes round once in twelve laps. Draw it as a shorter, thicker hand in INK – to R * 0.5, 4 thick – under the red one. Then finish the middle with a small filled circle of radius 4 in INK, on top of both hands.

tests.label: after 30 seconds the fast hand has been round three times
and the slow hand is a quarter of the way round: three laps of twelve
the slow hand is drawn before the fast one
tests.why: Whatever is drawn first is underneath.

tests.label: a draw_circle after the hands caps the centre
tests.why: draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 4.0, INK) as the last line of _draw().

hints: slow_turn() returns seconds / (LAP * 12.0).
The order in _draw() is the order of the stack: slow hand, then fast hand, then draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 4.0, INK).
steps.explain: The cap hides the untidy place where two lines of different widths meet. It is the smallest thing on the dial and it is what makes it look made. Three shapes share one point here, and the only thing that decides which you see is which was drawn last.

steps.title: Read it out
steps.task: Write time_text(s: float) -> String, which turns 7.3 into "7.3 s": one decimal place, a space, an s. Draw time_text(seconds) in white, size 12, under the dial – a baseline about 22 pixels below the rim, starting a little left of centre.

tests.label: time_text(83.46) rounds to one decimal: "83.5 s"
_draw() writes time_text(seconds) with draw_string
tests.why: draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(-18, R + 22), time_text(seconds), HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: it still runs, and _draw() has no error

hints: "%.1f s" % s – %.1f is a float with one decimal place.
Last line of _draw(): draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(-18, R + 22), time_text(seconds), HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)
steps.explain: A working stopwatch in about forty lines, with no image and no node but itself. Look back at its shape, because it is the shape of every drawn widget: two variables of state, four small functions that answer questions, and a _draw() that reads from back to front like a list of layers. Try it at LAP := 1.0.

title: A screen that keeps its pixels
intro: The view beside the editor is 320 × 180 screen pixels. Treat it as a monitor. By the end, a tiny game 100 × 50 art pixels in size will fit itself into a window at the largest whole scale, centre itself with bars, walk a sprite across without a shimmer, and refit when the window changes.
starter:
extends Node2D

const VIEW := Vector2(100, 50)   # the game's own size, in art pixels
const SPRITE := [
	"..oooo..",
	".oyyyyo.",
	"oyoyyoyo",
	"oyyyyyyo",
	"oyoyyoyo",
	"oyyooyyo",
	".oyyyyo.",
	"..oooo..",
]
const INK := {"o": Color("#3a2b30"), "y": Color("#f2c14e")}

var screen := Vector2(320, 180)  # the window the game has been given
var n := 1                       # screen pixels per art pixel
var pos := Vector2(10, 30)       # where the sprite is, in art pixels

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner

func whole_scale(view: Vector2, room: Vector2) -> int:
	return 1

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, screen), Color.BLACK)
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(4, 176), "x%d" % n, 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

steps.title: The biggest whole scale
steps.task: Finish whole_scale(view, room) so it returns how many whole times view fits inside room, both ways at once – and 0 if it does not fit even once. Then, in _ready(), set n from it using VIEW and screen. These sizes are Vector2s, so the division leaves a fraction: floori() rounds a float down to an int.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const VIEW := Vector2(100, 50)   # the game's own size, in art pixels
const SPRITE := [
	"..oooo..",
	".oyyyyo.",
	"oyoyyoyo",
	"oyyyyyyo",
	"oyoyyoyo",
	"oyyooyyo",
	".oyyyyo.",
	"..oooo..",
]
const INK := {"o": Color("#3a2b30"), "y": Color("#f2c14e")}

var screen := Vector2(320, 180)  # the window the game has been given
var n := 1                       # screen pixels per art pixel
var pos := Vector2(10, 30)       # where the sprite is, in art pixels

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner
	n = whole_scale(VIEW, screen)

func whole_scale(view: Vector2, room: Vector2) -> int:
	return mini(floori(room.x / view.x), floori(room.y / view.y))

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, screen), Color.BLACK)
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(4, 176), "x%d" % n, 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: 100 x 50 fits a 320 x 180 screen 3 whole times
64 x 36 fits 5 times
the narrower side decides: 2 in a 250-wide window
a game bigger than the screen fits 0 times
_ready() sets n to 3

hints: Across, the answer is floori(room.x / view.x). Down, the same with y. The game has to fit both ways, so return the smaller with mini().
In _ready(): n = whole_scale(VIEW, screen).
steps.explain: The label in the corner now reads x3: 320 / 100 is 3.2 and 180 / 50 is 3.6, and the whole part of the smaller one is 3. This is integer scale mode. Change VIEW to Vector2(64, 36) for a moment and it reads x5, with nothing left over.

steps.title: Centre it
steps.task: At x3 the game is 300 × 150 screen pixels, in a window of 320 × 180. Write view_rect() -> Rect2: the rectangle of the screen the game is drawn in, VIEW * n in size and centred in screen. Then fill it with Color("#7fae72") in _draw(), after the black.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const VIEW := Vector2(100, 50)   # the game's own size, in art pixels
const SPRITE := [
	"..oooo..",
	".oyyyyo.",
	"oyoyyoyo",
	"oyyyyyyo",
	"oyoyyoyo",
	"oyyooyyo",
	".oyyyyo.",
	"..oooo..",
]
const INK := {"o": Color("#3a2b30"), "y": Color("#f2c14e")}

var screen := Vector2(320, 180)  # the window the game has been given
var n := 1                       # screen pixels per art pixel
var pos := Vector2(10, 30)       # where the sprite is, in art pixels

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner
	n = whole_scale(VIEW, screen)

func whole_scale(view: Vector2, room: Vector2) -> int:
	return mini(floori(room.x / view.x), floori(room.y / view.y))

func view_rect() -> Rect2:
	var drawn := VIEW * n
	return Rect2((screen - drawn) / 2.0, drawn)

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, screen), Color.BLACK)
	draw_rect(view_rect(), Color("#7fae72"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(4, 176), "x%d" % n, 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: view_rect() is 300 x 150, starting at (10, 15)
_draw() fills view_rect()
tests.why: Add draw_rect(view_rect(), Color("#7fae72")) after the black rectangle.

hints: The spare room is screen - drawn, where drawn is VIEW * n. Half of it goes on each side, so the top-left corner is (screen - drawn) / 2.0.
return Rect2((screen - drawn) / 2.0, drawn) – a Rect2 can be made from a position and a size.
steps.explain: A green field with a black border ten pixels wide at the sides and fifteen above and below: that is aspect keep with integer scaling, and those bars are the pixels that 3.2 and 3.6 threw away.

steps.title: One art pixel, n screen pixels
steps.task:
Now draw inside it. Write art_rect(x: float, y: float) -> Rect2: the square of screen pixels that art pixel (x, y) of the game covers. Art pixel (0, 0) is the top-left corner of view_rect(), and every art pixel is n across.

Then write draw_sprite(at: Vector2), which walks the rows of SPRITE and draws one art_rect for each letter that INK has a colour for, and call it from _draw() with pos.

tests.label: art pixel (0, 0) is the 3 x 3 square at (10, 15)
art pixel (4, 2) is the 3 x 3 square at (22, 21)
the sprite is drawn one art_rect at a time
tests.why: Inside the two loops: draw_rect(art_rect(at.x + x, at.y + y), INK[row[x]])

hints: art_rect is one line: start at view_rect().position, go Vector2(x, y) * n further, and the size is Vector2(n, n).
Two loops: for y in range(SPRITE.size()):, take var row: String = SPRITE[y], then for x in range(row.length()):. A dot is not in INK, so test with INK.has(row[x]) before drawing.
The square to draw is art_rect(at.x + x, at.y + y) and its colour is INK[row[x]].
steps.explain: A face, eight art pixels across and twenty-four screen pixels wide, every one of its squares the same size. Nothing here ever multiplies by anything but n, and n is an int: that is the whole of integer scaling. Each draw_rect is what Nearest filtering does for one texel.

steps.title: Walk
steps.task: Make the face drift to the right. Add const SPEED := 5.0 (art pixels a second) and a _process(delta) that moves pos.x by SPEED * delta, wraps it with wrapf so it comes back in at -8.0 after leaving at VIEW.x, and asks for a new drawing. Then look hard at the edges of the face while it moves.

tests.label: after 0.625 seconds at 5 a second, pos.x is 13.125
it wraps round and stays between -8 and VIEW.x
asks for a new drawing with queue_redraw()
tests.why: Without it _draw() runs once and the face never moves on screen.

hints: wrapf(value, low, high) brings a value that has passed high back round to low.
pos.x = wrapf(pos.x + SPEED * delta, -8.0, VIEW.x), then queue_redraw() on the next line.
steps.explain: It moves – and it is soft. The outline swells and thins as it goes, and the eyes blur. At five art pixels a second, pos.x is a fraction for almost every frame, so every square of the face is drawn across the boundary between screen pixels. That shimmer is what an unsnapped sprite looks like in a real game too.

steps.title: Snap the drawing
steps.task: Fix the shimmer without touching pos. Write drawn_at() -> Vector2, which returns pos rounded to whole art pixels, and draw the sprite there instead. pos itself must keep its fraction, or the walk will no longer be five art pixels a second.

tests.label: with pos.x at 13.125, drawn_at() is (13, 30)
pos.x itself is still 13.125
at 13.75 it is drawn at (14, 30)
the sprite is drawn at drawn_at()
tests.why: In _draw(): draw_sprite(drawn_at())

hints: A Vector2 rounds both of its numbers at once: pos.round().
In _draw(), change draw_sprite(pos) to draw_sprite(drawn_at()). Leave _process alone.
steps.explain: Crisp again, and now it moves a whole art pixel at a time, five times a second. That step is not a fault: it is how every sprite on a real pixel screen has always moved. To see why the rounding does not go in _process, try it there for a moment – pos.x = roundf(pos.x + SPEED * delta) – and watch the face stop dead.

steps.title: Resize the window
steps.task:
Last, let the window change. Add a list of sizes and a counter:

const WINDOWS := [Vector2(320, 180), Vector2(255, 180), Vector2(200, 120), Vector2(128, 72)]
var which := 0

In _process, when ui_accept has only now been pressed (Space, or the A button), move which on to the next size, going back to the first after the last; set screen to it and work out n again. One of those windows leaves an odd number of pixels spare, so make view_rect() round its corner down with .floor().

tests.label: one press: the window is 255 x 180
and the game drops to x2
centred on a whole pixel: view_rect() starts at (27, 40), not (27.5, 40)
second press, 200 x 120: still x2, bars above and below only
third press, 128 x 72: x1
fourth press: back to 320 x 180 at x3

hints: The press: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):. Going round a list is which = (which + 1) % WINDOWS.size().
Inside that if, after moving which: screen = WINDOWS[which] and n = whole_scale(VIEW, screen).
In view_rect(): ((screen - drawn) / 2.0).floor(). With 55 pixels spare, half is 27.5, and a game that starts on a half pixel is soft all over.
steps.explain: Click the view and press Space. The window shrinks, the game steps down from x3 to x2 to x1, and at every size the face is made of equal squares. That is stretch mode, aspect keep and integer scale mode, in about forty lines – and the same half-pixel trap as a centred sprite, caught by one floor(). What Godot adds is doing it for every node, on the graphics card.

title: A tone you can see
intro: The script is one Node2D in a small game view. The drawing is already written: it samples a function wave() across the screen and joins the dots, then shows a caption. Across the five steps you give it a waveform to draw. Use the arrow keys (or the buttons under the view) in the last two steps.

steps.title: A sine
steps.task: wave(t, kind) should give the height of the wave t whole cycles in, between -1 and 1. Return a sine: sin of TAU times t. The line on the view stops being flat.

tests.label: a quarter of the way round is the peak, 1.0
three quarters is the trough, -1.0
it starts at 0
and repeats every whole cycle

hints: TAU is one full turn in radians, so TAU * t is the angle after t cycles.
return sin(TAU * t)
steps.explain: Three smooth waves across the view: CYCLES is 3.0, so the picture holds three cycles. Change it to 6.0 and the same wave is twice the pitch – frequency is how many cycles fit in a second, or here, in a screen.

steps.title: Four shapes
steps.task: Make wave obey its kind parameter with a match: "sine" as now; "square" is 1.0 in the first half of each cycle and -1.0 in the second (use fposmod(t, 1.0)); "triangle" is asin(sin(TAU * t)) * (2.0 / PI); "saw" climbs from -1 to 1 across the cycle. Any other name should give a sine. Then change shape at the top to try each.

tests.label: square is 1 in the first half
and -1 in the second
and it repeats
a triangle peaks at 0.25 too
but climbs in a straight line: 0.5 at 0.125
a saw is -0.5 a quarter of the way
and starts at -1
an unknown name falls back to a sine
and so does no name at all

hints: A match on kind with a branch for each name, each with its own return, and _: last for the sine.
The square is return 1.0 if fposmod(t, 1.0) < 0.5 else -1.0. The saw is fposmod(t, 1.0) * 2.0 - 1.0.
steps.explain: Edit shape at the top – "sine", "square", "triangle", "saw" – and the picture changes: the same notes, with a different character. A speaker plays the square as buzzy because of the sharp corners. The _: branch is the one that catches any name nobody thought of, and a function with a default parameter keeps working when it is called without one.

steps.title: An envelope
steps.task: Add envelope(x: float) -> float, where x is how far through the sound (0.0 to 1.0): minf(1.0, x / 0.15) times pow(1.0 - x, 2.2). Then in _draw() multiply the wave's height by envelope(x / 320.0), so that the tone swells and fades across the view.

tests.label: it starts silent
and ends silent
at the end of the attack the rise is complete
half way through the attack it is half risen
after the peak it only falls
_draw() uses the envelope
tests.why: Multiply the wave by envelope(x / 320.0) inside the loop.

hints: minf(1.0, x / 0.15) rises to 1 and stays there; pow(1.0 - x, 2.2) falls from 1 to 0.
In _draw(): var env := envelope(x / 320.0) and multiply by env in the line that works out y.
steps.explain: The tone now rises in the first few cycles and fades to nothing by the right edge, with no hard edge at either end: that is the picture of "no click". Change 0.15 and 2.2 in the function and watch it turn from a swell into a pluck.

steps.title: Loudness, in decibels
steps.task: Give the sound a volume in dB. Add var volume_db := 0.0 and gain(db: float) -> float returning pow(10.0, db / 20.0). Make the left and right arrow keys step the volume by 3 dB (move_left down, move_right up) using Input.is_action_just_pressed, never above 0 or below -24. Multiply the height by gain(volume_db) in _draw() and call queue_redraw() when it changes.

tests.label: 0 dB is unchanged
-6 dB is about half
-20 dB is a tenth
a tap on move_left makes it 3 dB quieter
and another, 6 dB
move_right brings it back up by 3
it never goes below -24
and never above 0

hints: In _process: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("move_left"):, then volume_db = maxf(volume_db - 3.0, -24.0) and queue_redraw(). The right one mirrors it with minf.
In _draw(), the height gains a factor: * gain(volume_db).
steps.explain: Click the view and tap the arrow keys. Each press of ← takes 3 dB off, and every second press halves the height of the wave: 6 dB is half, as the table said. Because dB add rather than multiply, the volume stays a plain number you can add to and clamp, and gain turns it back into the multiplier a speaker needs.

steps.title: Pitch, in semitones
steps.task: Add var semitone := 0 and ratio(semitones: int) -> float returning pow(2.0, semitones / 12.0) (use float() – the division is the trap from Chapter D). Make move_up and move_down raise and lower semitone by one, and draw the wave with CYCLES * ratio(semitone) cycles instead of CYCLES. Show the semitone count in the caption.

tests.label: no semitones: the same pitch
twelve semitones: an octave, twice the frequency
minus twelve: half
a fifth is a ratio of about 1.498
a tap on move_up is one semitone up
and move_down takes it back
the wave is drawn at CYCLES * ratio(semitone)
tests.why: That is what makes the picture change with the note.

hints: pow(2.0, float(semitones) / 12.0), and two more ifs in _process for move_up and move_down.
In _draw(), before the loop: var cycles := CYCLES * ratio(semitone), and use cycles where CYCLES was.
steps.explain: Tap ↑ twelve times and the waves are twice as close together, then twelve times down and they are back: an octave up and down. Every key on a keyboard is this one multiplication, and a game that does it with pitch_scale needs a single recording of a note. Together with the shape, envelope and loudness this is the whole tone: the game builds every sound in it from the same four ideas.

title: A layout engine in miniature
intro: The view stands for a window you can resize with ← and → (or the buttons under it) in step 4. A row of four boxes is drawn across it; every box has a minimum width and some are allowed to expand. The drawing is written for you. The sums – where Godot's containers and anchors do theirs – are yours.

steps.title: Every child, its minimum
steps.task: Write widths(total) so it returns an array with each child's "min", in order, ignoring total for now. Loop over KIDS and append. Four boxes appear, packed at the left edge – though not yet in the right places.

tests.label: every child gets its minimum width
one width for each child

hints: Start with var out := [], loop for k in KIDS: and out.append(k["min"]); then return out.
Return after the loop, not inside it.
steps.explain: Nothing is drawn yet, because the boxes need positions too. That comes next. What you wrote is the first half of what any container does: ask every child how small it can be.

steps.title: Put them in a row
steps.task: Write starts(ws): for each width, the x where that child begins. The first is 0, and each next one starts after the one before plus SEP. The row now appears, with its gaps.

tests.label: each child starts after the one before plus the gap
the first child starts at 0
no children, no positions

hints: Keep a running x. For each width: append x, then move it on by that width and SEP.
out.append(x) then x += w + SEP, inside for w in ws:.
steps.explain: Four boxes in a row, 8 pixels apart, and a good deal of unused room on the right. This is a HBoxContainer with no child asking for space: everything is as small as it can be.

steps.title: Share what is left
steps.task: Make widths(total) use total. Work out the leftover: total minus every minimum minus the gaps (there is one fewer gap than children). If it is above zero, share it equally among the children whose "expand" is true and add each one's share to its minimum. If it is not, everyone stays at the minimum.

tests.label: at 320: 124 left over, 62 each to Label and Gap
at 400 they get 102 each
at 196 there is nothing left to share
and below that nobody shrinks past the minimum
the row fills the whole width exactly

hints: The row needs SEP * (KIDS.size() - 1) plus every "min". Count the children with "expand" as you add them up.
Share is (total - needed) / growers, but only when there are growers and total > needed. Then each child's width is its minimum, plus the share if it expands.
steps.explain: The row now fills the view exactly. Orange boxes expand, blue ones keep their size, which is SIZE_EXPAND_FILL against none. You have written what a HBoxContainer does: minimums first, gaps next, the leftover shared among those who asked, and nobody pushed below their minimum.

steps.title: Resize the window
steps.task: Add min_width(), the smallest the row can be: every minimum plus the gaps (196 here). Then in _process(delta) read Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right") and change width by that times 80 times delta, keeping it between min_width() and 320, and call queue_redraw(). Hold the arrow keys and watch the boxes re-flow.

tests.label: the row's minimum width is 196
holding left, the window stops at the row's minimum
holding right, it grows back to 320 and no more
in half a second it narrows by 40
asks for a new drawing with queue_redraw()
tests.why: The boxes only move if _draw() runs again.

hints: min_width() is the first half of widths: SEP * (KIDS.size() - 1) plus every minimum. widths can call it.
width = clampf(width + Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right") * 80.0 * delta, min_width(), 320.0), then queue_redraw().
steps.explain: Click the view and hold ←. The orange boxes shrink first, then stop at their minimum, and the row stops narrowing at 196. It is exactly what you see when you drag the edge of a window onto an interface in a container. The clamp is what a container cannot do without: it never goes below what its children need.

steps.title: A footer on the bottom edge
steps.task: Add anchored(parent: Vector2, anchors: Array, offsets: Array) -> Rect2. anchors is [left, top, right, bottom] (each 0 to 1) and offsets the same in pixels; the rectangle runs from parent * anchor + offset on each side. Then in _draw() draw a bar with anchors [0, 1, 1, 1] and offsets [8, -30, -8, -8] in a parent of Vector2(width, 180): it should hug the bottom and narrow with the row.

tests.label: a bar along the bottom edge of a 320 by 180 parent
in a narrower parent the same anchors give a narrower bar
anchors at the middle keep a 40 by 20 box centred
anchors 0,0,1,1 and no offsets fill the parent
the footer is drawn inside the row's current width
tests.why: Pass Vector2(width, 180) as the parent so that it follows the resize.

hints: Each side is parent.x * anchors[0] + offsets[0] for left, and the same with parent.y and index 1 for top. The size is right minus left, bottom minus top.
In _draw(): draw_rect(anchored(Vector2(width, 180), [0, 1, 1, 1], [8, -30, -8, -8]), Color("#e0808f"))
steps.explain: A pink bar hugs the bottom with an 8-pixel margin either side, and as you narrow the window with ← it narrows too. That is PRESET_BOTTOM_WIDE with margins. Try anchors of [0.5, 1, 0.5, 1] and offsets of [-40, -30, 40, -8] for a button that stays at the bottom centre instead. This is one function and the whole of what anchors and offsets are.

title: A save that still loads
intro: Six steps that end in a pair of functions, to_json() and from_json(), which survive a missing field, a wrong type, a silly number and a save from an older version. The file itself would be two more lines of FileAccess around them.

steps.title: Out as text
steps.task: Write to_json() -> String, which returns state as JSON text. Then make _ready() print what it returns, in place of pass, so you can see the save beside the editor.

tests.label: to_json() returns the state as JSON text
the text has the 10 coins in it
_ready() prints the save

hints: One line in the body: return and a call to JSON.stringify.
return JSON.stringify(state), and in _ready(), print(to_json()).
steps.explain: That line of text is the whole save. Change the 10 in default_state() and watch it change. Notice that the function returns the text and does not write it anywhere: whatever puts it on a disk is a separate, smaller job, and this half can be checked without one.

steps.title: Back in, carefully
steps.task: Now the other direction. Write from_json(text: String) -> Dictionary. It parses the text; if what comes out is not a Dictionary, it returns default_state(); otherwise it returns what it parsed. In _ready(), add a second line that prints what from_json makes of "this is not a save".

tests.expr: from_json("this is not a save") == default_state()
tests.label: text that is not JSON gives the default state
a list is JSON, but not a save: the default state again
a real save is read: 99 coins
_ready() prints what the bad text loaded as

hints: Keep the parsed value in a variable typed Variant: it might be anything, including null.
if typeof(parsed) != TYPE_DICTIONARY: then return default_state(). After that, return parsed.
steps.explain: The second line of output is a new game, which is the right thing to load from rubbish. One question – is it a Dictionary? – catches the empty file, the half-written file and the file that is somebody's shopping list. What it does not catch is a Dictionary with the wrong things in it, and that is the next three steps.

steps.title: Defaults for the gaps
steps.task: A save of {"coins": 99} has no day, and the first thing to ask for one would stop the game. Write sanitize(s: Dictionary) -> Dictionary: start from default_state(), and for each key of the default, take the value from s if s has that key. Keys the default does not have are left behind. Make from_json return the sanitised Dictionary, and print what it makes of '{"coins": 99, "cheat": true}'.

tests.label: a save with no day gets the default day, 1
and keeps its own 99 coins
a key the game does not know is left behind
an empty save loads as the default state
sanitize() can be called with a Dictionary directly
_ready() prints the third load

hints: for key in d: walks the keys of the default. Inside, if s.has(key): copy s[key] into d[key].
In from_json, the last line becomes return sanitize(parsed).
steps.explain: The direction of the copy is the idea. You did not take the file's Dictionary and fill its holes; you took your own and let the file fill in what it could. So the result always has exactly the default's keys – look for cheat in the output – and a field you add to default_state() next month is present in every old save the day you add it.

steps.title: Numbers you can rely on
steps.task:
Look at the third line of output: 99.0 coins, and nothing stops a save saying -5 or "lots". A loop treats every key alike, and they are not alike. Replace the loop for the three numbers with a check each:

  • coins – if the file's value is a number: a whole number, never below 0
  • day – if it is a number and at least 1: a whole number. Anything else keeps the default.
  • volume – if it is a number: kept between 0.0 and 1.0

Keep copying name as it comes for now. A small helper, is_number(v: Variant) -> bool, will save typing the same test three times. Do not copy version at all: whatever the file said, what you hand back is in today's shape.

tests.label: 99 coins come back as the int 99, not 99.0
-5 coins become 0
coins that are not a number keep the default
day 7 comes back as the int 7
day 0 is refused: the default, 1
a day of true is not a number
a volume of 7 is pulled down to 1.0
a volume of -1 is pulled up to 0.0
a volume that is not a number keeps the default
the version handed back is always today's

hints: The helper is one line: return typeof(v) in [TYPE_INT, TYPE_FLOAT]. Give it s.get("coins"), which is null when the key is missing, and null is not a number.
Coins: if is_number(s.get("coins")): then d["coins"] = maxi(0, int(s["coins"])). Volume is the same shape with clampf(s["volume"], 0.0, 1.0) and no int().
Day has two conditions: if is_number(s.get("day")) and s["day"] >= 1:. The order matters – and stops at the first false, so >= is never asked of a String.
steps.explain: Two different answers to a bad number, chosen on purpose. Coins and volume are clamped: there is a nearest sensible value, so use it. The day is refused: day 0 is not nearly day 1, it is a broken file, and the default is the honest result. Deciding which each field gets is the real work of a sanitiser. The typing is the easy part.

steps.title: Text you can rely on
steps.task: The name is shown on screen, so a wrong one is visible. Accept the file's name only if it is a String and has something in it besides spaces; trim the spaces from its ends, and keep at most 16 characters. Anything else keeps the default.

tests.label: a good name is kept
a name that is a number keeps the default
a name of nothing but spaces keeps the default
spaces at the ends are trimmed
a long name is cut to 16 characters

hints: The type test for text is typeof(s.get("name")) == TYPE_STRING.
.strip_edges() removes spaces from both ends, and .substr(0, 16) keeps the first sixteen characters.
if typeof(s.get("name")) == TYPE_STRING and s["name"].strip_edges() != "": then d["name"] = s["name"].strip_edges().substr(0, 16).
steps.explain: Sixteen is not a magic number: it is whatever fits the widest label the name appears in. A sanitiser is where a limit like that belongs, because it is the one place every name passes through on its way in.

steps.title: A save from last year
steps.task: Version 1 of this game kept its money under "gold" and wrote no version number. Write migrate(s: Dictionary) -> Dictionary: work out the save's version (1 when there is no number saying otherwise), and if it is below 2 and there is gold, move it to coins and erase gold. Return s. Then have from_json migrate before it sanitises, and print what it makes of '{"gold": 45, "day": 3, "name": ""}'.

tests.label: an old save's 45 gold loads as 45 coins
and there is no gold left in the result
what comes out is version 2
a version 2 save is not migrated: its coins stay 3
migrate() works on a Dictionary directly
today's save loads back as exactly today's state
_ready() prints the old save, loaded

hints: Start with var v := 1, and replace it with int(s["version"]) only if is_number(s.get("version")).
Inside if v < 2: – if s.has("gold"):, then s["coins"] = s["gold"] and s.erase("gold").
In from_json: return sanitize(migrate(parsed)). Migrate first, so the sanitiser only ever has to know today's names.
steps.explain: Read the last line of output: an old save with the money under the wrong name and an empty name arrives as 45 coins, day 3, and "Wren". Parse, check, migrate, sanitise – four small stages, each of which can only make the data more trustworthy, and none of which touches a disk. To finish it for a real project you would wrap the two ends in the FileAccess functions from earlier: write_save(to_json()) and state = from_json(read_save()).

title: A lighthouse that keeps time
intro: The picture is drawn for you: the starter's _draw() reads seven variables and paints what they say. Nothing moves yet because nothing changes them. In five steps you make each one keep time. The view beside the editor restarts whenever you stop typing.
starter:
extends Node2D

const DAY := 16.0            # real seconds for one day and night
const BLINK := 0.5           # seconds between flips of the lamp
const HORN_COOLDOWN := 2.0   # seconds before the horn can sound again

var clock_t := 0.0     # seconds into the day
var blink_t := 0.0     # seconds since the lamp last flipped
var lamp_on := false
var horn_left := 0.0   # seconds of cooldown still to run
var horns := 0
var echo := false
var speed := 1.0

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	queue_redraw()

func is_night() -> bool:
	return false

func _draw() -> void:
	var night := is_night()
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#1d2440") if night else Color("#9fd3e6"))
	# the sun by day and the moon by night, crossing the sky as the hours pass
	var across := fmod(clock_t, DAY / 2.0) / (DAY / 2.0)
	draw_circle(Vector2(320.0 * across, 34), 9, Color("#e8ecf5") if night else Color("#ffd75e"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 140, 320, 40), Color("#24506a"))     # the sea
	draw_rect(Rect2(152, 62, 16, 78), Color("#f3efe4"))     # the tower
	draw_rect(Rect2(147, 50, 26, 12), Color("#b8432f"))     # the lamp room
	if lamp_on:
		draw_circle(Vector2(160, 56), 5, Color("#ffe98a"))
		if night:
			draw_circle(Vector2(160, 56), 22, Color(1.0, 0.9, 0.4, 0.35))
	if echo:
		draw_arc(Vector2(160, 56), 30, 0, TAU, 32, Color.WHITE, 2)
		draw_arc(Vector2(160, 56), 44, 0, TAU, 32, Color(1, 1, 1, 0.5), 2)
	# the horn's cooldown, as a bar that empties
	draw_rect(Rect2(10, 10, 60.0 * horn_left / HORN_COOLDOWN, 5), Color.WHITE)
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 172), "horn x%d   speed x%d" % [horns, int(speed)], 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

steps.title: A day that comes round
steps.task: Make clock_t count the seconds of the day, and come back to 0 when it reaches DAY so that tomorrow follows today. Then make is_night() true for the second half of the day. Watch the sun: it should cross in eight seconds, and the moon should follow it.

and it is day
ten seconds in, it is night

steps.title: Flash on a beat
steps.task: Make the lamp flash. Each frame, add delta to blink_t. When it reaches BLINK, take BLINK off it – keeping whatever was left over, not setting it to zero – and flip lamp_on. The lamp shows as a small light by day and throws a glow at night.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const DAY := 16.0            # real seconds for one day and night
const BLINK := 0.5           # seconds between flips of the lamp

var clock_t := 0.0     # seconds into the day

tests.label: after 1.5 s of uneven frames the lamp has flipped three times, and is on
half a second later it is off
and half a second after that, on again
blink_t never stays above BLINK

hints: Three lines after the clock: add to blink_t, then if blink_t >= BLINK: with two lines inside.
Inside the if: blink_t -= BLINK and lamp_on = not lamp_on.
If the first check fails and the others pass, you are setting blink_t = 0.0. With frames of uneven length that throws time away, and the lamp falls behind.

steps.title: A horn with a cooldown
steps.task: Give the keeper a foghorn. Each frame, run horn_left down by delta, never below 0. When ui_accept (the space bar) is pressed and horn_left is 0, add one to horns and set horn_left to HORN_COOLDOWN. Click the view and press space: the count at the bottom goes up, the white bar fills and drains, and pressing again too soon does nothing.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const DAY := 16.0            # real seconds for one day and night
const BLINK := 0.5           # seconds between flips of the lamp
const HORN_COOLDOWN := 2.0   # seconds before the horn can sound again

var clock_t := 0.0     # seconds into the day

func _ready() -> void:

tests.label: pressing space sounds the horn: horns is 1
and the cooldown is running
pressing again a second later does nothing
left alone, the cooldown runs out and stops at 0
and then the horn sounds again

hints: The countdown is one line: horn_left = maxf(0.0, horn_left - delta).
The press: if Input.is_action_pressed("ui_accept") and horn_left <= 0.0: – then count the horn and start the cooldown.

steps.title: An echo, with await

extends Node2D

const HORN_COOLDOWN := 2.0   # seconds before the horn can sound again

var lamp_on := false

tests.label: as the horn sounds, echo is true
and the horn was still counted
a quarter of a second later it is still ringing
after half a second it has stopped
waits with await get_tree().create_timer(…).timeout
tests.why: This step is about the one-line timer: await get_tree().create_timer(0.5).timeout

hints: A new function at the left edge: func sound_horn() -> void:. Move horns += 1 into it, and call sound_horn() where that line was.
Its body is four lines: count, echo = true, the wait, echo = false.

steps.title: Wind the day forward
steps.task: Let the keeper hurry the day. Each frame, set speed to 8.0 while ui_right (the right arrow) is held, and to 1.0 otherwise. steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const DAY := 16.0            # real seconds for one day and night
