tests.label: one second with the arrow held moves the day on by eight
let go, and one second is one second again
speed is back to 1.0
the horn's cooldown ignores the speed: a hurried second takes one second off it
and the lamp is still flashing in real time

hints: First line after queue_redraw(): speed = 8.0 if Input.is_action_pressed("ui_right") else 1.0.
Then one change to the clock's line: delta * speed where delta was. Leave the other two deltas alone.
steps.explain: There are now two kinds of time in one small script, and you can see both at once: the sun on game time, the lamp and the white bar on real time. Which clock a thing belongs to is a decision about the game, not about the code – a crop grows in game time, a button's cooldown runs in real time – and here it is one * speed. Set the speed to 0.0 while a key is held and you have a pause that stops the day and nothing else.

title: A Game store, a step at a time
intro: Your script plays the autoload. It will hold a day and some coins, announce each real change, and let a HUD keep up. At the end you can freeze it into text and thaw it again, and the listeners will notice.

steps.title: One door
steps.task: The starter calls change("coins", 5), and there is no such function. Write change(key: String, value) so that it stores the value in state. Everything that changes the state will go through it from now on. Watch the output pane print the dictionary.

tests.label: change("coins", 5) has stored 5
change works for any key
the state is printed

hints: The function takes a String key and a value with no type, so it can store ints and bools alike.
state[key] = value, indented under func change(key: String, value) -> void:.
steps.explain: One line, and one idea: callers do not write state["coins"] = 5 themselves, they ask. That gives you a single place where a change is known about, and a single place to put everything that should happen when one occurs. Little Hours does this in _changed(), which you will see in a moment.

steps.title: Announce it
steps.task: Declare signal state_changed(key: String, value) and emit it from change() after storing. To watch it work, give the script a method _announce(key, value) that prints changed coins to 5 (with the real key and value), keep a count of announcements in var heard := 0, and connect the signal to _announce at the top of _ready().
steps.solution:
extends Node

signal state_changed(key: String, value)

var state := {"day": 1, "coins": 0}
var heard := 0

func change(key: String, value) -> void:
	state[key] = value
	state_changed.emit(key, value)

func _announce(key: String, value) -> void:
	heard += 1
	print("changed ", key, " to ", value)

func _ready() -> void:
	state_changed.connect(_announce)
	change("coins", 5)
	print(state)

tests.label: the announcement is printed
heard counts one announcement
declares the signal state_changed
emits it

hints: The connect line goes first in _ready(), before change is called, or the first change is not heard.
state_changed.emit(key, value) at the end of change; state_changed.connect(_announce) at the start of _ready.
steps.explain: The store now talks, and it does not know who is listening: here it is a method on itself, in the real game it is the HUD. Try moving the connect line below the call to change and watch heard go back to 0. A signal only reaches what is already connected.

steps.title: Only real changes
steps.task: Setting coins to the value it already has is not news. Make change() return early, saying nothing, when state[key] already equals value. The starter script changes coins once; the checks call it again with the same number and with a new one.

tests.label: setting 5 again says nothing: still one announcement
setting 6 is news: two announcements
and 6 again is not
a key that did not exist yet counts as a change

hints: Compare with state.get(key) rather than state[key]: get gives null for a key that is not there yet, and a new key should count as a change.
if state.get(key) == value: then return, before the assignment.
steps.explain: Without that guard a loop that sets coins sixty times a second would announce sixty times a second, and every listener would redraw for nothing. Little Hours has the same worry in its farm code, which writes the save only on the frame a plot actually changes (Chapter T).

steps.title: A listener that reacts
steps.task: Add an inner class Hud extends RefCounted with a var shown := "". Its _init(game) connects game.state_changed to its own method _on_changed(key, value), which sets shown to text like coins: 5. In _ready(), make one with var hud := Hud.new(self) before the first change.

tests.label: the HUD heard the change in _ready
and the next one too
an unchanged value leaves it as it was
prints what the HUD shows

hints: Declare var hud: Hud beside the other variables so that _ready and the checks can both reach it, then assign it in _ready.
Inside Hud: func _init(game) -> void: with game.state_changed.connect(_on_changed); and shown = "%s: %s" % [key, value].
steps.explain: This is the shape of a real HUD: it is handed the store, connects once, and from then on keeps itself up to date. The store never mentions Hud – delete the class and everything above still runs. Add a second listener, a Chime that plays a sound, and the store still does not change.

steps.title: A snapshot to save
steps.task: Write snapshot() -> String, which returns the whole state as a JSON string, and restore(text: String), which reads such a string back and sets every key through change(). Going through the front door matters: the HUD must hear about the restored values.

tests.label: the snapshot is JSON that carries the coins
restore sets the state from text
and the HUD heard it, through change()
text that is not a save changes nothing
_ready saves, changes, restores and prints

hints: JSON.stringify(state) makes the text, and JSON.parse_string(text) reads it back – and returns null if the text is not JSON.
In restore: check typeof(data) == TYPE_DICTIONARY first, then for key in data: and change(key, data[key]).
steps.explain: Now the store is something you could save and load (Chapter S). JSON brings numbers back as floats, which is one reason a real game cleans what it loads. Watch the order in the output: _ready sets coins to 5, takes a snapshot, wrecks the coins, restores, and the state is back. Because restore calls change, any HUD sees each value arrive. A restore that wrote straight into state would leave the display showing 99.

title: A seed shop that runs on a table
intro: Five steps: defaults under every entry, a fallback for an id nobody has heard of, a line of text for the shop, a check for the table, and then a new crop added without writing any code.

steps.title: Defaults underneath
steps.task: The tomato's entry is only a name. Write of(id: String) -> Dictionary, which returns a crop in full: a copy of DEFAULT with the crop's own entry laid over it. Then make _ready() print of("tomato") and look at what the tomato has gained.

tests.label: a tomato keeps its own name
a tomato takes the default 20 seconds
a pumpkin's own price wins over the default
asking about the pumpkin did not change what a carrot costs
DEFAULT itself is untouched: of() works on a copy
_ready() prints the tomato in full

hints: Three moves: var crop: Dictionary = DEFAULT.duplicate(), then a for key in CROPS[id]: loop that copies each value into crop, then return crop.
Inside the loop: crop[key] = CROPS[id][key]. If the carrot's price comes out as 15, you wrote into DEFAULT itself – start from DEFAULT.duplicate().
steps.explain: The printed tomato has a grow time, a price and a season it never mentioned. Order matters: defaults first, the entry second, so the entry wins. And duplicate() matters: without it every lookup would write into the one shared DEFAULT, and the pumpkin's price would leak into every crop asked for after it. In Godot a const dictionary is read-only, so there the mistake is an error instead of a leak.

steps.title: Nobody sells turnips
steps.task: Ask for a crop that is not in the table: add print(of("turnip")) to _ready(). If your of() indexes CROPS[id], the script stops. Make an unknown id safe: it gets the defaults, and its "name" is the id itself, so of("turnip")["name"] is "turnip". Crops that are in the table must keep their real names, and nothing may be added to CROPS.

tests.label: an unknown crop is named after its id
and has the default grow time
a known crop still has its real name
and its own values
the table itself did not gain a turnip

hints: CROPS.get(id, {}) gives the entry, or an empty dictionary when there is none. A loop over an empty dictionary does nothing, so the rest of the function needs no if.
Set crop["name"] = id straight after the duplicate(), before the loop. A real entry's name then overwrites it; a missing entry leaves it.
steps.explain: Showing the id where a name should be is a choice. A blank would hide the mistake and a crash would punish the player for it; turnip in lower case in the middle of a shop reads as exactly what it is, a bug, to whoever sees it first. Decide what "not found" means for each table you write.

steps.title: A line for the shop
steps.task: Write describe(id: String) -> String, which gives one line of the shop's list: Carrot: 15 s to grow, 5 coins. Build it from of(id), so that it works for every crop. Then replace the two prints in _ready() with a loop over CROPS that prints the line for each crop.

tests.label: describe() works for a crop that is not in the table too
_ready() prints a line for every crop in the table
the list is a loop over CROPS, not three prints
tests.why: Loop over the table: for id in CROPS:

hints: A format string does the work: "%s: %d s to grow, %d coins" % [crop["name"], crop["grow"], crop["price"]]. %d writes a float as a whole number.
In _ready(): for id in CROPS: and, under it, print(describe(id)). Looping over a dictionary gives its keys, in the order they were written.
steps.explain: Look for a crop's name in the code you have written. There is none. describe() knows what a crop looks like, not which crops exist, and _ready() asks the table. That is the whole idea of the chapter in two functions.

steps.title: Check the table
steps.task:
Write problems(table: Dictionary) -> Array, which looks at every entry of a table shaped like CROPS and returns a list of sentences, in the table's order:

  • an entry without a "name" gives "leek: no name";
  • then, for each key of the entry that is neither "name" nor a key of DEFAULT, "leek: unknown key grwo".

A table with nothing wrong gives an empty array. After the shop's list, make _ready() print Problems: followed by problems(CROPS).

tests.label: the shop's own table has no problems
an entry with no name is reported
a misspelt key is reported
every problem is listed, not only the first
_ready() prints Problems: and the list

hints: Start with var found: Array = [], loop for id in table:, and return found at the end. Each problem is found.append("%s: no name" % id).
The inner loop: for key in table[id]: then if key != "name" and not DEFAULT.has(key): and append "%s: unknown key %s" % [id, key].
steps.explain: Because problems() takes the table as an argument, it can be tried on tables that are wrong without breaking the real one – which is how the checks beside the editor tested it, and how you would test it yourself (Chapter W). The misspelt key is the one to care about: "grwo": 9.0 does not fail anywhere. The crop just quietly takes twenty seconds.

steps.title: A new crop, no new code
steps.task: The shop is getting sunflowers: called Sunflower, 30 seconds to grow, 12 coins, in any season. Put them on sale. Do not touch a function.

tests.label: a sunflower takes 30 seconds
and costs 12 coins
in any season
the shop lists it
and the table still has no problems

hints: One new line inside CROPS, shaped like the others. The key is "sunflower".
"sunflower": {"name": "Sunflower", "grow": 30.0, "price": 12}, – no season, because "any" is the default.
steps.explain: One line, and the shop sells sunflowers: listed, priced, checked. Now misspell price as prise in your new entry and read the last line of the output. That is the bargain of a table in code – nothing stops the typo, so you write the thing that does.

title: A test runner, and the bug it finds
intro: The script below works out the season from the day number, and somebody says the seasons change on the wrong day. In five steps you build check(), make failures speak, add a report, use them to find and fix the bug, and then teach the runner about floats.
starter:
extends Node

const SEASONS := ["Spring", "Summer", "Autumn", "Winter"]
const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5
const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0

var checks := 0
var fails := 0

# Days count from 1. Days 1 to 5 are Spring, 6 to 10 Summer, and so on;
# after Winter the year starts again.
func season_of(day: int) -> String:
	return SEASONS[(day / DAYS_PER_SEASON) % SEASONS.size()]

# How much of the day has gone, from 0.0 to 1.0.
func day_fraction(clock_t: float) -> float:
	return clock_t / DAY_LENGTH

func _ready() -> void:
	pass

steps.title: One check
steps.task: Write check(what: String, got, want) -> bool. It adds one to checks and returns true when got equals want, false when it does not. Then use it in _ready(): check that season_of(1) is "Spring", and print what check() returns.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const SEASONS := ["Spring", "Summer", "Autumn", "Winter"]
const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5
const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0

var checks := 0
var fails := 0

# Days count from 1. Days 1 to 5 are Spring, 6 to 10 Summer, and so on;
# after Winter the year starts again.
func season_of(day: int) -> String:
	return SEASONS[(day / DAYS_PER_SEASON) % SEASONS.size()]

# How much of the day has gone, from 0.0 to 1.0.
func day_fraction(clock_t: float) -> float:
	return clock_t / DAY_LENGTH

func _ready() -> void:
	print(check("day 1 is Spring", season_of(1), "Spring"))

func check(what: String, got, want) -> bool:
	checks += 1
	return got == want

tests.label: _ready() makes at least one check
check() returns true when got equals want
and false when it does not
every call adds one to checks

hints: The first line is func check(what: String, got, want) -> bool:. got and want have no type on purpose: a check has to compare anything with anything.
Two lines in the body: checks += 1 and return got == want. In _ready(): print(check("day 1 is Spring", season_of(1), "Spring")).
steps.explain: It prints true, so the first day of the year is right. Look at the three arguments, because every check anybody writes has them: what is being claimed, in words; what the code gave; what it should have given. The words are not used yet. They are for the moment a check fails, which is next.

steps.title: Make a failure speak
steps.task:
A bare false is no help in a list of a hundred checks. When a check fails, check() must also add one to fails and print a line of this shape: FAIL probe: got Summer, wanted Spring. A check that passes prints nothing.

Then, in _ready(), stop printing what check() returns, and add a second check: the last day of Spring, day 5, is still "Spring".
steps.solution:
extends Node

const SEASONS := ["Spring", "Summer", "Autumn", "Winter"]
const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5
const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0

var checks := 0
var fails := 0

# Days count from 1. Days 1 to 5 are Spring, 6 to 10 Summer, and so on;
# after Winter the year starts again.
func season_of(day: int) -> String:
	return SEASONS[(day / DAYS_PER_SEASON) % SEASONS.size()]

# How much of the day has gone, from 0.0 to 1.0.
func day_fraction(clock_t: float) -> float:
	return clock_t / DAY_LENGTH

func _ready() -> void:
	check("day 1 is Spring", season_of(1), "Spring")
	check("day 5 is still Spring", season_of(5), "Spring")

func check(what: String, got, want) -> bool:
	checks += 1
	if got == want:
		return true
	fails += 1
	print("FAIL  %s: got %s, wanted %s" % [what, got, want])
	return false

tests.label: _ready() checks day 1 and day 5
a check that passes leaves fails alone
a check that fails adds one to fails
and prints FAIL, what was claimed, what it got and what was wanted
check() still returns true or false

hints: Deal with the good case first and leave: if got == want: then return true. Everything after that is the failure.
The failure is three lines: fails += 1, then print("FAIL %s: got %s, wanted %s" % [what, got, want]), then return false.
steps.explain: Your new check has failed, and look at how much the line tells you: FAIL day 5 is still Spring: got Summer, wanted Spring. Which claim, what happened, what should have. That is a bug report, written by a program. Do not fix anything yet. One failing check is a clue; a few more will show the shape of the bug.

steps.title: A report at the end
steps.task: Write summary(total: int, failed: int) -> String, the last line of a test run. With no failures it reads 5 checks passed; with some, 2 of 5 checks FAILED. Make it the last thing _ready() prints, using the two counters.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const SEASONS := ["Spring", "Summer", "Autumn", "Winter"]
const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5
const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0

var checks := 0
var fails := 0

# Days count from 1. Days 1 to 5 are Spring, 6 to 10 Summer, and so on;
# after Winter the year starts again.
func season_of(day: int) -> String:
	return SEASONS[(day / DAYS_PER_SEASON) % SEASONS.size()]

# How much of the day has gone, from 0.0 to 1.0.
func day_fraction(clock_t: float) -> float:
	return clock_t / DAY_LENGTH

func _ready() -> void:
	check("day 1 is Spring", season_of(1), "Spring")
	check("day 5 is still Spring", season_of(5), "Spring")
	print(summary(checks, fails))

func check(what: String, got, want) -> bool:
	checks += 1
	if got == want:
		return true
	fails += 1
	print("FAIL  %s: got %s, wanted %s" % [what, got, want])
	return false

func summary(total: int, failed: int) -> String:
	if failed == 0:
		return "%d checks passed" % total
	return "%d of %d checks FAILED" % [failed, total]

tests.label: _ready() prints the summary
and it is summary(checks, fails) that is printed
tests.why: End _ready() with print(summary(checks, fails))

hints: An if failed == 0: with one return inside it and another after it. Each is a format string: "%d checks passed" % total.
Two values need an array: "%d of %d checks FAILED" % [failed, total]. The last line of _ready() is print(summary(checks, fails)).
steps.explain: 1 of 2 checks FAILED. The summary is a pure function of two numbers, which is why the page could test it with numbers of its own. The loud word matters too: a person, or a script, can look for FAILED in a thousand lines of output and know the answer. Little Hours' suite ends with these same two sentences.

steps.title: Corner the bug
steps.task: Now use it. Bugs in sums like this live at the edges, so add checks on both sides of each: day 6 is "Summer", day 20 (the last day of the year) is "Winter", and day 21 is "Spring" again. Read the FAIL lines together, find the mistake in season_of(), and fix it. You are done when all five checks pass.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const SEASONS := ["Spring", "Summer", "Autumn", "Winter"]
const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5
const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0

var checks := 0
var fails := 0

# Days count from 1. Days 1 to 5 are Spring, 6 to 10 Summer, and so on;
# after Winter the year starts again.
func season_of(day: int) -> String:
	return SEASONS[((day - 1) / DAYS_PER_SEASON) % SEASONS.size()]

# How much of the day has gone, from 0.0 to 1.0.
func day_fraction(clock_t: float) -> float:
	return clock_t / DAY_LENGTH

func _ready() -> void:
	check("day 1 is Spring", season_of(1), "Spring")
	check("day 5 is still Spring", season_of(5), "Spring")
	check("day 6 is Summer", season_of(6), "Summer")
	check("day 20 is Winter", season_of(20), "Winter")
	check("day 21 is Spring again", season_of(21), "Spring")
	print(summary(checks, fails))

func check(what: String, got, want) -> bool:
	checks += 1
	if got == want:
		return true
	fails += 1
	print("FAIL  %s: got %s, wanted %s" % [what, got, want])
	return false

func summary(total: int, failed: int) -> String:
	if failed == 0:
		return "%d checks passed" % total
	return "%d of %d checks FAILED" % [failed, total]

tests.label: _ready() makes at least five checks
and none of them fails
season_of(5)  →  "Spring" (the last day of Spring)
season_of(20)  →  "Winter" (the last day of the year)
the report says they passed

hints: With the new checks in, two fail: day 5 comes out as Summer and day 20 as Spring. Both are the last day of a season, and both come out as the season after. Every season is starting one day early.
Days count from 1, and the sum treats them as counting from 0. Work it through by hand for day 5: 5 / 5 is 1, which is Summer. What number should be divided instead?
(day - 1) / DAYS_PER_SEASON: day 1 becomes 0, day 5 becomes 4, and 4 / 5 is 0.
steps.explain: An off-by-one, the commonest bug there is, and it hid behind the two checks anybody would write first: day 1 and day 6 were right all along. It took the edges to show it. Now the important part: the five checks stay. Nobody will ever have to think about this bug again, because if a later change brings it back, the last line of the output will say so. That is what a test is for.

steps.title: Nearly equal
steps.task: The other function in the script returns a float. A third of the way through the day, day_fraction(160.0) should be about 0.333. Try it with check() first and read the FAIL line. Then write check_near(what: String, got: float, want: float) -> bool, which counts and reports exactly as check() does but passes when the two are within 0.001 of each other, and use it for that check instead.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const SEASONS := ["Spring", "Summer", "Autumn", "Winter"]
const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5
const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0

var checks := 0
var fails := 0

# Days count from 1. Days 1 to 5 are Spring, 6 to 10 Summer, and so on;
# after Winter the year starts again.
func season_of(day: int) -> String:
	return SEASONS[((day - 1) / DAYS_PER_SEASON) % SEASONS.size()]

# How much of the day has gone, from 0.0 to 1.0.
func day_fraction(clock_t: float) -> float:
	return clock_t / DAY_LENGTH

func _ready() -> void:
	check("day 1 is Spring", season_of(1), "Spring")
	check("day 5 is still Spring", season_of(5), "Spring")
	check("day 6 is Summer", season_of(6), "Summer")
	check("day 20 is Winter", season_of(20), "Winter")
	check("day 21 is Spring again", season_of(21), "Spring")
	check_near("a third of the day has gone", day_fraction(160.0), 0.333)
	print(summary(checks, fails))

func check(what: String, got, want) -> bool:
	checks += 1
	if got == want:
		return true
	fails += 1
	print("FAIL  %s: got %s, wanted %s" % [what, got, want])
	return false

func check_near(what: String, got: float, want: float) -> bool:
	checks += 1
	if absf(got - want) < 0.001:
		return true
	fails += 1
	print("FAIL  %s: got %s, wanted about %s" % [what, got, want])
	return false

func summary(total: int, failed: int) -> String:
	if failed == 0:
		return "%d checks passed" % total
	return "%d of %d checks FAILED" % [failed, total]

tests.label: _ready() now makes at least six checks
and none of them fails
check_near() passes when the two are within 0.001
0.1 + 0.2 is near enough to 0.3
it adds one to checks
and one to fails when the two are further apart
a failure prints FAIL, the claim and what it got

hints: Copy check() and change two things: the types of the parameters, and the test. "Within 0.001" is absf(got - want) < 0.001 – the size of the difference, whichever way round.
If the report still says a check failed, the old check("…", day_fraction(160.0), 0.333) is still in _ready(). Replace it with the check_near version.
steps.explain: The FAIL line you saw said it all: got 0.33333333333333, wanted 0.333. A float is almost never exactly the number you would write down, so == is the wrong question for one; even 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false. Godot has is_equal_approx(a, b) for the same job with a tolerance of its own. You now have a whole test runner: a check, a check for floats, counters and a report. The real one in Little Hours is not much bigger.

title: A release gate, a step at a time
intro: Five steps to a script that decides whether a build may go out. At the end it refuses a release whose version code did not rise, refuses one with the checklist unfinished, and lets a good one through.

steps.title: Take a version apart
steps.task: Write parse_version(text: String) -> Array. It takes a version name such as "2.9.0" and returns its three numbers as ints: [2, 9, 0]. Then, in _ready(), print what it makes of "2.9.0".

tests.label: parse_version("2.9.0") is [2, 9, 0] – numbers, not text
_ready() prints [2, 9, 0]

hints: text.split(".") gives the pieces as text: "2", "9", "0". Each one needs int(…) round it.
Start with var parts := [], loop with for piece in text.split("."):, and parts.append(int(piece)) inside.
steps.explain: The output shows [2, 9, 0] with no quotes round the numbers: they are ints now, and ints compare the way you expect. Had you returned the pieces as they came, it would have printed ["2", "9", "0"] – look for those quotes whenever a comparison surprises you.

steps.title: Which is newer
steps.task: Write is_newer(a: String, b: String) -> bool: true when version a is later than version b. Compare the first numbers; only if they are equal look at the second; only if those are equal, the third. Two equal versions are not newer than each other. Print is_newer("2.10.0", "2.9.0") from _ready().

tests.label: is_newer("2.10.0", "2.9.0") – ten is more than nine
a version is not newer than itself
is_newer("1.12.0", "2.0.0") is false – the first number decides

hints: Parse both, then walk the three positions with for i in 3:. The first position where the numbers differ settles it.
Inside the loop: if pa[i] != pb[i]: return pa[i] > pb[i]. After the loop they were all equal, so return false.
steps.explain: The loop returns at the first difference and never looks further, which is why 3.0.0 beats 2.99.99. Try replacing the body with return a > b and watch the second check fail: that is the text comparison from earlier in the chapter.

steps.title: The gate
steps.task:
Write problems(version: String, code: int) -> Array. It returns a list of reasons this release may not go out, compared with shipped, and an empty list when there are none:

  • if code is not greater than the shipped code: "code 38 did not rise" (with the code you were given)
  • if version is not newer than the shipped version: "version 2.8.15 is not newer" (with the version you were given)

In that order. Print problems("2.9.0", 38) from _ready().

tests.label: a newer version with a higher code has no problems

tests.expect: ["code 7 did not rise", "version 1.0.0 is not newer"]
tests.label: both problems are reported, code first
_ready() prints the problems of 2.9.0 with code 38

hints: Start with var out := [], append a message for each rule that is broken, and return out. The shipped numbers are shipped["code"] and shipped["version"].
if code <= shipped["code"]: out.append("code %d did not rise" % code), then the same shape with not is_newer(version, shipped["version"]) and "version %s is not newer" % version.
steps.explain: The function returns reasons rather than true or false. A gate that only says no leaves you guessing; one that returns a list can be printed, counted and tested, and an empty list still means yes. The same shape – "give me everything that is wrong" – is how the checkers in Chapter Y work.

steps.title: A checklist
steps.task:
Version numbers are not the only thing that must be right. Add a checklist as a dictionary, every item starting as done:

var done := {"tests pass": true, "bundle signed": true, "notes written": true}

Write mark(item: String, ok: bool) -> void, which records an item as done or not. Then make problems() add "not done: " followed by the item for every item that is false, after the version problems. In _ready(), mark "notes written" as false, print problems("2.9.0", 39), and mark it true again.

tests.label: with everything done, a good release still has no problems
mark("bundle signed", false) records it
problems() now reports: not done: bundle signed

tests.expect: ["code 38 did not rise", "not done: bundle signed"]
tests.label: version problems come first, the checklist after
mark("bundle signed", true) clears it
and the release is clean again
_ready() shows the unfinished notes blocking 2.9.0

hints: mark is one line: done[item] = ok.
At the end of problems(), before the return: for item in done: and, inside, if not done[item]: out.append("not done: " + item).
steps.explain: Looping over a dictionary gives its keys in the order they were written, so the report reads in the order of the list. Add a fourth item to done – "played on a phone": false – and the gate starts refusing without another line of code. That is the point of holding the checklist as data.

steps.title: Ship it, or refuse
steps.task:
Write release(version: String, code: int) -> bool. If there are problems it prints REFUSED 2.9.0 (38) (with the version and code it was given), then each problem on its own line after two spaces and a dash, and returns false. If there are none it stores the new version and code in shipped, prints Released 2.9.0 (39) and returns true.

Finish _ready() by trying two releases: release("2.9.0", 38), then release("2.9.0", 39).

tests.label: _ready() shows 2.9.0 (38) refused with its reason, then 2.9.0 (39) released
shipped now holds 2.9.0 and 39
releasing the same build a second time is refused
a refused release changes nothing
after releasing 2.9.1 (40), that is what shipped holds

hints: Ask problems(version, code) once and keep the answer in a variable. If it is not empty: print the heading, loop over it printing " - " and each problem, and return false.
The heading is print("REFUSED %s (%d)" % [version, code]). On the happy path: shipped = {"version": version, "code": code}, the Released line, return true.
steps.explain: Read the output from the top: one build refused for its code, one released. The gate updates shipped only on success, so the second release of the same build is refused by the very rule that let the first through – the behaviour of a real store, in a dozen lines. The script Little Hours releases with, described next, is this idea with a real export in the middle.

title: A room checker, a step at a time
intro: Five steps to a tool that validates a table of rooms: impossible sizes, exits to rooms that do not exist, doors you cannot come back through, rooms nobody can reach – and a report with an exit code at the end. ROOMS has one of each mistake in it; GOOD has none.

steps.title: Impossible sizes
steps.task: problems(rooms) returns a list of messages and so far finds nothing. Make it look at every room in the table and, for any whose "w" or "h" is zero or less, add the room's id followed by : size must be positive – for example garden: size must be positive.

tests.label: the garden, 12 by 0, is reported
the hall, 8 by 6, is not
a width below zero counts too
the GOOD table has no problems
the output names the garden

hints: Looping over a dictionary gives its keys: for id in rooms:, and then rooms[id] is that room's own dictionary.
Inside the loop: if rooms[id]["w"] <= 0 or rooms[id]["h"] <= 0: and out.append("%s: size must be positive" % id).
steps.explain: One line of output, and it names the room. Every message a checker writes should start with where, because the person reading it is about to go there. Give the shed a width of 0 in ROOMS and it joins the list without the code changing.

steps.title: Doors to nowhere
steps.task:
Each room's "exits" is a small dictionary from a direction to the id of the room it leads to. Inside your loop, check every exit: if the room it names is not in the table, add a message in this form:

hall: exit up leads to attic, which is not a room

tests.expr: problems(ROOMS).has("hall: exit up leads to attic, which is not a room")
tests.label: the hall's exit to the attic is reported

tests.expr: problems(ROOMS).has("hall: exit east leads to kitchen, which is not a room")
tests.label: its exit to the kitchen is not
the garden's size is still reported
the GOOD table still has no problems
the output mentions the attic

hints: A second loop inside the first: for way in room["exits"]: gives each direction, and room["exits"][way] is the id it leads to. rooms.has(…) says whether that id is in the table.
The message has three blanks, so the format takes an array: "%s: exit %s leads to %s, which is not a room" % [id, way, to].
steps.explain: This is the commonest mistake in any table that refers to itself: a name typed slightly wrong, or a room deleted while a door still points at it. The game would only find it when a player walked through that door. Notice the checker reports the garden and the attic – all the problems, not the first.

steps.title: No way back
steps.task:
If you can walk from the kitchen to the garden, you should be able to walk back. For each exit that does lead to a real room, check that the other room has some exit leading back to this one. If it has none, report it with the room you started in first:

kitchen: no way back from garden

An exit to a room that does not exist already has its own message and should not get this one as well.

tests.expr: problems(ROOMS).has("kitchen: no way back from garden")
tests.label: kitchen to garden is one-way, and reported

tests.expr: problems(ROOMS).has("shed: no way back from garden")
tests.label: so is shed to garden

tests.expr: problems(ROOMS).has("hall: no way back from kitchen")
tests.label: hall to kitchen has a way back and is not reported

tests.expr: problems(ROOMS).has("hall: no way back from attic")
tests.label: the missing attic gets only its own message
the GOOD table still has no problems
the output shows a one-way door

hints: Add an elif to the check from the last step, so it only runs when the other room exists. The other room's exits are rooms[to]["exits"].
A dictionary's .values() is the list of things it leads to, so the test is elif not rooms[to]["exits"].values().has(id):.
steps.explain: The elif matters twice. It stops one mistake producing two messages, and it stops the checker itself falling over: rooms["attic"] does not exist, and asking for its exits would be an error. A checker runs on data that is wrong by definition, so it has to be more careful than the game.

steps.title: Rooms nobody can reach
steps.task:
The shed has a door out, but no room has a door in. Write reachable(rooms, start) -> Array: the ids of every room you can get to by walking through exits from start, including start itself. Ignore exits to rooms that do not exist.

Then, at the end of problems(), after the loop, add a message for each room that is not reachable from START:

shed: cannot be reached from hall

tests.label: three rooms can be reached from the hall
the garden is one of them, by way of the kitchen
the shed is not
from the shed you can reach the shed and the garden
two rooms that lead to each other do not send it round for ever

tests.expr: problems(ROOMS).has("shed: cannot be reached from hall")
tests.label: problems() reports the shed
ROOMS now has five problems in all
the GOOD table still has no problems

hints: Keep two lists: seen, every room found so far, and todo, rooms whose exits you have not looked at yet. Both start as [start]. While todo is not empty, take one room off it and look at its exits.
For each exit of that room: if the room it leads to is in the table and not in seen, append it to both lists. todo.pop_back() takes the last room off the list. When the loop ends, return seen.
steps.explain: This "flood fill" is one of the most useful dozen lines in games: it is also how you find every tile a character can walk to, or every square a spilled colour should fill. The seen list is what keeps it from walking hall, kitchen, hall, kitchen for ever. Give the garden an exit "east": "shed" and count the problems again.

steps.title: A report and an exit code
steps.task:
Make it a tool another program could run. Write report(rooms) -> int. It prints each problem on its own line after two spaces, then a summary:

  • with problems: 5 problems in 4 rooms, and it returns 1
  • with none: 2 rooms, no problems, and it returns 0

Then change _ready() to call report(ROOMS) in place of its loop.

output: shed: cannot be reached from hall
tests.label: _ready() prints the problems, indented, and then: 5 problems in 4 rooms
report(ROOMS) returns 1
report(GOOD) returns 0
a clean table gets the line: 2 rooms, no problems
tests.why: When nothing is wrong, print the number of rooms and " rooms, no problems".

tests.label: problems() itself is unchanged

hints: Ask problems(rooms) once and keep the list. Print each line with print(" ", line). rooms.size() is the number of rooms.
After the loop: if the list is empty, print the clean summary and return 0; otherwise print found.size(), " problems in ", rooms.size(), " rooms" and return 1.
steps.explain: Change _ready() to report(GOOD) to see the other summary. The return value is the exit code from earlier in the chapter: in a --script tool the last line would be quit(report(rooms)), and a release script would refuse to continue on a 1. You have written, in about forty lines, a tool that makes a whole class of bug impossible to ship.

title: Catch the lanterns: a whole game
intro: Click the game view and use the arrow keys (or A and D); on a phone, the buttons under it. Catch five lanterns before the twenty seconds run out. You will build the whole thing in six small steps – a clock, a player, a falling thing, a rule, a result and a restart – and every part of it is something an earlier chapter taught.

steps.title: A clock that stops
steps.task: The bar along the top is the time left, drawn from time_left, which starts at TIME. At the moment nothing changes it. In _process, take delta off it every frame, but never let it go below zero, and ask for a redraw so the bar shrinks. Remember that _draw runs once and then only when asked.

tests.label: after two seconds, 18 are left
far past twenty seconds it rests at 0, not below

hints: time_left has to fall by exactly the time the frame took. That is delta.
time_left = maxf(0.0, time_left - delta) and then queue_redraw().
steps.explain: The bar runs down smoothly and stops at the left edge. Like the clock in Chapter T, it is seconds added up from delta, never frames counted, so it takes twenty seconds on every screen. maxf(0.0, …) is what stops it overshooting. Everything that follows is this one number, time_left, plus other numbers beside it: that is what state is.

steps.title: Move with input
steps.task: Add a player. Declare const SPEED := 120.0 and var player_x := 160.0, and move player_x by the horizontal axis of the move_left and move_right actions times SPEED and delta. Keep it between 8 and 312 so the player cannot leave the screen, and draw it as a 16 by 12 rectangle with its top at y = 148. Click the view and use the arrow keys.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const TIME := 20.0
const SPEED := 120.0

var time_left := TIME
var player_x := 160.0

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	time_left = maxf(0.0, time_left - delta)
	var dir := Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right")
	player_x = clampf(player_x + dir * SPEED * delta, 8.0, 312.0)
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(10, 10, 300.0 * time_left / TIME, 6), Color("#f2a65a"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(player_x - 8, 148, 16, 12), Color("#7fc8a9"))

tests.label: holding right for a second moves it 120 pixels
it stops at the right edge
and at the left edge

hints: Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right") is -1, 0 or 1, as in Chapter K. Multiply by SPEED and by delta.
player_x = clampf(player_x + dir * SPEED * delta, 8.0, 312.0), and a draw_rect in _draw with player_x - 8 as its left.
steps.explain: Input changes state, and the picture follows. The drawing code never moves the player; it only reads player_x. Keeping those two jobs apart is the habit this whole chapter is about, and it is what lets you test the movement without looking at it, as the checks beside the steps do.

steps.title: Lanterns fall
steps.task: Lanterns drift down from the top, one at a time. Put where each one starts in a table: const DROPS := [40.0, 200.0, 120.0, 280.0, 80.0]. Keep var drop := 0 (which entry is falling) and var lantern := Vector2(DROPS[0], 0.0). Every frame move lantern.y down by FALL (60 a second) times delta; when it reaches GROUND (160), call a new function next_lantern() that moves on to the next entry, wrapping to the first after the last, and puts the lantern back at the top. Draw it as a circle.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const TIME := 20.0
const SPEED := 120.0
const FALL := 60.0
const GROUND := 160.0
const DROPS := [40.0, 200.0, 120.0, 280.0, 80.0]

var time_left := TIME
var player_x := 160.0
var drop := 0
var lantern := Vector2(DROPS[0], 0.0)

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	time_left = maxf(0.0, time_left - delta)
	var dir := Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right")
	player_x = clampf(player_x + dir * SPEED * delta, 8.0, 312.0)
	lantern.y += FALL * delta
	if lantern.y >= GROUND:
		next_lantern()
	queue_redraw()

func next_lantern() -> void:
	drop = (drop + 1) % DROPS.size()
	lantern = Vector2(DROPS[drop], 0.0)

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(10, 10, 300.0 * time_left / TIME, 6), Color("#f2a65a"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(player_x - 8, 148, 16, 12), Color("#7fc8a9"))
	draw_circle(lantern, 5.0, Color("#ffd166"))

tests.label: after a second it has fallen 60 pixels
after three seconds it is the second lantern
which has only just started to fall

hints: Declare FALL and GROUND as constants. lantern.y += FALL * delta moves it, and if lantern.y >= GROUND: notices it has landed.
drop = (drop + 1) % DROPS.size() wraps round; then lantern = Vector2(DROPS[drop], 0.0).
steps.explain: The level is a table. The code never says "40, then 200": it says "the next entry", so a longer or different table is a different game with no new code. That is the data-tables habit, and it is what Chapter V builds up into resources. The % makes the list a ring. Notice the lantern lands at x = 40 on the left while you stand in the middle: nothing happens when it lands. That is next.

steps.title: Catch one
steps.task: When a lantern lands, it is caught if it is within CATCH (16) pixels of player_x. Count catches in var caught := 0, by way of a function catch_lantern() that adds one. Whatever happens, the lantern then moves on with next_lantern(). Show the count with draw_string.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const TIME := 20.0
const SPEED := 120.0
const FALL := 60.0
const GROUND := 160.0
const CATCH := 16.0
const DROPS := [40.0, 200.0, 120.0, 280.0, 80.0]

var time_left := TIME
var player_x := 160.0
var caught := 0
var drop := 0
var lantern := Vector2(DROPS[0], 0.0)

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	time_left = maxf(0.0, time_left - delta)
	var dir := Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right")
	player_x = clampf(player_x + dir * SPEED * delta, 8.0, 312.0)
	lantern.y += FALL * delta
	if lantern.y >= GROUND:
		if absf(lantern.x - player_x) <= CATCH:
			catch_lantern()
		next_lantern()
	queue_redraw()

func catch_lantern() -> void:
	caught += 1

func next_lantern() -> void:
	drop = (drop + 1) % DROPS.size()
	lantern = Vector2(DROPS[drop], 0.0)

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(10, 10, 300.0 * time_left / TIME, 6), Color("#f2a65a"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(player_x - 8, 148, 16, 12), Color("#7fc8a9"))
	draw_circle(lantern, 5.0, Color("#ffd166"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 32), "Caught " + str(caught), HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: a lantern still in the air has not been caught
a lantern landing on the player is caught
the next one lands out of reach and is missed

hints: absf(lantern.x - player_x) <= CATCH is "close enough". Check it inside the if that notices the landing, before next_lantern().
if absf(lantern.x - player_x) <= CATCH: then catch_lantern(). The function itself is one line: caught += 1.
steps.explain: Walk left a little under a second to meet the first lantern at x = 40 and the counter ticks to 1. The rule lives in a function of its own, catch_lantern(), rather than as a bare caught += 1 in the middle of _process, because the next step will want to hang a consequence on it. A name for each thing that happens is what keeps a loop readable once it has ten of them.

steps.title: Win or lose
steps.task: Give the game a result. Add const GOAL := 5 and var phase := "playing" (the other values are "won" and "lost"). Catching GOAL lanterns while playing sets "won"; time_left reaching 0 while playing sets "lost". When the phase is not "playing", _process should do nothing but redraw: the world freezes. Change what is drawn so the text says who won.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const TIME := 20.0
const SPEED := 120.0
const FALL := 60.0
const GROUND := 160.0
const CATCH := 16.0
const GOAL := 5
const DROPS := [40.0, 200.0, 120.0, 280.0, 80.0]

var phase := "playing"      # "playing", "won" or "lost"
var time_left := TIME
var player_x := 160.0
var caught := 0
var drop := 0
var lantern := Vector2(DROPS[0], 0.0)

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if phase != "playing":
		queue_redraw()
		return
	time_left = maxf(0.0, time_left - delta)
	var dir := Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right")
	player_x = clampf(player_x + dir * SPEED * delta, 8.0, 312.0)
	lantern.y += FALL * delta
	if lantern.y >= GROUND:
		if absf(lantern.x - player_x) <= CATCH:
			catch_lantern()
		next_lantern()
	if time_left <= 0.0 and phase == "playing":
		phase = "lost"
	queue_redraw()

func catch_lantern() -> void:
	caught += 1
	if caught >= GOAL and phase == "playing":
		phase = "won"

func next_lantern() -> void:
	drop = (drop + 1) % DROPS.size()
	lantern = Vector2(DROPS[drop], 0.0)

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(10, 10, 300.0 * time_left / TIME, 6), Color("#f2a65a"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(player_x - 8, 148, 16, 12), Color("#7fc8a9"))
	draw_circle(lantern, 5.0, Color("#ffd166"))
	var text := "Caught %d of %d" % [caught, GOAL]
	if phase == "won":
		text = "You caught them all!"
	elif phase == "lost":
		text = "Time is up."
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 32), text, HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: with no one catching anything, time runs out and the phase is lost
and the frozen game catches nothing more
once lost, even five catches cannot make it won

hints: Put if phase != "playing": at the top of _process, with queue_redraw() and return inside it.
In catch_lantern: if caught >= GOAL and phase == "playing": then phase = "won". After the clock: if time_left <= 0.0 and phase == "playing": then phase = "lost".
steps.explain: A phase string is the smallest state machine there is, and the early return is the pause button of the whole game: when the phase is not playing, nothing moves. That is exactly how Little Hours stops its clock at nightfall. The phase == "playing" checks are what make a result final; try taking one away and let the clock run out after you have won, and watch the win turn into a loss.

steps.title: Play again
steps.task: A game with no way back is a demo. Write restart(), which puts every piece of state back as it started – phase, time, player, count and the lantern sequence – and call it from _process when the game is over and ui_accept (Space, or the round button under the view) has just been pressed.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const TIME := 20.0
const SPEED := 120.0
const FALL := 60.0
const GROUND := 160.0
const CATCH := 16.0
const GOAL := 5
const DROPS := [40.0, 200.0, 120.0, 280.0, 80.0]

var phase := "playing"      # "playing", "won" or "lost"
var time_left := TIME
var player_x := 160.0
var caught := 0
var drop := 0
var lantern := Vector2(DROPS[0], 0.0)

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if phase != "playing":
		if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):
			restart()
		queue_redraw()
		return
	time_left = maxf(0.0, time_left - delta)
	var dir := Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right")
	player_x = clampf(player_x + dir * SPEED * delta, 8.0, 312.0)
	lantern.y += FALL * delta
	if lantern.y >= GROUND:
		if absf(lantern.x - player_x) <= CATCH:
			catch_lantern()
		next_lantern()
	if time_left <= 0.0 and phase == "playing":
		phase = "lost"
	queue_redraw()

func restart() -> void:
	phase = "playing"
	time_left = TIME
	player_x = 160.0
	caught = 0
	drop = 0
	lantern = Vector2(DROPS[0], 0.0)

func catch_lantern() -> void:
	caught += 1
	if caught >= GOAL and phase == "playing":
		phase = "won"

func next_lantern() -> void:
	drop = (drop + 1) % DROPS.size()
	lantern = Vector2(DROPS[drop], 0.0)

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(10, 10, 300.0 * time_left / TIME, 6), Color("#f2a65a"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(player_x - 8, 148, 16, 12), Color("#7fc8a9"))
	draw_circle(lantern, 5.0, Color("#ffd166"))
	var text := "Caught %d of %d" % [caught, GOAL]
	if phase == "won":
		text = "You caught them all! Press Space."
	elif phase == "lost":
		text = "Time is up. Press Space."
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 32), text, HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: first the game is lost
pressing accept starts a fresh game: playing, nothing caught, time back near 20
and a new game can be won
and restarted again

hints: restart() should set every variable that changes while playing back to the value it was declared with.
In the not-playing branch of _process: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"): then restart().
steps.explain: A complete little game: state in variables, a clock, input, a table of data, a rule, a result and a way to go again. Play it. Then notice how few kinds of thing there are, and that they are the five habits of this chapter's first section. restart() is also the honest list of your state: if you forget to reset something, the second game plays differently from the first, which is how you find out what you forgot to write down. Little Hours has the same function on a grander scale, which is what a "new game" really does.

title: Build a dog that follows
intro: A room seen from above at a quarter of its size, with the game's own speeds and distances. The blue dot is you – click the view and walk with the arrow keys. The brown dot is the dog, and by the end it will walk at your heel, run when it is left behind, and chase a ball.
starter:
extends Node2D

# The game's own numbers, in world pixels. The view shows a room
# 1280 wide and 720 tall at a quarter of its size.
const ZOOM := 0.25
const SPEED := 280.0        # how fast you walk
const HEEL_BACK := 120.0    # how far behind you the dog wants to be
const DOG_WALK := 200.0     # the dog's own walking pace
const CATCH_UP := 330.0     # the dog's run: faster than you
const RUN_BEHIND := 150.0   # further from its spot than this, it runs
const KEEP_UP := 1.12       # walking with you: your pace and a bit

var you := Vector2(300, 360)
var lead_dir := Vector2.RIGHT     # the way you last walked
var lead_speed := 0.0             # how fast you are going now
var dog := Vector2(900, 600)
var target := Vector2(900, 600)   # where the dog is heading: the ring
var running := false

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	var move := Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down")
	you += move * SPEED * delta
	you = you.clamp(Vector2(20, 20), Vector2(1260, 700))
	lead_speed = move.length() * SPEED
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#d9c7a8"))
	draw_arc(target * ZOOM, 5, 0, TAU, 16, Color("#8a7a5c"), 1)
	draw_circle(dog * ZOOM, 5, Color("#e9a23b") if running else Color("#7a4322"))
	draw_circle(you * ZOOM, 6, Color("#3d5a80"))

steps.title: Find the heel spot
steps.task: The dog needs somewhere to want to be. Keep lead_dir up to date: whenever you are moving, it becomes the direction of move, with length one. Write heel() -> Vector2, the point HEEL_BACK pixels behind you along that direction. Then, every frame, make the dog's target the heel spot. Walk about: the ring should trail behind you, and stay behind when you turn.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

# The game's own numbers, in world pixels. The view shows a room
# 1280 wide and 720 tall at a quarter of its size.
const ZOOM := 0.25
const SPEED := 280.0        # how fast you walk
const HEEL_BACK := 120.0    # how far behind you the dog wants to be
const DOG_WALK := 200.0     # the dog's own walking pace
const CATCH_UP := 330.0     # the dog's run: faster than you
const RUN_BEHIND := 150.0   # further from its spot than this, it runs
const KEEP_UP := 1.12       # walking with you: your pace and a bit

var you := Vector2(300, 360)
var lead_dir := Vector2.RIGHT     # the way you last walked
var lead_speed := 0.0             # how fast you are going now
var dog := Vector2(900, 600)

Try adding that to heel().

steps.title: Walk to it
steps.task: Now move the dog. Every frame, after the target is set, step dog towards target at DOG_WALK pixels a second – no further than the target itself, so it arrives and stops and does not jitter back and forth across it.

dog = dog.move_toward(target, DOG_WALK * delta), on the line before queue_redraw().
steps.explain: The dog crosses the room and sits on the ring. Now walk away from it in a straight line and watch the gap grow: 200 against your 280. The game's dog once walked at 130, which its comment calls "a dog on a lead being dragged"; 200 is better and still not enough. The game's own walking does the same thing by hand – to.normalized() * minf(speed * delta, to.length()) – because it also has furniture to slide along.

steps.title: Run when left behind
steps.task: Give it a second gear. Each frame, set running to whether the dog is more than RUN_BEHIND pixels from its target, and move it at CATCH_UP when it is running and DOG_WALK when it is not. The dog turns amber while it runs.

extends Node2D

# The game's own numbers, in world pixels. The view shows a room
# 1280 wide and 720 tall at a quarter of its size.
const ZOOM := 0.25
const SPEED := 280.0        # how fast you walk
const HEEL_BACK := 120.0    # how far behind you the dog wants to be
const DOG_WALK := 200.0     # the dog's own walking pace
const CATCH_UP := 330.0     # the dog's run: faster than you
const RUN_BEHIND := 150.0   # further from its spot than this, it runs
const KEEP_UP := 1.12       # walking with you: your pace and a bit

var you := Vector2(300, 360)
var lead_dir := Vector2.RIGHT     # the way you last walked
var lead_speed := 0.0             # how fast you are going now
var dog := Vector2(900, 600)
var target := Vector2(900, 600)   # where the dog is heading: the ring

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func heel() -> Vector2:

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
