tests.label: starting far from its spot, the dog is running
and has covered 33 pixels in a tenth of a second: CATCH_UP
once it has arrived it is not running
and it is at your heel

hints: dog.distance_to(target) is how far it has to go. Comparing that with RUN_BEHIND gives a bool you can store straight into running.
Pick the speed in one line: var speed := CATCH_UP if running else DOG_WALK, and use speed * delta in move_toward.
steps.explain: It hurries across the room and drops to a walk for the last stretch. Walk in a long straight line, though, and watch the colour: brown, amber, brown, amber. It falls behind at a walk, sprints, catches up, and falls behind again. The game's comment describes exactly this – "walk, fall behind, run, walk" – and says it "read as a slow dog with a fast setting". Two speeds are not enough for walking with somebody.

steps.title: Keep pace
steps.task: Move the choice of speed into its own function, speed_now() -> float, and use it in _process. Running, it returns CATCH_UP. Otherwise it starts from DOG_WALK – but if you are going faster than DOG_WALK / KEEP_UP, the dog walks at your speed (lead_speed) times KEEP_UP instead, and never faster than CATCH_UP.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

# The game's own numbers, in world pixels. The view shows a room
# 1280 wide and 720 tall at a quarter of its size.
const ZOOM := 0.25
const SPEED := 280.0        # how fast you walk
const HEEL_BACK := 120.0    # how far behind you the dog wants to be
const DOG_WALK := 200.0     # the dog's own walking pace
const CATCH_UP := 330.0     # the dog's run: faster than you
const RUN_BEHIND := 150.0   # further from its spot than this, it runs
const KEEP_UP := 1.12       # walking with you: your pace and a bit

var you := Vector2(300, 360)
var lead_dir := Vector2.RIGHT     # the way you last walked
var lead_speed := 0.0             # how fast you are going now
var dog := Vector2(900, 600)
var target := Vector2(900, 600)   # where the dog is heading: the ring
var running := false

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func heel() -> Vector2:
	return you - lead_dir * HEEL_BACK

func speed_now() -> float:
	if running:
		return CATCH_UP
	var speed := DOG_WALK
	if lead_speed > speed / KEEP_UP:
		speed = minf(lead_speed * KEEP_UP, CATCH_UP)
	return speed

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	var move := Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down")
	you += move * SPEED * delta
	you = you.clamp(Vector2(20, 20), Vector2(1260, 700))
	lead_speed = move.length() * SPEED
	if move != Vector2.ZERO:
		lead_dir = move.normalized()
	target = heel()
	running = dog.distance_to(target) > RUN_BEHIND
	dog = dog.move_toward(target, speed_now() * delta)
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#d9c7a8"))
	draw_arc(target * ZOOM, 5, 0, TAU, 16, Color("#8a7a5c"), 1)
	draw_circle(dog * ZOOM, 5, Color("#e9a23b") if running else Color("#7a4322"))
	draw_circle(you * ZOOM, 6, Color("#3d5a80"))

tests.label: while you stand still, the dog's pace is DOG_WALK
after two seconds of walking, the dog is still at your heel
walking with you, its pace is yours times KEEP_UP: 313.6
and it did not need to run

hints: Deal with running first: if running: then return CATCH_UP. The rest of the function is about walking.
Start with var speed := DOG_WALK. Then if lead_speed > speed / KEEP_UP: replace it with minf(lead_speed * KEEP_UP, CATCH_UP), and return speed.
In _process, the two lines that chose and used speed become one: dog = dog.move_toward(target, speed_now() * delta).
steps.explain: Walk the length of the room: the dog stays on the ring and stays brown. This is the game's _speed_now() with its lookups written out. Turn sharply and the ring jumps 240 pixels to your other side, further than RUN_BEHIND, so the dog still runs when it really has been left behind. Change KEEP_UP to 1.0 and it will hold whatever gap it has without ever closing it; that extra 12% is what makes it catch up.

steps.title: Throw the ball
steps.task: Add var mode := "follow", and only aim at the heel and decide about running while the mode is "follow". Then write fetch(): it sets the mode to "wander", puts target at a random spot at least 60 pixels in from the walls of the 1280 × 720 room, sets running to true, and 3.4 seconds later puts the mode back to "follow". Call it when ui_accept (Space) has just been pressed.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

# The game's own numbers, in world pixels. The view shows a room
# 1280 wide and 720 tall at a quarter of its size.
const ZOOM := 0.25
const SPEED := 280.0        # how fast you walk
const HEEL_BACK := 120.0    # how far behind you the dog wants to be
const DOG_WALK := 200.0     # the dog's own walking pace
const CATCH_UP := 330.0     # the dog's run: faster than you
const RUN_BEHIND := 150.0   # further from its spot than this, it runs
const KEEP_UP := 1.12       # walking with you: your pace and a bit

var you := Vector2(300, 360)
var lead_dir := Vector2.RIGHT     # the way you last walked
var lead_speed := 0.0             # how fast you are going now
var dog := Vector2(900, 600)
var target := Vector2(900, 600)   # where the dog is heading: the ring
var running := false
var mode := "follow"

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func heel() -> Vector2:
	return you - lead_dir * HEEL_BACK

func speed_now() -> float:
	if running:
		return CATCH_UP
	var speed := DOG_WALK
	if lead_speed > speed / KEEP_UP:
		speed = minf(lead_speed * KEEP_UP, CATCH_UP)
	return speed

func fetch() -> void:
	mode = "wander"
	target = Vector2(randf_range(60, 1220), randf_range(60, 660))
	running = true
	get_tree().create_timer(3.4).timeout.connect(func() -> void: mode = "follow")

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	var move := Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down")
	you += move * SPEED * delta
	you = you.clamp(Vector2(20, 20), Vector2(1260, 700))
	lead_speed = move.length() * SPEED
	if move != Vector2.ZERO:
		lead_dir = move.normalized()
	if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):
		fetch()
	if mode == "follow":
		target = heel()
		running = dog.distance_to(target) > RUN_BEHIND
	dog = dog.move_toward(target, speed_now() * delta)
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#d9c7a8"))
	draw_arc(target * ZOOM, 5, 0, TAU, 16, Color("#8a7a5c"), 1)
	draw_circle(dog * ZOOM, 5, Color("#e9a23b") if running else Color("#7a4322"))
	draw_circle(you * ZOOM, 6, Color("#3d5a80"))

tests.label: to begin with the dog is following
Space throws the ball: the mode is "wander"
and the dog is running

tests.expr: target.x >= 60.0 and target.x <= 1220.0 and target.y >= 60.0 and target.y <= 660.0
tests.label: towards a spot at least 60 pixels in from the walls
two seconds later it is still off after the ball
after 3.4 seconds it is following again
and comes back to your heel

hints: Wrap the two lines that set target and running in if mode == "follow":. The move_toward line stays outside it – the dog always walks to its target, whoever chose it.
A random spot: Vector2(randf_range(60, 1220), randf_range(60, 660)). Check the key in _process with if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):.
The game's way to come back: get_tree().create_timer(3.4).timeout.connect(func() -> void: mode = "follow"). A countdown variable you subtract delta from works as well.
steps.explain: Press Space and the ring jumps somewhere, the dog tears after it, waits there, and then remembers you. Notice what you did not write: any code for moving the dog to the ball. It already walks to target; fetching only changed who sets the target. That is the whole design of Pet.gd – a treat, a brushing, the zoomies and the cat bringing you a present are each a mode, a spot and a speed.

title: Build the start of a life
intro: The questions, the answer they add up to, the save they are written into and the numbers they change – with the game's own names and values. Each step prints something new in the output beside the editor.

steps.title: Keep each answer
steps.task: Write pick_answer(step_id: String, key: String), which records in picks the answer a question got, under that question's id. Write tally() -> Dictionary, which counts from picks how many times each manner was chosen. In _ready(), answer five questions – "q0" bold, "q1" banter, "q2" bold, "q3" steady, "q4" banter – then go back and change "q2" to banter, and print tally().

tests.label: five questions have an answer, though one was answered twice
tally() counts banter three times
the first answer to q2 is no longer counted: bold once
steady once
now change q0 from bold to romantic
nobody is bold any more

hints: Assigning to a key that is already in a dictionary replaces what was there, which is exactly the behaviour you want: picks[step_id] = key.
tally() starts with var out := {} and walks picks.keys(). For each one, the manner is picks[step_id].
Counting into a dictionary: out[key] = int(out.get(key, 0)) + 1. get with a second argument gives 0 the first time a manner turns up.
steps.explain: Six taps, five answers: the second answer to "q2" replaced the first, so bold is counted once and banter three times. The first version of the game kept a running total and added one on every tap, so the bold answer you took back would still have counted. Nothing in your code remembers a total at all: it is counted fresh from the answers each time it is asked for.

steps.title: Who came out
steps.task: Write winner() -> String: the manner with the highest count in tally(). Walk DYNAMICS in its own order and only change your mind when a count is strictly greater than the best so far, so that a tie goes to whichever is listed first. With no answers at all, return "steady". In _ready(), print "Manner: " followed by the winner.

tests.label: with banter chosen three times, winner() is "banter"
change q1 to steady: banter 2, steady 2, bold 1
a tie goes to the manner listed first: still "banter"
change q2 to steady as well: steady 3
now winner() is "steady"
wipe every answer
with nothing answered, winner() falls back to "steady"

hints: Keep two variables as you loop: the best manner so far and its count. Start them at "steady" and 0.
Loop over DYNAMICS, not over the tally. The tally's order depends on which answer happened to be given first; the constant's order is always the same, and that is what makes a tie predictable.
if int(counts.get(key, 0)) > best_n: – then store the new count and the new key. >, not >=: with >= a tie would go to the last one listed.
steps.explain: Five questions and four manners means ties are common – two, two and one – so the tie-break is part of the design and worth deciding on purpose. The game's _tally_winner() does what you wrote: it walks the answers in the order the cards list them and keeps the first one that nobody beats.

steps.title: Start the life
steps.task:
Write begin_life(answers: Dictionary, dyn: String), which copies what the player said into state:

  • "name" – trimmed of spaces at both ends and cut to 16 characters, but only if anything is left after trimming
  • "mode" – the one in answers, or "cosy" if there is none
  • "dynamic" – dyn if it is one of DYNAMICS, otherwise "steady"
  • "created" – true

In _ready(), call it with {"name": " Ada ", "mode": "cosy"} and winner(), then print state.

tests.label: the name is "Ada", with the spaces trimmed off
the dynamic is the winner, "banter"
created is true
begin again with a blank name, hustle, and a manner that does not exist
a blank name changes nothing
the mode is "hustle"
an unknown manner becomes "steady"
begin again as Maximilian-Alexander, with no mode given
a long name is cut to 16 characters
and the mode falls back to "cosy"

hints: answers.get("name", "") gives an empty string when there is no name. .strip_edges() trims it; .substr(0, 16) keeps the first sixteen characters.
Only write the name inside if nm != "":. The mode is one line: state["mode"] = str(answers.get("mode", "cosy")).
A choice in one expression: state["dynamic"] = dyn if DYNAMICS.has(dyn) else "steady".
steps.explain: Look at the printed state: that dictionary is the whole of who you are, and in the game it is what gets written to the save file. Notice how defensive the function is for something only one card ever calls. A name of spaces, a missing mode, a manner that is not on the list – each has an answer. A save lasts for months and passes through every version of the game on the way, so the function that starts one should not be the place that lets nonsense in.

steps.title: Make the mode matter
steps.task:
Give the mode its numbers. Write three functions that read state["mode"], each with a match:

  • mode_price_mult() -> float – 1.3 for "hustle", 0.9 for "cosy", otherwise 1.0
  • mode_event_gap() -> float – 16.0 for "story", 34.0 for "hustle", otherwise 25.0
  • mode_day_scale() -> float – 0.8 for "cosy", 1.15 for "hustle", otherwise 1.0

Then add const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0 and day_seconds() -> float, how long a day really takes: DAY_LENGTH divided by the day scale. In _ready(), print "A day lasts ", day_seconds() and " seconds".

tests.label: in cosy, what you sell goes for 0.9 of its price
events are 25 seconds apart
and a day lasts 600 seconds
begin again in hustle
hustle sells at 1.3
with 34 seconds between events
and a day of about 417 seconds
begin again in story
story sells at the plain price
with events only 16 seconds apart
and the clock at its ordinary speed

hints: A match compares one value against several, top to bottom: match state["mode"]: and then, indented, a line for each case such as "hustle": return 1.3.
The last branch is _: return 1.0. The underscore matches anything, so the function always returns something.
day_seconds() is one line: return DAY_LENGTH / mode_day_scale(). Both are floats, so the division keeps its fraction.
steps.explain: Ten minutes, eight, or just under seven: the same 480 seconds of clock, run at three speeds. The game never works out day_seconds() – it multiplies each frame's delta by mode_day_scale() as it adds it to the clock, which comes to the same thing. Notice which mode gets which kindness: story has the shortest gap, because its promise is that the street comes to you; hustle has the best prices and the least time.

steps.title: The first steps
steps.task: Last, the short list a new player is walked through. Add const FIRST_STEPS := ["step_walk", "step_use", "step_door", "step_meet"]. Write first_step(id: String), which adds the id to state["first_steps"] unless it is already there, and first_steps_left() -> Array, the ids in FIRST_STEPS that have not been done, in that order. In _ready(), tick "step_walk" twice – the game calls it every time you arrive anywhere – and print first_steps_left().

tests.label: after a walk, three steps are left
ticking the same step twice wrote it once
now meet somebody before trying a door
the list keeps its own order: use, then door

hints: first_step is a guard and one line: if done.has(id): return, then done.append(id), where done is state["first_steps"].
first_steps_left() builds a new array: loop over FIRST_STEPS and append every id that state["first_steps"] does not have.
steps.explain: What is saved is the short list of things done; what is left is worked out from it. And because first_step() does nothing the second time, the game can call it from the busiest places it has – every arrival, every door – without a thought. Nothing here blocks the player or checks an order: somebody who meets a neighbour before opening a door finds that line already gone. The character's first-day thoughts in Tutorial.gd lean on this same list. Each thought names the step that ends it and the thought that must come before it, and she says the next one only when the screen has been quiet for 1.2 seconds.

title: Build the day clock
intro: The same clock, with a day twenty seconds long so you can watch one go by. Your script is one Node2D; the view beside the editor restarts each time you stop typing.
starter:
extends Node2D

const DAY_LENGTH := 20.0   # seconds; the game's day is 480

var clock_t := 0.0

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	pass

steps.title: Let time pass
steps.task: Make clock_t count seconds. _process(delta) runs every frame and delta is how long the last frame took, so adding it up gives time that does not depend on the frame rate.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const DAY_LENGTH := 20.0   # seconds; the game's day is 480

var clock_t := 0.0

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	clock_t += delta

tests.label: after four seconds of frames, clock_t is 4.0

hints: Replace pass with one line that adds delta to clock_t.
clock_t += delta
steps.explain: Nothing shows yet – the node has nothing to draw – but the number is moving. Counting frames instead (clock_t += 1) would make the day twice as fast on a 120 Hz screen.

steps.title: Hold the night
steps.task: The day must end. Add var night_held := false. When clock_t reaches DAY_LENGTH, pin it there and set night_held to true; and at the top of _process, do nothing at all while the night is held.

tests.label: four seconds in, the night is not held
long after nightfall, clock_t is exactly DAY_LENGTH
and night_held is true

hints: Two ifs. The first, before anything else: if night_held: then return.
The second, after adding delta: if clock_t >= DAY_LENGTH: – set clock_t = DAY_LENGTH and night_held = true.
steps.explain: This is the game's _process almost line for line. The early return is called a guard: it deals with the special case first so the rest of the function can forget about it.

steps.title: Read the time
steps.task:
Write three functions that read the clock without changing it:

  • day_fraction() -> float – clock_t / DAY_LENGTH, clamped to 0–1 with clampf
  • phase() -> String – "Morning" below 0.2, "Daytime" below 0.55, "Evening" below 0.75, otherwise "Night"
  • clock_text() -> String – the fraction stretched from 360 minutes (06:00) to 1320 (22:00), as "HH:MM"

tests.label: the day starts at 06:00
and it is Morning
a quarter of the day in, day_fraction() is 0.25
the clock reads 10:00
and it is Daytime
at 0.6 of the day it is Evening
and the clock reads 15:36
the day ends at 22:00, Night

hints: phase() is a ladder of ifs, smallest limit first, each returning as soon as it fits. Keep the fraction in a variable so you ask for it once.
For the clock: var mins := int(lerpf(360.0, 1320.0, day_fraction())), then hours are mins / 60 and minutes mins % 60.
Two digits each: "%02d:%02d" % [mins / 60, mins % 60].
steps.explain: mins / 60 is whole-number division because both sides are int: 936 / 60 is 15, not 15.6. That is a trap everywhere else in GDScript (Chapter D) and exactly what a clock wants.

steps.title: Paint the sky
steps.task: Now show it. Add sky_color() -> Color that blends from Color("#fff4e2") at sunrise to Color("#8e98dc") at nightfall, using .lerp() and the day fraction. In _draw(), fill the 320 × 180 view with it and write clock_text() in the corner. A drawing is kept until you ask for a new one, so call queue_redraw() in _process – first thing, before the guard.

tests.label: at sunrise the sky is #fff4e2
at nightfall it is #8e98dc
_draw() fills the view with draw_rect
tests.why: Drawing calls only work inside _draw().

tests.label: asks for a new drawing with queue_redraw()
tests.why: Without it _draw() runs once and the sky never changes.

hints: a.lerp(b, t) gives the colour a share t of the way from a to b: Color("#fff4e2").lerp(Color("#8e98dc"), day_fraction()).
In _draw(): draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), sky_color()), then draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 24), clock_text()).
If the sky stays one colour, _draw() is running only once. Put queue_redraw() on the first line of _process.
steps.explain: Watch it run: twenty seconds from cream to indigo, and then it holds. The game does this with seven colours in a Gradient instead of two and a lerp, and gives the result to a CanvasModulate instead of drawing a rectangle – but the idea is this one line, colour = f(day_fraction()).

title: Build a room you can rearrange
intro: A small room with a save of four pieces, and five empty functions. Fill them in one at a time and you will be able to pick the furniture up with the mouse or a finger, carry it, and put it down so that it stays put. The mouse is already wired to your functions, and so is Space, which leaves the room and comes back.

steps.title: Build from the save
steps.task: The room is empty because build() does nothing. Make it empty sprites and then add one entry for each piece in decor: a dictionary with the piece's "uid" and "k", a "rect" of the catalogue's size centred on its saved x and y, and a "z" that is the y of the rect's bottom edge. A piece whose k is not in CATALOG is skipped.

tests.label: three pieces are on screen: the hatstand is not in the catalogue and is left out
the sofa's rect is 64 by 28, centred on (120, 90)
the lamp's z is its bottom edge: 92 + 20
build the room a second time
and there are still three pieces, not six

hints: Start with sprites.clear(), then for e in decor:. Skip a piece the catalogue does not know with if not CATALOG.has(e["k"]): continue.
The size is CATALOG[e["k"]]["size"] and the middle is Vector2(e["x"], e["y"]). A rect centred on a point starts half its size up and to the left: Rect2(centre - size * 0.5, size).
The bottom edge is centre.y + size.y * 0.5. Append {"uid": e["uid"], "k": e["k"], "rect": …, "z": …}.
steps.explain: A sofa, with a lamp and a plant standing in front of it. They overlap the right way round because _draw() paints the pieces in order of z, smallest first, and you set z to the bottom edge – the game's rule, z_index equal to where the art meets the floor (Chapter L). The hatstand shows why build() checks the catalogue: a save lasts longer than any one version of the game, and a piece that has since been removed should be left out, not crash the room. The game does the same check twice, once when the save is loaded and once here.

steps.title: What is under the finger
steps.task: Write piece_at(p): the uid of the piece whose rect contains the point p, or "" if there is none. Where two pieces overlap, the one in front wins – the one with the larger z.

tests.label: the middle of the sofa is the sofa, "d2"
where the lamp stands in front of the sofa, it is the lamp, "d1"
where the plant stands in front of the sofa, it is the plant, "d3"
bare floor is ""

hints: Go through every entry in sprites; do not stop at the first hit. s["rect"].has_point(p) says whether the point is inside.
Keep the best so far in two variables, best (a uid, starting at "") and best_z (starting below any real z, say -1.0).
if s["rect"].has_point(p) and s["z"] >= best_z: – then remember this piece's z and uid. Return best after the loop.
steps.explain: Nothing looks different yet, but the room can now answer the question every tap and every drag starts with. "The first one in the list" and "the last one in the list" would both be wrong here – the lamp is listed before the sofa and the plant after it, and both stand in front. What the player sees on top is decided by z, so what a press picks must be decided by z as well. The game's own furniture goes a step further and tests the painted pixels, because a box round a lamp is mostly empty air.

steps.title: Pick it up
steps.task: Write begin_drag(p). It sets dragging_uid to whatever piece_at(p) finds, which may be nothing. If there is nothing it returns false. Otherwise it stores in drag_offset the vector from the finger to the middle of the piece, and returns true. Press a piece: it gets a white outline.

tests.label: pressing bare floor picks nothing up: false
pressing the lamp at (144, 100) returns true
and the lamp, "d1", is in the hand
drag_offset is from the finger to the lamp's middle: (2, -8)
pressing bare floor again returns false
and leaves the hand empty

hints: The first line can be dragging_uid = piece_at(p). If that is "", return false straight away.
The middle of the piece is entry(dragging_uid)["rect"].get_center(). From the finger to there is that minus p.
steps.explain: The outline is the starter's _draw() noticing dragging_uid. The offset is the detail that makes a drag feel right. You almost never press a thing dead in its middle; without the offset, the piece would jump so that its middle was under your finger the moment it moved. Remember where you took hold of it and it moves as if you were holding it there. The piece stays outlined when you let go, because letting go is step five.

steps.title: Carry it
steps.task: Write drag_to(p). With nothing in the hand it does nothing. Otherwise the piece's new middle is the finger plus drag_offset, kept inside BOUNDS and rounded to whole pixels. Give the piece's entry a new "rect" centred there and a new "z". Do not touch decor.

tests.label: call drag_to with nothing in the hand
nothing moves: the lamp is still at (146, 92)
pick the lamp up at (144, 100)
carry it to (200, 140)
its middle keeps its offset from the finger: (202, 132)
and its z follows it down the room: 152
carry it far outside the room
it stops at the corner of BOUNDS: (310, 170)
the save has not changed: x is still 146

hints: Begin with the guard: if dragging_uid == "": return. Then var s := entry(dragging_uid) – this is the very dictionary that sits in sprites, so changing it changes what is drawn.
The new middle in one line: (p + drag_offset).clamp(BOUNDS.position, BOUNDS.end).round(). BOUNDS.end is the bottom-right corner.
The size has not changed: var size: Vector2 = s["rect"].size. Then s["rect"] = Rect2(centre - size * 0.5, size) and s["z"] = centre.y + size.y * 0.5, exactly as in build().
steps.explain: Drag the lamp down the room and it stays in front of the sofa; drag it up to the wall and it slips behind, because its z is recalculated on every move. Now drag something, let go, and press Space. It jumps back. The room was built again from the save, and the save was never told. That is the bug the game's set_editing comment records – "drawn in its new place but saved in its old one" – and you have just reproduced it on purpose.

steps.title: Put it down
steps.task: Write end_drag(). With nothing in the hand it does nothing. Otherwise it takes the middle of the piece being carried, snaps its x and its y to the nearest multiple of SNAP, writes them into that piece's entry in decor, empties the hand, and builds the room again.

tests.label: pick the lamp up
carry it until its middle is at (202, 132)
and let go
the save now says (204, 132): 202 snapped to the grid of six
the hand is empty
leave the room and come back: the lamp is where you put it
and where it used to stand there is only the sofa

hints: Snapping a number to a grid: divide by the grid, round, multiply back. roundf(centre.x / SNAP) * SNAP.
Find the save's entry with a loop: for e in decor: and if e["uid"] == dragging_uid: – then set e["x"] and e["y"].
Finish with dragging_uid = "" and build(), in that order, so the room that is built has nothing in the hand.
steps.explain: Drop a piece and watch it shift by a pixel or two as it finds the grid; press Space and it does not move. The save and the screen now agree, and they agree because the screen was made from the save, not because you were careful to change both. The game moves the one sprite on a drop instead of rebuilding the room, which is quicker and means the same thing. To finish the job as the game does, try an add_decor(k) that appends {"uid": …, "k": k, "x": 160.0, "y": 110.0} with a uid nobody else has, and calls build(). The uid is what lets two lamps be two different lamps.

title: Build the evening caller
intro: A model of the whole decision in plain variables: who is eligible, who is best, and the timer that offers them a chance. Randomness is passed in as a number so you can test it.

steps.title: Once a day
steps.task: Write evening_had_today() -> bool, true when state["evening"] is a dictionary whose "day" is today's. It will not exist at first. Then write evening_begun(id), which stores {"day": today, "with": id} in state["evening"].

tests.label: with no evening recorded, it has not happened today
record an evening with bo
now it has
and it remembers who
move on to day 6
tomorrow it is open again, with nothing cleared

hints: Fetch the dictionary with a default: state.get("evening", {}). Compare its "day" (default -1) with state["day"].
var e: Dictionary = state.get("evening", {}) then return int(e.get("day", -1)) == int(state["day"]).
steps.explain: The last check moves the day on by hand and the answer flips back with no reset code anywhere. That is the whole trick. The helpers set_day() and friends are only there so the checks can change the world; they are not part of the rule.

steps.title: The best-known visitor
steps.task: Write best_known() -> String: loop over heard and return the id with the most beats heard, but only counting someone with EVENING_KNOWN or more. Nobody qualifying gives "". Start a variable most at EVENING_KNOWN - 1 and use a strict comparison.

tests.label: bo and cy both have 3 beats; the first listed wins
give cy a fourth beat
now cy wins
forget everybody
with nobody known, the answer is empty
ada has one beat
one beat is not enough
di has two beats
two beats is enough

hints: Keep two variables: best := "" and most := EVENING_KNOWN - 1. Loop with for id in heard:.
Inside the loop: if int(heard[id]) > most: then update both most and best.
steps.explain: Starting most one below the threshold means the same > that finds the best also rejects anybody who is not known well enough. The tests change heard as they go; the real game does the same thing, only one conversation at a time.

steps.title: Who might come
steps.task: Write evening_caller(fraction: float) -> String, where fraction is the day fraction. It returns "" if the player has not been created (state["created"] false), an evening has already happened today, or fraction is below EVENING_FROM. Otherwise it returns best_known(). Put the guards first, each as its own if. The checks use the small helpers at the top of the script to change the day and who is known between questions.

tests.label: at half the day, nobody comes
just before 0.66, still nobody
at 0.66, bo may call
an evening with bo happens
after it, nobody else is let in that day
the next day comes
the door is open again
no character yet
before a character exists, nobody calls

hints: Two guard clauses that return "", then return best_known().
if not bool(state.get("created", false)) or evening_had_today(): return ""
steps.explain: A function with a list of early returns reads like a checklist, and each line can be tested alone, which is what the last four checks do. The test is fraction < EVENING_FROM, so exactly 0.66 is allowed – edges are worth testing both sides of.

steps.title: The timer and the toss
steps.task: Write tick(delta: float, fraction: float, roll: float) -> String. Subtract delta from event_t; while it is still above zero return "". At zero or below, refill it with EVENT_GAP, then ask evening_caller(fraction). If there is a caller and roll is below 0.5, record evening_begun(caller) and return the caller's id; otherwise return "small", a small event.

tests.label: one second in, the timer has not run out
and counted down to 4
it runs out, the toss fails (0.9), so a small event happens
and the timer is refilled
too early in the day, a lucky toss still only gives a small event
late in the day and a lucky toss, bo calls
the next try the same day is small again

hints: Subtract first, return early, then reset the timer before you roll anything.
var caller := evening_caller(fraction) then if caller != "" and roll < 0.5:.
steps.explain: This is _tick_events without the room and overlay checks. In the game roll is randf() and the gap carries up to 45 random seconds; passing them in as arguments is the usual way to make random code testable. Notice that three separate guards – time, who, and chance – turn a rare event into one that feels like a surprise without being unfair.

title: Build a farm plot
intro: A small working farm in plain variables: twelve plots, one function for every tap, a growth rule that reads the clock, a harvest and a night. The checks use wait() and set_clock() from the top of the script to move time.
starter:
extends Node

const FARM_COLS := 4
const FARM_ROWS := 3
const CROPS := {
	"carrot": {"name": "Carrot", "grow": 15.0},
	"tomato": {"name": "Tomato", "grow": 20.0},
	"strawberry": {"name": "Strawberry", "grow": 25.0},
	"sunflower": {"name": "Sunflower", "grow": 30.0},
	"pumpkin": {"name": "Pumpkin", "grow": 40.0},
}

var farm: Array = []
var bag := {}
var day := 1
var clock_t := 0.0

# Helpers for the checks, not part of the rule: they move the clock.
func wait(seconds: float) -> void:
	clock_t += seconds

func set_clock(t: float) -> void:
	clock_t = t

func _ready() -> void:
	pass

steps.title: A grid of plots
steps.task: Write _fresh_plot(), which returns a new dictionary with the keys state ("grass"), crop (""), planted_at (0.0), watered and ready (both false). Then _fresh_farm(), which loops FARM_COLS * FARM_ROWS times and returns an array of them. Call it in _ready() and keep the result in farm.

tests.label: the farm has 12 plots (4 columns by 3 rows)
the first is bare grass
the last one is not ready
every plot starts the same

hints: Build the array with a for i in range(...) loop and append. Make the plot inside the loop, by calling the function each time.
a.append(_fresh_plot()) inside the loop, and farm = _fresh_farm() in _ready().
steps.explain: A plot is not a class, just a dictionary with five keys. Because the loop calls _fresh_plot() every time, each plot is its own dictionary; appending one dictionary twelve times would give twelve names for the same plot. The next step will prove it.

steps.title: Dig, plant, water
steps.task: Write act(i: int, crop: String = "carrot"), the one function every tap goes through. Ignore an i outside the farm. Otherwise match on the plot's state: grass becomes "tilled"; tilled becomes "planted", with the crop stored and planted_at set to clock_t; planted and not yet watered becomes watered.

tests.label: dig plot 0
plot 0 is tilled
plot 1 is still grass, so the plots are separate dictionaries
plant a tomato in plot 0
plot 0 holds a planted tomato
water it
it is watered
a plot that does not exist is ignored, not an error
and so is a negative one

hints: Start with a guard: if i < 0 or i >= farm.size(): return. Then var plot: Dictionary = farm[i] and match plot["state"]:.
Three branches, "grass":, "tilled": and "planted":. Each only edits plot[...], which is the same dictionary that lives in farm.
steps.explain: This is _farm_act in Main with the sound and the messages taken out. The plot is edited in place because plot is a reference to the dictionary in the array, not a copy. The game keeps planting in a separate card where you pick a seed, but it writes the same four fields.

steps.title: Let it grow
steps.task: Write tick() -> bool. For every plot that is planted, watered and not yet ready, look up its grow time in CROPS. If clock_t - planted_at has reached it, set ready to true. Return true if any plot changed. Also: if planted_at is later than clock_t, it is from before this morning, so set it to 0.0 first.

tests.label: dig plot 0
plant a carrot
fifteen seconds pass, unwatered
an unwatered crop does not grow, however long it waits
now water it
it has been in the ground for 15 seconds, so watering it makes it ready
plot 0 is ready
a second tick changes nothing, so no second signal
dig plot 1
plant a pumpkin (40 seconds)
water it
39 seconds pass
not yet
one more
the pumpkin is ready at exactly 40
late in the evening
dig plot 2
plant a tomato at 400
water it
a new morning: the clock starts again
the tomato is not ready at 00:00
twenty seconds of the new day
it ripens after its own 20, not after waiting for the clock to pass 420

hints: Start the loop body with a continue for plots that are not growing: if plot["state"] != "planted" or not plot["watered"] or plot["ready"]: continue.
var grow := float(CROPS[plot["crop"]]["grow"]), then the carry-over fix, then if clock_t - float(plot["planted_at"]) >= grow:.
steps.explain: Look at what is not here: no timer per plant, no countdown stored. Each plot only remembers when it was planted, and every tick asks whether enough time has gone by. That is the same "store the moment, not the remainder" idea as clock_t itself (C). It also means a crop you water late is ready at once if its time is already up: the time counts from planting, not from watering. The carry-over check is the bug the game's own comment records: the clock restarts every morning and is not saved, so without it an evening planting would wait all of the next day.

steps.title: Pick it
steps.task: Extend the "planted" branch of act: a watered plot that is ready is harvested. Write harvest(i) to add one of its crop to bag (a dictionary of counts), then put the plot back to "tilled" with no crop, not watered and not ready. A watered crop that is not ready does nothing.

tests.label: dig
plant
water
pressing on a watered crop that is not ready does nothing
it is still planted
wait
it ripens
press it again: harvest
one carrot is in the bag
the plot is bare soil, with no crop
and neither watered nor ready
replant it straight away
a pumpkin this time

hints: In the "planted" branch: if not plot["watered"]: water it, elif plot["ready"]: call harvest(i).
bag[crop] = int(bag.get(crop, 0)) + 1 adds to a count that may not exist yet. Then reset the four fields, leaving state as "tilled" so the soil is ready for a new seed.
steps.explain: One tap does a different thing depending on the plot’s state: that is a small state machine, grass to tilled to planted to ready and back to tilled. The plot returns to tilled, not grass, so a farmer is never made to dig the same ground twice.

steps.title: Sleep on it
steps.task: Write advance_day(): add one to day, set clock_t back to 0.0, and make every plot that is planted and watered ready.

tests.label: dig plot 0
plant
water plot 0
dig plot 1
plant plot 1 and leave it dry
dig plot 2 and leave it empty
the day goes on
go to bed
it is day 2
the clock is back to zero
the watered tomato finished growing overnight
the dry one did not
and bare soil never does

hints: One loop over farm with a single if that checks two keys.
if plot["state"] == "planted" and plot["watered"]: plot["ready"] = true
steps.explain: You have the whole farm: a grid of dictionaries, one function for every tap, a growth rule that reads the clock, and a night that finishes what you watered. Watering is the only thing the rule asks of you, and it is the reason to come to the farm before bed.

title: Build an evening visitor
intro: A basement, a clock and a ghost who keeps the game's rules: evenings only, looked for every so often, one piece of story a day. The day here is sixteen seconds long and starts at midday, so evening is two seconds away each time the view restarts.
starter:
extends Node2D

const DAY_LENGTH := 16.0   # seconds; the game's day is 480
const BEATS := 3           # pieces of her story; the game counts a list
const BASE_Y := 120.0      # where her feet are

var day := 1
var clock_t := 8.0         # midday, so evening is two seconds away
var ghost := {"met": false, "heard": 0, "day": 0}

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	clock_t += delta
	if clock_t >= DAY_LENGTH:   # the game waits for you to sleep; here morning comes by itself
		clock_t = 0.0
		day += 1
	queue_redraw()

func day_fraction() -> float:
	return clampf(clock_t / DAY_LENGTH, 0.0, 1.0)

func ghost_may_appear() -> bool:
	return false

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#2b2a3a"))    # the basement wall
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 130, 320, 50), Color("#3b3948"))   # and its floor
	var label := "Day %d   %d%% of the day   heard %d of %d" % [day, int(day_fraction() * 100), ghost["heard"], BEATS]
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 18), label, 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)
	if ghost_may_appear():
		draw_ghost(Vector2(230, BASE_Y))

func draw_ghost(feet: Vector2) -> void:
	var shape := [Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(-14, -34), Vector2(-9, -44), Vector2(0, -48), Vector2(9, -44), Vector2(14, -34), Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Vector2(0, 0), Vector2(-7, -6)]
	var outline := []
	for p in shape:
		outline.append(feet + p)
	draw_colored_polygon(outline, Color(1, 1, 1, 0.72))   # 0.72: the game's own number
	draw_circle(feet + Vector2(-5, -32), 2, Color("#2b2a3a"))
	draw_circle(feet + Vector2(5, -32), 2, Color("#2b2a3a"))

steps.title: Evenings only
steps.task: The room is drawn and the clock runs, but ghost_may_appear() always says no. Make it say yes once 0.62 of the day has gone, as the game does. day_fraction() is already written.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const DAY_LENGTH := 16.0   # seconds; the game's day is 480
const BEATS := 3           # pieces of her story; the game counts a list
const BASE_Y := 120.0      # where her feet are

var day := 1
var clock_t := 8.0         # midday, so evening is two seconds away
var ghost := {"met": false, "heard": 0, "day": 0}

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:

	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 18), label, 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)
	if ghost_may_appear():
		draw_ghost(Vector2(230, BASE_Y))

func draw_ghost(feet: Vector2) -> void:
	var shape := [Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(-14, -34), Vector2(-9, -44), Vector2(0, -48), Vector2(9, -44), Vector2(14, -34), Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Vector2(0, 0), Vector2(-7, -6)]
	var outline := []
	for p in shape:
		outline.append(feet + p)
	draw_colored_polygon(outline, Color(1, 1, 1, 0.72))   # 0.72: the game's own number

tests.label: a second in (56% of the day) she may not appear
two seconds in (62%) she may

hints: The whole body is one comparison, returned. A comparison is already a bool, so there is no need for if.
return day_fraction() >= 0.62
steps.explain: Watch the percentage in the corner: at 62 she is there, and at morning she is gone, both on the very frame the answer changes. That is correct and a little mechanical. The next step makes her less punctual, the way the game does.

steps.title: Look every so often
steps.task: Stop asking every frame. Add const GHOST_CHECK := 2.0 (the game's is 12), var _ghost_t := 0.0 and var showing := false. Write _tick_ghost(delta): count _ghost_t down by delta; while it is above zero, return; otherwise wind it back up to GHOST_CHECK and set showing to what ghost_may_appear() says. Call it from _process, and make _draw go by showing instead of asking for itself.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const DAY_LENGTH := 16.0   # seconds; the game's day is 480
const BEATS := 3           # pieces of her story; the game counts a list
const BASE_Y := 120.0      # where her feet are
const GHOST_CHECK := 2.0   # seconds between looks; the game's is 12

var day := 1
var clock_t := 8.0         # midday, so evening is two seconds away
var ghost := {"met": false, "heard": 0, "day": 0}
var _ghost_t := 0.0
var showing := false

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	clock_t += delta
	if clock_t >= DAY_LENGTH:   # the game waits for you to sleep; here morning comes by itself
		clock_t = 0.0
		day += 1
	_tick_ghost(delta)
	queue_redraw()

func day_fraction() -> float:
	return clampf(clock_t / DAY_LENGTH, 0.0, 1.0)

func ghost_may_appear() -> bool:
	return day_fraction() >= 0.62

func _tick_ghost(delta: float) -> void:
	_ghost_t -= delta
	if _ghost_t > 0.0:
		return
	_ghost_t = GHOST_CHECK
	showing = ghost_may_appear()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#2b2a3a"))    # the basement wall
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 130, 320, 50), Color("#3b3948"))   # and its floor
	var label := "Day %d   %d%% of the day   heard %d of %d" % [day, int(day_fraction() * 100), ghost["heard"], BEATS]
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 18), label, 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)
	if showing:
		draw_ghost(Vector2(230, BASE_Y))

func draw_ghost(feet: Vector2) -> void:
	var shape := [Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(-14, -34), Vector2(-9, -44), Vector2(0, -48), Vector2(9, -44), Vector2(14, -34), Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Vector2(0, 0), Vector2(-7, -6)]
	var outline := []
	for p in shape:
		outline.append(feet + p)
	draw_colored_polygon(outline, Color(1, 1, 1, 0.72))   # 0.72: the game's own number
	draw_circle(feet + Vector2(-5, -32), 2, Color("#2b2a3a"))
	draw_circle(feet + Vector2(5, -32), 2, Color("#2b2a3a"))

hints: A countdown is three moves: take delta off, leave early if there is time left, wind it up again. _ghost_t -= delta, then if _ghost_t > 0.0: and return.
After the guard: _ghost_t = GHOST_CHECK and showing = ghost_may_appear(). Then one line in _process: _tick_ghost(delta).
In _draw, the line if ghost_may_appear(): becomes if showing:.
steps.explain: She now turns up a fraction late – whenever the next look happens to fall – and lingers a moment into the morning before she is noticed and removed. Change GHOST_CHECK to 6.0 to see it clearly. The gate is now run once every two seconds instead of sixty times a second, and the drawing reads a plain variable.

steps.title: Let her drift
steps.task: She stands like a signpost. Add const BOB := 5.0 and var _t := 0.0, add delta to _t every frame, and write ghost_y() -> float: BASE_Y plus sin(_t * 1.6) * BOB, rounded to a whole pixel with roundf. Draw her with her feet at ghost_y().
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const DAY_LENGTH := 16.0   # seconds; the game's day is 480
const BEATS := 3           # pieces of her story; the game counts a list
const BASE_Y := 120.0      # where her feet are
const GHOST_CHECK := 2.0   # seconds between looks; the game's is 12
const BOB := 5.0           # pixels up and down

var day := 1
var clock_t := 8.0         # midday, so evening is two seconds away
var ghost := {"met": false, "heard": 0, "day": 0}
var _ghost_t := 0.0
var showing := false
var _t := 0.0

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	clock_t += delta
	if clock_t >= DAY_LENGTH:   # the game waits for you to sleep; here morning comes by itself
		clock_t = 0.0
		day += 1
	_t += delta
	_tick_ghost(delta)
	queue_redraw()

func day_fraction() -> float:
	return clampf(clock_t / DAY_LENGTH, 0.0, 1.0)

func ghost_may_appear() -> bool:
	return day_fraction() >= 0.62

func _tick_ghost(delta: float) -> void:
	_ghost_t -= delta
	if _ghost_t > 0.0:
		return
	_ghost_t = GHOST_CHECK
	showing = ghost_may_appear()

func ghost_y() -> float:
	return roundf(BASE_Y + sin(_t * 1.6) * BOB)

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#2b2a3a"))    # the basement wall
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 130, 320, 50), Color("#3b3948"))   # and its floor
	var label := "Day %d   %d%% of the day   heard %d of %d" % [day, int(day_fraction() * 100), ghost["heard"], BEATS]
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 18), label, 0, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)
	if showing:
		draw_ghost(Vector2(230, ghost_y()))

func draw_ghost(feet: Vector2) -> void:
	var shape := [Vector2(-14, 0), Vector2(-14, -34), Vector2(-9, -44), Vector2(0, -48), Vector2(9, -44), Vector2(14, -34), Vector2(14, 0), Vector2(7, -6), Vector2(0, 0), Vector2(-7, -6)]
	var outline := []
	for p in shape:
		outline.append(feet + p)
	draw_colored_polygon(outline, Color(1, 1, 1, 0.72))   # 0.72: the game's own number
	draw_circle(feet + Vector2(-5, -32), 2, Color("#2b2a3a"))
	draw_circle(feet + Vector2(5, -32), 2, Color("#2b2a3a"))

tests.label: at the start she is at BASE_Y
a second later she has sunk the full 5 pixels, to 125
two seconds after that she has risen to 115
she is drawn at ghost_y()
tests.why: In _draw: draw_ghost(Vector2(230, ghost_y()))

hints: _t += delta goes in _process, beside the clock. It is a second clock that never resets.
func ghost_y() -> float: with the body return roundf(BASE_Y + sin(_t * 1.6) * BOB).
In _draw: draw_ghost(Vector2(230, ghost_y())).
steps.explain: sin swings smoothly between −1 and 1 for ever, so multiplying it by 5 gives a rise and fall of five pixels each way, and the 1.6 sets how quickly: one full bob in a little under four seconds. This is the line from Ghost.gd. The roundf matters in pixel art – take it out and a sprite sits between pixels and blurs (Chapter P).

steps.title: One piece a day
steps.task: Now give her something to say. Write ghost_can_hear() -> bool: true while ghost["heard"] is below BEATS and ghost["day"] is before today. Write hear_ghost() -> String: if she cannot be heard, return ""; otherwise add one to heard, write today into day, set met, and return "Piece 1 of 3" with the right numbers in it. Then in _process, when she is showing and ui_accept has just been pressed, call it and print what comes back unless it is empty.

hints: ghost_can_hear() is two comparisons joined with and: ghost["heard"] < BEATS and ghost["day"] < day.
hear_ghost() starts with a guard – if not ghost_can_hear(): return "" – then ghost["heard"] += 1, ghost["day"] = day, ghost["met"] = true, and returns "Piece %d of %d" % [ghost["heard"], BEATS].
In _process, after _tick_ghost(delta): if showing and Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"): then var piece := hear_ghost() and, if piece != "", print(piece).
steps.explain: Click the view, wait for her and press Space. Press it again: nothing, because ghost["day"] now equals today. Nobody clears that at midnight; when day goes up, the comparison comes out true by itself. But she is still standing there with nothing to say, which the game does not allow. One more step.

steps.title: Only with something to say
steps.task: The game's ghost appears only when she has something for you. Add that to the gate: ghost_may_appear() should be true when it is late enough and she can be heard. Nothing else needs to change.

hints: Keep the evening test and add the other one. As two guards: if day_fraction() < 0.62: return false, then return ghost_can_hear().
Or as one line: return day_fraction() >= 0.62 and ghost_can_hear().
steps.explain: Play it through: she comes at evening, you press Space, and within two seconds she has gone – not because anything told her to leave, but because the next look found the gate shut. Three evenings later the gate never opens again. You changed one function and the appearing, the leaving and the ending all followed, because everything else asks that function. The game's gate has three more reasons for her to come after this one; each is one more or.

title: Build a heart meter
intro: Twelve days of calling on Tobias, printed a day at a time. The play-through in _ready() is already written and so is most of the scaffolding; what is missing is every rule. As you add them, watch the twelve lines change.

steps.title: Remember each heart
steps.task: Twelve days and the warmth is still 0.0. The fault is in heart(): it hands back a brand new dictionary every time, so whatever warm_heart() adds is thrown away. Make it keep one heart per person in hearts – create it the first time that id is asked for, and return the same one ever after.

tests.label: a new life, open to several
a heart starts at stage 0
asking for hal's heart puts it in hearts
a good moment with hal…
…is still there when you look again: warmth 1.0

hints: Two lines before the return: if hearts does not have this id yet, put a new heart there. Then return what is stored, not a new one.
if not hearts.has(id): then hearts[id] = {"stage": 0, "warmth": 0.0, "last": 0}, and finally return hearts[id].
steps.explain: The numbers climb now: 2.0, 4.0, up to 24.0. Nothing in warm_heart() changed. It always wrote to the dictionary it was given; the dictionary now happens to be the one in hearts, because a dictionary is passed by reference, not copied. This make-it-when-first-asked pattern is exactly the game's heart(). But Tobias is still a stranger, and you are getting two moments a day.

steps.title: One moment a day
steps.task: Write heart_spent_today(id) -> bool: true when that heart's last is today (or later). Then make warm_heart() refuse – return false and change nothing – when the day is spent. When it does go ahead it should also write today into last, and lift stage to 1 if it was below: you have met.

hints: heart_spent_today is one comparison: return heart(id)["last"] >= day.
Put the refusal first in warm_heart, before anything is changed: if heart_spent_today(id): return false.
After adding the warmth: h["last"] = day, then if h["stage"] < 1: and h["stage"] = 1.
steps.explain: One a day: 1.0, 2.0, up to 12.0, and the word has changed to met. Look at what you did not write: nothing clears "spent" in the morning. sleep() adds one to day, and last >= day stops being true. Storing when instead of whether is one of the most useful habits in game code – the game uses it for hearts, neighbours, side jobs and the ghost.

steps.title: Cross the lines
steps.task: Warmth is at 12 and he is still only "met". At the end of a successful warm_heart(), look at the next stage – the one after the heart's current stage. If there is one, and the warmth has reached what ROMANCE_NEEDS asks for it, move up to it. One step per moment, never more, and no error once the last stage is reached.

tests.label: a new life, open to several
a moment worth 2.0 with hal
2.0 is not yet 3: still met
a night passes
one more, to exactly 3.0
reaching 3 is enough: flirting
a night passes
an absurdly good day, to 23.0
moves up one stage only: dating, not together
a night passes
the next day
together
a night passes
a moment after the last stage is not an error
and you are still together

hints: Work out the next stage's number first: var next: int = h["stage"] + 1. The warmth it needs is ROMANCE_NEEDS[next].
There is no stage 5. Ask whether next is inside the list before you use it as an index: if next < ROMANCE_STAGES.size() and h["warmth"] >= ROMANCE_NEEDS[next]:
Inside that if: h["stage"] = next. It goes just before return true.
steps.explain: Flirting on day 3, dating on day 7, together on day 12 – read straight off ROMANCE_NEEDS. Once you are together, next is 5 and the list has no entry 5. That is why the size test comes first: and gives up at the first false, so the list is never asked. Swap the two halves and the check for "a moment after the last stage" fails with an out-of-bounds error. To retune the whole romance you would now change three numbers in one line at the top.

steps.title: Some people suit you
steps.task: Make the pace depend on who it is. Write affinity(id) -> float: look the person up in CANDIDATES; 1.5 if their warms_to is your dynamic, 0.6 if their wary_of is, otherwise 1.0. Then have warm_heart() add base times that, instead of base.

tests.label: a new life, steady and kind
tobias warms to steady: 1.5
hal is wary of steady: 0.6
del is neither: 1.0
a moment worth 2.0 with tobias
comes to 3.0
which is flirting on the first day
another life, one who says the thing
now hal warms to you
and tobias is the wary one
a moment worth 5.0 with tobias
comes to only 3.0

hints: Fetch the person once: var c: Dictionary = CANDIDATES[id]. Then two ifs that each return, and a plain return 1.0 at the bottom for everybody else.
if c["warms_to"] == dynamic: return 1.5, then if c["wary_of"] == dynamic: return 0.6.
In warm_heart the line becomes h["warmth"] += base * affinity(id).
steps.explain: Steady suits Tobias: flirting on day 2, dating on day 5, together on day 8. Now change "steady" in _ready() to "bold", the manner he is wary of. Twelve days gets you to dating and no further – slower, and still moving. That is the design in the game's comment: a small multiplier changes how many days it takes, and it is never zero, so nobody is quietly impossible.

steps.title: Only one thing starts
steps.task: The last line of the output asks about Hal, and at the moment the answer is true even though you have moved in with Tobias. Write may_court(id) -> bool. If romance_style is "none" or "partner": false. If it is "several": true. Otherwise ("one"): false if anybody other than id in hearts has reached flirting, and true if not. Then make warm_heart() refuse when may_court(id) is false.

hints: Deal with the three easy answers first, each with its own return. What is left is the "one" case, and that needs a loop over hearts.keys().

In the loop, skip the person you were asked about with if other == id: continue. For anybody else, if heart(other)["stage"] >= ROMANCE_STAGES.find("flirting"): return false. If the loop finishes without returning, return true.
In warm_heart, one more guard at the very top: if not may_court(id): return false.
steps.explain: "And Hal? false". The rule lives in one function and is asked at the place where the change would be made, so no button anywhere can get round it. Change "one" to "several" in _ready() and Hal says yes again. What you have is the game's romance, short of two things: a count of afternoons out, and one line that writes the person's id into together_with when the stage reaches the end – which is all "moving in" is.

title: Build a bag, a stove and a market
intro: A day with a bag: the farm, the stove, the market, the grocer's. The day is already written in _ready(), and every function it calls is there but empty. Fill them in one at a time and watch the day start to work.
starter:
extends Node

const RECIPES := {
	"Pancakes": ["carrot"],
	"Tomato Soup": ["tomato"],
	"Roast Dinner": ["carrot", "tomato"],
}
const PRICE_CROP := 12   # what the market pays
const PRICE_DISH := 30
const GROCER_STOCK := {"carrot": 18, "tomato": 18, "pumpkin": 26}   # what the grocer charges

var state := {}

func new_game() -> void:
	state = {"coins": 0, "crops": {}, "dishes": {}}

func add_item(kind: String, key: String, n: int = 1) -> void:
	pass

func count_of(kind: String, key: String) -> int:
	return 0

func cook(dish: String) -> bool:
	return false

func sell_one(kind: String, key: String, price: int) -> bool:
	return false

func buy_crop(key: String) -> bool:
	return false

func _ready() -> void:
	new_game()
	# A morning on the farm…
	add_item("crops", "carrot", 2)
	add_item("crops", "tomato")
	print("Carrots: ", count_of("crops", "carrot"), "   bag: ", state["crops"])
	# …the stove…
	print("Cook a Roast Dinner: ", cook("Roast Dinner"))
	print("Cook another: ", cook("Roast Dinner"))
	print("Bag: ", state["crops"], " ", state["dishes"])
	# …the market…
	print("Sell the dinner: ", sell_one("dishes", "Roast Dinner", PRICE_DISH))
	print("Sell it again: ", sell_one("dishes", "Roast Dinner", PRICE_DISH))
	print("Coins: ", state["coins"])
	# …and the grocer's on the way home.
	print("Buy a pumpkin: ", buy_crop("pumpkin"))
	print("Buy another: ", buy_crop("pumpkin"))

	print("Sell the pumpkin: ", sell_one("crops", "pumpkin", PRICE_CROP), "   coins: ", state["coins"])

steps.title: Things in, things out
steps.task: Write the two functions the rest will stand on. add_item(kind, key, n) adds n to the count of key in state[kind] – starting from 0 if it is not there yet – and if that leaves none, removes the key altogether. n may be negative: that is how things are taken out. count_of(kind, key) returns how many there are, and 0 for something that is not in the bag.
steps.solution:
extends Node

const RECIPES := {
	"Pancakes": ["carrot"],
	"Tomato Soup": ["tomato"],
	"Roast Dinner": ["carrot", "tomato"],
}
const PRICE_CROP := 12   # what the market pays
const PRICE_DISH := 30
const GROCER_STOCK := {"carrot": 18, "tomato": 18, "pumpkin": 26}   # what the grocer charges

var state := {}

func new_game() -> void:
	state = {"coins": 0, "crops": {}, "dishes": {}}

func add_item(kind: String, key: String, n: int = 1) -> void:
	var bag: Dictionary = state[kind]
	bag[key] = bag.get(key, 0) + n
	if bag[key] <= 0:
		bag.erase(key)

func count_of(kind: String, key: String) -> int:
	return state[kind].get(key, 0)

func cook(dish: String) -> bool:
	return false

func sell_one(kind: String, key: String, price: int) -> bool:
	return false

func buy_crop(key: String) -> bool:
	return false

func _ready() -> void:
	new_game()
	# A morning on the farm…
	add_item("crops", "carrot", 2)
	add_item("crops", "tomato")
	print("Carrots: ", count_of("crops", "carrot"), "   bag: ", state["crops"])
	# …the stove…
	print("Cook a Roast Dinner: ", cook("Roast Dinner"))
	print("Cook another: ", cook("Roast Dinner"))
	print("Bag: ", state["crops"], " ", state["dishes"])
	# …the market…
	print("Sell the dinner: ", sell_one("dishes", "Roast Dinner", PRICE_DISH))
	print("Sell it again: ", sell_one("dishes", "Roast Dinner", PRICE_DISH))
	print("Coins: ", state["coins"])
	# …and the grocer's on the way home.
	print("Buy a pumpkin: ", buy_crop("pumpkin"))
	print("Buy another: ", buy_crop("pumpkin"))
	print("Coins: ", state["coins"], "   bag: ", state["crops"])
	print("Sell the pumpkin: ", sell_one("crops", "pumpkin", PRICE_CROP), "   coins: ", state["coins"])

tests.label: the day begins: prints Carrots: 2
then, with an empty bag…
put in 3 pumpkins
count_of says 3
put in one more, leaving n out

take all 4 out
count_of says 0
and the name has gone from the bag
put Pancakes in the dishes
the kinds are kept apart

hints: Start by getting hold of the right dictionary: var bag: Dictionary = state[kind]. Reading a key that may be missing is bag.get(key, 0).
bag[key] = bag.get(key, 0) + n, then if bag[key] <= 0: and bag.erase(key).
count_of is one line: return state[kind].get(key, 0).
steps.explain: The first line of output has come alive: two carrots, and the bag printed as a dictionary. You never wrote "if there are no carrots yet" – get(key, 0) made the first carrot the same as every other. And bag is the very dictionary inside state, not a copy, which is why changing it was enough. The rest of the day still says false.

steps.title: Cook
steps.task: Write cook(dish). Look up what the dish needs in RECIPES. If any ingredient is missing, return false and leave the bag exactly as it was. Otherwise take one of each ingredient out of "crops", add one of the dish to "dishes", and return true. Use count_of and add_item – they are the only things that should touch the bag.

tests.label: the day: one Roast Dinner cooks, a second does not
then, with an empty bag…
one carrot and no tomato
a Roast Dinner cannot be cooked
and the carrot has not been used up trying
add a tomato
now it cooks
there is one Roast Dinner in the dishes
and both crops have gone
no carrot left for Pancakes

hints: Two loops over the same list. The first only checks, and returns false the moment something is missing. Only if it gets all the way through does the second loop take anything.
var needs: Array = RECIPES[dish], then for crop in needs: with if count_of("crops", crop) <= 0: return false inside.
The second loop: for crop in needs: and add_item("crops", crop, -1). After it, add_item("dishes", dish) and return true.
steps.explain: One dinner cooks; the second is refused because the only tomato went into the first, and the bag line shows a single carrot left and a dish where there was none. If you wrote it as one loop – check a crop, take it, on to the next – the check "the carrot has not been used up trying" will have caught you. Look first, then act: it is the simplest way to make sure a thing either happens completely or does not happen.

steps.title: Sell one
steps.task: Write sell_one(kind, key, price), the market's one function. If there is none of that thing in the bag, return false and pay nothing. Otherwise take one out, add price to state["coins"], and return true.

tests.label: the day: the dinner sells once, for 30
then, with an empty bag…
two lots of Pancakes
the first sells
30 coins
the second sells
60 coins
a third tap sells nothing
and pays nothing: still 60
the bag has no Pancakes line left
something you never had cannot be sold

hints: The refusal comes first, before anything changes: if count_of(kind, key) <= 0: return false.
Then add_item(kind, key, -1), state["coins"] += price, return true.
steps.explain: "Sell it again: false", and the coins stay at 30. That second line is a double tap: the same button pressed twice, faster than the card can redraw. Because the check, the taking and the paying are in one function, there is no moment between them for a second tap to land in. If a card did add_item(…, -1) itself and then added the coins itself, every card that sold anything would have to remember the check – and one day one would not.

steps.title: The grocer
steps.task: Write buy_crop(key), selling in reverse. If the grocer does not stock key, or you have fewer coins than its price in GROCER_STOCK, return false and change nothing. Otherwise take the price off your coins, put one in "crops", and return true.

tests.label: the day: one pumpkin bought, a second not, 4 coins left
then, with an empty bag and no coins…
a carrot cannot be bought
and does not turn up in the bag
make some Pancakes appear
and sell them for 30
now a pumpkin can be bought
30 − 26 leaves 4 coins
and there is a pumpkin in the bag
4 coins will not buy a carrot
and trying costs nothing
something the grocer does not stock cannot be bought

hints: Two refusals, then the exchange. The first refusal is if not GROCER_STOCK.has(key): return false.
Then var price: int = GROCER_STOCK[key] and if state["coins"] < price: return false.
Last: state["coins"] -= price, add_item("crops", key), return true.
steps.explain: The whole day runs. Read the last two lines of output: a pumpkin bought for 26 sells for 12, so standing between the shop and the market only loses money – that is the comment above the game's GROCER_STOCK, working. Now try the other way. In _ready(), buy a carrot instead, cook("Pancakes"), and sell the dish at PRICE_DISH: 18 in, 30 out. The economy pays for doing something, not for owning something. The game's grocer keeps its stock as a list so the shelf has an order; yours is a dictionary, and the rule is the same.

title: Build a day's work
intro: Two days of side hustles, printed line by line: a gallery, a print, a music commission and a stall. The jobs call five small rules that are there but empty, which is why at the moment the gallery can be opened as often as you like. Write the rules and the day sorts itself out.

steps.title: Once a day
steps.task: The first two lines of output are the bug: the gallery pays twice in one day. hustle is a dictionary meant to hold, for each job, the day it was last done. Write mark_hustle(id) to write today's day into it, and hustle_done(id) to say whether the day written there is today. A job that has never been done has nothing written; treat that as day −1.

tests.label: the day: the gallery will not open twice
then, starting again…
a job never done is not done today
the gallery opens
now it is done for today
it will not open again
so it paid once: 28 coins
other jobs are not affected
a night passes
tomorrow it is open again, with nothing reset

hints: mark_hustle is one assignment: hustle[id] = day.
hustle_done reads the day back with a fallback for "never": hustle.get(id, -1), and compares it with day.
return hustle.get(id, -1) >= day
steps.explain: "Gallery again: false", and at the bottom "Day 2. Gallery: true" – open again after a night, though you wrote nothing that runs at night. Imagine the other way of doing it: a done_today flag per job and a function that clears them all each morning. It works until somebody adds a job and forgets the clearing, or a save is loaded on a different day. A date cannot go stale like that.

steps.title: Paper and strings
steps.task: Paid work spends materials. Write buy_supply(kind, n): the cost is the price of that kind in SUPPLY_PRICE times n. If you cannot afford it – or the cost is 0, because the shop sells no such thing – return false and change nothing; otherwise pay and add n to supplies[kind]. Then use_supply(kind): if there is none, false; otherwise take one and return true.

tests.label: the day: no print without paper; with paper, a print
then, starting again with no coins…
there is no paper to use
and none can be bought
earn 25 coins
two lots of paper can be bought
for 20, leaving 5
there are 2 in stock

nor anything the shop does not sell

and a refused job uses no paper

steps.task: Now write a whole job from the pieces. music_commission() pays 12 coins plus 3 for every point of practice, where practice is stat("dj"). The _ branch is not laziness: a save from an older version, or a typing mistake, gets a sensible answer instead of a crash. The game adds two things to what you have built: a 1.35 bonus on one kind of work for players who once named a trade, and a pile of washing on the first job of each day.

title: Build the repair list
intro: The rule in plain variables: a list of repairs, a house with three lists in it, and the functions that work out what is next, how far away it is, and what happens when you pay. The repairs here are the first three; the checks use a helper, set_coins(), to change your money.

steps.title: What comes next
steps.task: Write next_repair() -> Dictionary. Loop over REPAIRS in order and return the first one whose id is not in house["repairs"]. If every one is done, return an empty dictionary {}.

mark gate as done

hints: A for r in REPAIRS: loop with an if not house["repairs"].has(...) inside it. The return {} goes after the loop.
if not house["repairs"].has(r["id"]): return r
steps.explain: Look at what is not stored: there is no "current repair" variable. The state is the list of what is done, and the next one is worked out from it, as the clock does in C. The array's order is the story's order, which is why the gate (60) comes after the window (90).

steps.title: How far off
steps.task: Write repair_goal() -> Dictionary. If there is no next repair, return {}. Otherwise return a dictionary with the keys id, name, cost, have (the coins you hold), short (how many more you need, never below zero) and ready (true when you can afford it).

steps.explain: The game's HUD shows have / cost beside the coins, and a glow when ready is true, all from this one answer. maxi(0, ...) is the little guard that keeps "short" from reading "-60 more" when you are rich.

steps.title: A line about money
steps.task: Write goal_note() -> String: empty if there is no goal; "That is enough for X." if it is ready; otherwise "N more for X.", where X is the repair's name in lower case (.to_lower()) and N is short. Then with_goal(line), which returns the line with the note on the end after two spaces, or the line alone if the note is empty.

mark gate as done

and the note is empty

"%d more for %s." % [g["short"], name], and in with_goal: return line if note == "" else "%s %s" % [line, note].
steps.explain: This is what turns a number into a distance. The game says "Sold the tomato for twelve coins" and then how far that leaves you from the draught, on every line that pays you. Every income in J goes through with_goal. Because it takes the line as an argument, the one function serves the stall, the kitchen and the concert alike.

steps.title: Pay for it
steps.task: Write has_keepsake(id) (is it in house["keepsakes"]) and do_repair() -> String. It returns "" if nothing is left or you cannot afford it, with nothing changed. Otherwise it takes the cost from coins, appends the repair's id to house["repairs"], adds its found keepsake to house["keepsakes"] unless you already have it, and returns the repair's name.

var found := str(r.get("found", "")) then if found != "" and not has_keepsake(found): append it.
steps.explain: All the checks come first and all the changes after, so a refusal never leaves a half-done repair. The game's comment calls its refusal "a safety net": the card already greys out a row you cannot afford, but the rule does not trust the card. The found lookup uses .get(..., "") so that a repair with nothing to find would still work.

steps.title: Show it to somebody
steps.task: Write has_shown(id) and show_keepsake(id: String, room: String) -> String. Look up SHOWINGS[id] (an empty dictionary if there is none). Return "" if there is no showing, you do not have the keepsake, you have shown it already, or the showing names a room and you are not in it.
