Everything else, from the HUD pill to which rows of the card are greyed out, is worked out from them.

title: Build the mailbox
intro: The same mailbox with three letters instead of sixty, so you can watch the pool come round. By the end you can read a letter, see that reading it twice counts once, and go to bed to get the next.
starter:
extends Node

const LETTERS := [
	{"from": "The Doormat", "text": "Wipe your feet. That is all."},
	{"from": "A Snail", "text": "Crossing the path. Back by Friday."},
	{"from": "The Stairs", "text": "Thirteen of us. We counted twice."},
]

var day := 1
var mail_read := 0   # the day whose letter has been read

func _ready() -> void:
	pass

steps.title: One letter a day
steps.task: Write letter_for(d: int) -> Dictionary. Day 1 gets the first letter, day 2 the second, and the day after the last one starts the pool again. A day below 1 counts as day 1. Then, in _ready(), print the sender for days 1 to 5, each as Day 1: The Doormat.

tests.label: day 1 gets the first letter
day 3 gets the third
day 4 starts the pool again
day 8 is the second letter, third time round
a day below 1 counts as day 1

hints: The position in the array is the day minus one, because arrays count from 0. % gives the remainder after dividing, so % LETTERS.size() keeps any number inside the array.
var i := (maxi(1, d) - 1) % LETTERS.size(), then return LETTERS[i].
In _ready(): for d in range(1, 6): and print("Day %d: %s" % [d, letter_for(d)["from"]]). range(1, 6) stops before 6.
steps.explain: Look at days 1 and 4 in the output: the same sender. Three letters, so the remainder goes 0, 1, 2, 0, 1. Add a fourth letter to LETTERS and watch day 4 change and day 5 become the Doormat – the function did not have to be told how many there are.

steps.title: Is there post?
steps.task: Add has_unread_mail() -> bool: there is post when the day whose letter was read is behind today. It is one comparison of the two variables. At the end of _ready(), print the answer as Post waiting: true.

tests.label: there is post exactly when mail_read is behind day
has_unread_mail() compares mail_read with day
tests.why: Compare the two variables – do not return a fixed answer.

hints: A comparison is already a bool, so the function is one line with return and <.
return mail_read < day, and in _ready(): print("Post waiting: %s" % has_unread_mail()).
steps.explain: mail_read starts at 0 and day at 1, so the very first morning already has post without anybody arranging it. Change mail_read to 1 at the top and the last line flips to false.

steps.title: Open the box
steps.task: Add var letters_read := 0 and open_mailbox() -> String. It returns today's letter as "sender: text". If the letter was unread, it also marks it read – copy day into mail_read – and adds one to letters_read. Opening the box a second time must give the same letter and count nothing. In _ready(), print open_mailbox() twice, then Letters read: 1.

tests.label: open_mailbox() returns today's letter as "sender: text"
after opening the box, no post is waiting
opening it again does not count again

output: The Doormat: Wipe your feet. That is all.

hints: Fetch the letter first with letter_for(day). Then one if: only when has_unread_mail() is true do the two bits of bookkeeping.
Inside the if: mail_read = day and letters_read += 1.
After the if: return "%s: %s" % [letter["from"], letter["text"]].
steps.explain: The letter prints twice and the count says 1. That is the game's _build_mail(): show the letter every time, do the counting only when has_unread_mail() says it is new. Marking it read is what makes the next call different – the function changes the answer to its own question.

steps.title: A new morning
steps.task: Add sleep(), which moves day on by one and touches nothing else. At the end of _ready(), call it, print Day 2, post waiting: true from the two things you already have, and open the box once more.

tests.label: sleep() moves the day on by one
and in the morning there is post again
the new day's letter counts once
two nights without looking is still only one letter

output: A Snail: Crossing the path. Back by Friday.

hints: sleep() is one line: day += 1. Do not reset mail_read – that is the point.
In _ready(): sleep(), then print("Day %d, post waiting: %s" % [day, has_unread_mail()]), then print(open_mailbox()).
steps.explain: sleep() never mentions the post, and yet the post came back: day moved, mail_read stayed, and the comparison turned true by itself. Now call sleep() twice in a row before opening the box. You get the Stairs, and the Snail is never seen – a missed day leaves no backlog, because only today's letter can be asked for. That is the game's mailbox, whole.

title: Build a house you can walk through
intro: Four rooms on a plan three squares by two – the same arrangement the house has on the real plan, shrunk – and a red dot that is you. By the end the doorways are worked out from the plan and the arrow keys walk you through them. The walking and the drawing are written already, at the bottom of the script; your four functions are at the top. Click the view before using the keys.

steps.title: Who owns a square
steps.task: Fill in room_at(cell): go through CELLS and return the name of the room whose rectangle contains that square, or "" if none does. A Rect2 answers the question itself, with has_point().

tests.label: square (0, 0) is the bedroom
so is (0, 1): the bedroom is two squares tall
(1, 1) is the kitchen
(2, 0) is the living room
(3, 0) is off the plan: nobody
so is (0, -1)

hints: for room in CELLS: gives you each name in turn, and CELLS[room] is that room's rectangle.
Inside the loop: if CELLS[room].has_point(cell): then return room. The return "" stays after the loop, for when nothing matched.
steps.explain: Every square of the plan now says who owns it – the drawing code asks room_at() six times. The bedroom and the living room say so twice, because each covers two squares. The game's version is map_room_at(), with Rect2i and Vector2i, the whole-number kinds, and a check that the room is on the right floor.

steps.title: Look over the wall
steps.task: Fill in beyond(room, dir, i): the room on the other side of square i of one wall. Start at the room's top-left square, CELLS[room].position. Move i squares along the wall – across for a north or south wall, down for a west or east one. Then step in the direction DIR_STEP[dir], and keep stepping while you are still inside the room's own rectangle. Return whoever owns the square you end on.

tests.label: east of the bedroom's top square: the bathroom
east of its bottom square: the kitchen
south of the bathroom: the kitchen
west of the living room's bottom square: the kitchen
south of the bedroom: nothing, not the bedroom itself
west of the bedroom: nothing

hints: A north or south wall runs across, so square i of it is Vector2(i, 0) from the corner; for a west or east wall it is Vector2(0, i). A step with a y in it (step.y != 0) means north or south.
var probe: Vector2 = cells.position + (Vector2(i, 0) if step.y != 0 else Vector2(0, i)) + step, where cells is CELLS[room] and step is DIR_STEP[dir].
Then while cells.has_point(probe): probe += step, and return room_at(probe).
steps.explain: Green bars have appeared on the plan wherever a wall has somebody behind it: the drawing code asks beyond() about every square of every wall. Look at the bedroom's east wall – two bars, one for each neighbour. The while matters for its south wall: one step south from the top-left square is still the bedroom, and without the loop the bedroom would find itself next door.

steps.title: List the ways out
steps.task: Fill in exits(room) so that it returns one dictionary for each opening: {"dir": …, "room": …, "from": …, "to": …}. Go through the four directions in DIR_STEP and, for each, through the squares of that wall – wall_len(room, dir) says how many there are. Where beyond() finds a room, add an opening. Square i of a wall n squares long runs from i / n to (i + 1) / n of it; make those floats.

tests.label: the bedroom has two ways out
the first: east to the bathroom, the top half of the wall
the second: east to the kitchen, the bottom half
the kitchen has three
the bathroom's south wall is all kitchen: from 0.0 to 1.0

hints: Start with var out: Array = [] and end with return out. In between, two loops: for dir in DIR_STEP: and inside it for i in n:, with var n := wall_len(room, dir).
Inside both loops: var other := beyond(room, dir, i), and only if other != "": append.
out.append({"dir": dir, "room": other, "from": float(i) / n, "to": float(i + 1) / n}). Without float(), 1 / 2 is 0.
steps.explain: The line under the plan now lists the ways out of the room you are in. This is the list the rest of the game works from. The game does one thing more: where several squares in a row lead to the same room it merges them into one wide opening – the second half of _edge_runs() above. With rooms this small there is nothing to merge.

steps.title: Go through
steps.task: Now make the walls let you through. leave(dir, along) is called whenever you walk into a wall, with how far along it you are. Look through exits(here) for an opening on that wall whose from–to spans along. If there is one, change here to its room and stand in the middle of it, Vector2(0.5, 0.5). If there is none, do nothing: it is a wall.

tests.label: walking east from the top of the bedroom leads to the bathroom
north of the bathroom is a wall: you stay
south of it is the kitchen
west of the kitchen is the bedroom
and the lower part of the bedroom's east wall leads back to the kitchen

hints: for e in exits(here): – each e is one of the dictionaries from the last step.
The test has three parts joined with and: e["dir"] == dir, along >= e["from"], along <= e["to"].
When it matches: here = e["room"], spot = Vector2(0.5, 0.5), then return so the loop stops at the first opening that fits.
steps.explain: Click the view and use the arrow keys. Walk east from the top of the bedroom and you are in the bathroom; from the bottom, the kitchen – along picks between two openings on one wall. Anywhere there is no green bar you stop. But every arrival drops you in the middle of the room, which is not how walking through a door feels.

steps.title: Arrive at the door
steps.task: Arrive where you would expect to. In leave(), remember the room you are leaving before you change here. You come in by the opposite wall – DIR_BACK[dir]. Look through the new room's exits for the opening on that wall that leads back to the room you left, and set spot to entry_point() of it. Keep the middle of the room as the fallback.

tests.label: walk east out of the bedroom, into the bathroom
you arrive at its west wall, not in the middle
turn round and you are back in the bedroom
in the bathroom's doorway: a quarter of the way down the east wall
go by the kitchen instead and you come back three quarters of the way down
bathroom to kitchen: you arrive at the middle of the kitchen's north wall

hints: Three new lines before the search: var from_room := here, var back: String = DIR_BACK[dir], and only then here = e["room"].
A second loop, inside the first one's if: for a in exits(here): – by now here is the new room.
if a["dir"] == back and a["room"] == from_room: then spot = entry_point(back, a["from"], a["to"]).
steps.explain: Walk from the bedroom into the kitchen and straight back: you return through the kitchen's doorway, in the lower half of the wall, not the bathroom's. That is the game's _go_through() – DIR_BACK, then exit_to(), then entry_point() – and it works for every pair of rooms because both openings came from the same shared edge. Now change the plan: make the kitchen Rect2(1, 1, 2, 1) and the living room Rect2(2, 0, 1, 1). The doorways move, the walking still works, and you did not touch a single rule.

title: Build a story that opens slowly
intro: Three invented neighbours – Ada, Bo and Cy – with four chapters each and the game's own two numbers. By the end you can live a month in one loop, visiting Ada daily and Bo now and then, and print what each of them has told you and what the rest is waiting for. The record-keeping helpers at the top are written for you.

steps.title: When a chapter opens
steps.task: Write two functions. stagger(id) -> int is the person's position in PEOPLE, wrapped with % STORY_PACE. beat_gate(id, index) -> Array returns what chapter number index waits for, as [day, closeness]: the first chapter (index 0) is [1, 0] for everybody; any later one is day 1 + stagger + index * STORY_PACE and closeness index * STORY_CLOSENESS. In _ready(), print one line per person with all four gates, like ada: [1, 0] [9, 2] [17, 4] [25, 6].

tests.label: ada is first in the list: no stagger
cy is third: two days late
everybody's first chapter is free: day 1, closeness 0
ada's second waits for day 9 and two days of talking
bo's second is a day behind hers
cy's fourth waits for day 27 and six days of talking

hints: PEOPLE.find(id) gives a position in the array, counting from 0. The stagger is that, % STORY_PACE.
beat_gate starts with the special case: if index <= 0: return [1, 0]. Then one return with an array of two sums.
For the printing: for id in PEOPLE:, start var line: String = id + ":", then for i in CHAPTERS: add " " + str(beat_gate(id, i)), and print(line) after the inner loop.
steps.explain: Read the three lines down, not across. The first column is the same for everybody – a first meeting always gives you something. After that each person runs a day behind the one before, so their news never lands on the same morning. Nothing is stored: a gate is arithmetic on a chapter number. Change STORY_PACE to 3 and every story in town speeds up at once.

steps.title: Days you spoke
steps.task: Closeness is the number of days on which you spoke to somebody, not the number of times. Write note_met(id): get their record with entry(id); if its "met_day" is already today, do nothing; otherwise set "met_day" to today and add one to "met". Write closeness(id) -> int, which returns "met". In _ready(), note that you met Ada twice and print Closeness with ada: 1.

tests.label: speaking to somebody twice in one day is one day of knowing them
the next day it counts again
and it is kept per person: nothing for bo

hints: var e := entry(id) gives you the dictionary itself, not a copy, so changing e["met"] changes the record.
The guard comes first: if e["met_day"] >= day: return.
Then e["met_day"] = day and e["met"] += 1. closeness is return entry(id)["met"].
steps.explain: Two calls, and the count is 1. "met_day" is a stamp: it remembers the last day that counted, so the function can tell a second visit today from a first visit tomorrow without anything being reset overnight. Remove the guard and watch the number become 2 – that is the bug it prevents, a friendship you could finish in an afternoon of tapping.

steps.title: Is there something new?
steps.task: Write can_hear(id) -> bool. The answer is no if they have told you everything ("heard" has reached CHAPTERS), and no if you already heard a chapter from them today ("day", the day you last heard one, is today). Otherwise ask beat_gate() about the next chapter – its index is the number you have heard – and say yes only if today has reached the gate's day and your closeness has reached the gate's closeness. Print Can hear ada: true at the end of _ready().

tests.label: on the first morning cy has something to tell you
the second chapter stays shut on day 21 if you have spoken on only one day
and opens once you have spoken on two
day 10 is too early for it, however often you have spoken
day 11 is not
never two chapters from one person in a day
and nothing once the story is all told

hints: Two guards first, each an if that returns false: e["heard"] >= CHAPTERS, and e["day"] >= day.
Then var gate := beat_gate(id, e["heard"]). gate[0] is the day it waits for and gate[1] the closeness.
return day >= gate[0] and closeness(id) >= gate[1]
steps.explain: It prints true, because it is day 1 and a first chapter is always free. The last line of the function is the whole rule: and, not or. Either half alone would let a player get the story by waiting, or by pestering.

steps.title: Hear it, and live a month
steps.task: Write hear(id) -> int. If can_hear(id) is false it returns 0. Otherwise it adds one to "heard", stamps "day" with today, counts the visit with note_met(id), and returns the number of the chapter just heard. Then live thirty days at the end of _ready(): a loop that, each day, notes you met Ada and hears her; on every fifth day (day % 5 == 0) does the same for Bo and prints a line like Day 5: ada 1/4, bo 1/4 using told(); and ends the day with sleep().

tests.label: hear() returns the number of the chapter: 1
ask again the same day and there is nothing: 0
hearing a chapter counts as having spoken
ten days on, having spoken once, still nothing
speak to them that day and the second chapter comes

hints: hear begins if not can_hear(id): return 0. After that nothing can go wrong: e["heard"] += 1, e["day"] = day, note_met(id), return e["heard"].
The loop: for n in 30: with note_met("ada") and hear("ada") on every pass, and sleep() as its last line.
Inside the loop, before sleep(): if day % 5 == 0: then note_met("bo"), hear("bo") and print("Day %d: %s, %s" % [day, told("ada"), told("bo")]).
steps.explain: Six lines, one every five days. Ada, seen daily, has told you everything by day 25. Bo's gates are only a day behind hers, but on day 15 he is still at 2/4 and on day 25 at 3/4: you have not spoken to him on enough days. He finishes on day 30, the first visit on which both halves of the rule are true. Cy, whom you never called on, is still at 0/4 and always will be.

steps.title: Say what it is waiting for
steps.task: Write hear_blocked_by(id) -> String, which says why there is nothing new: "" if there is something; "done" if the story is all told; "today" if you have already heard a chapter today; "closeness" if you do not know them well enough for the next one; and otherwise "time". Check them in that order. Then put it in the month's printed line, after each person: Day 15: ada 2/4 time, bo 2/4 closeness.

tests.label: nothing is in the way of a first chapter: ""
having just heard it: "today"
the next morning, one day of knowing them: "closeness"
speak to them, and what is left is "time"
on day 11 the way is clear again: ""
and when it is all told: "done"

hints: Start with if can_hear(id): return "". Everything after that line already knows the answer is no and only has to find out why.
The same tests as can_hear, in the same order, each returning its word: e["heard"] >= CHAPTERS is "done", e["day"] >= day is "today".

if closeness(id) < beat_gate(id, e["heard"])[1]: return "closeness", and a plain return "time" at the end. The print needs four %s after the day: told("ada"), hear_blocked_by("ada"), told("bo"), hear_blocked_by("bo").
steps.explain: Now the table explains itself. Ada is always waiting on time: you see her every day, so the calendar is the only thing in her way. Bo, on days 15 and 25, is waiting on closeness – the days have passed and you have not. The game turns those two words into two different sentences so that a silence reads as a person's reserve, not a fault. Try calling on Bo every third day (day % 3) and watch his reason change.

title: Build the camera and the view
intro: The view's fit, the zoom, the walkable floor and a camera that follows you, built up in five steps. The first three are functions you can check; the last two put them to work in a small room you can walk about in with the arrow keys.

steps.title: Fit the glass
steps.task: Write whole_scale(view: Vector2i, screen: Vector2i) -> int: how many whole times view fits inside screen, the smaller of the two ratios, rounded down, and never below 0. Then fit_view(screen: Vector2i) -> Vector2i: take the whole scale of MIN_VIEW on that screen (at least 1) and return the screen divided by it.

tests.label: a portrait view does not fit a 1920 by 1080 screen even once
1344 by 768 fits a 2688 by 1536 screen exactly twice
the shorter side limits it: only once
1920 by 1080 gets scale 2 and a 960 by 540 view
a tall modern phone: scale 2, view 1428 by 640
2400 by 1080: scale 2, view 1200 by 540
a screen too small for the minimum is not scaled down: scale 1, the view is the screen

hints: Divide each side of the screen by the same side of the view, turn each into a whole number with int(float(a) / float(b)), and take mini of the two.
var n: int = maxi(1, whole_scale(MIN_VIEW, screen)), then Vector2i(screen.x / n, screen.y / n).
steps.explain: Nothing is drawn yet, but this is the heart of how the game fills any phone. Every art pixel is drawn at a whole number of screen pixels, so the view is not a fixed size: it is the screen divided by that number. A 1920 by 1080 monitor gets a view of 960 by 540 at scale 2, and the numbers multiply back to the glass with no bars and no half pixels. A bigger minimum would force a smaller scale, which makes everything look smaller: the dial turns the opposite way from what you would guess.

steps.title: Lean in
steps.task: Write camera_zoom(art: int, lean: int) -> float: (art + lean) / art as a float, or 1.0 if art is zero or less. Then seen(view: Vector2, zoom: float) -> Vector2, the size of the world a view shows at that zoom: the view divided by the zoom, rounded up with .ceil().

tests.label: three screen pixels per art pixel plus one is 4 thirds
no lean, no zoom
a lean of 2 would be 5 thirds
a broken art size gives 1.0 rather than a divide by zero
at zoom 1.25 a 960 by 540 view shows 768 by 432 of the world
fractions round up, so the camera never shows less than it should

hints: Careful with integer division: convert with float(art + lean) / float(art). Put the guard first.
return (view / zoom).ceil() – a Vector2 divided by a float, then rounded up component by component.
steps.explain: In the game art is Assets.scaled(6), which is 3, and the lean is CAMERA_LEAN, 1, so the zoom is 4/3. It has to be a ratio of whole numbers like that: a zoom of 1.4 would put an art pixel on 4.2 screen pixels, which splits it, and pixel art smeared that way looks wrong. That is why the comment says there is nothing between 3/3, 4/3 and 5/3.

steps.title: Where you may walk
steps.task: The BOUND_ constants are now at the top of the script. Write bounds_for(room: Vector2i, wall_h: int) -> Rect2: the floor you can stand on. It starts BOUND_INSET_X in from the left and wall_h + BOUND_TOP_GAP down from the top, is BOUND_INSET_X clear of the right wall too, and stops BOUND_BOTTOM short of the bottom.

tests.label: the game's wide room: 48 in from each side, 267 down, ending 34 short of the bottom
a room half as wide has bounds half as wide, less the margins
and the little room used next

hints: A Rect2 is Rect2(x, y, width, height). The top is float(wall_h) + BOUND_TOP_GAP. The width loses the inset twice.
Rect2(BOUND_INSET_X, top, float(room.x) - BOUND_INSET_X * 2.0, float(room.y) - top - BOUND_BOTTOM)
steps.explain: Nothing is hard-coded to one room size, which is the reason the game computes these instead of writing numbers down: every room is a different size now. The original portrait numbers, 432 and 878, are exactly what this gives for a 1344-tall room with a 384 wall.

steps.title: A camera that follows
steps.task: Now a small world to walk about in: a room 640 wide and 240 tall seen through a 320 by 180 view, at the zoom from step 2. Add the constants WALL_H (60), ROOM (Vector2i(640, 240)), VIEW (Vector2(320, 180)) and SPEED (120.0), and the variables zoom, bounds, player and cam, set up in _ready from your three functions. Start player in the middle of the floor, 60 above its bottom edge, and cam on the player. In _process, move player.x with Input.get_axis("ui_left", "ui_right") at SPEED per second, clamped to bounds, then set cam from follow(), which is the player's position but clamped so that the part of the world the camera shows (half of seen() each side) never leaves the room. Draw the room through cam and zoom.

tests.label: you start in the middle of the floor
60 up from the bottom of the walkable floor
the camera starts on you
hold right for a long time: you stop at the right edge of the floor
but the camera stops 120 short of the room's end, so no edge shows
hold left: you stop at the left edge of the floor
and the camera stops 120 in from the left

hints: follow(): var half := VIEW / zoom / 2.0, then clampf(player.x, half.x, ROOM.x - half.x) and the same for y.
Screen position of a world point: (p - cam) * zoom + VIEW / 2.0. Draw everything with that, scaling sizes by zoom, and call queue_redraw() in _process.
steps.explain: Walk to each end and watch the green line, the edge of the floor you may stand on. The camera stops 120 short of each end of the room, half of what it sees, so the edge of the world never comes into view. In the game the same thing is done by giving the Camera2D four limit_ numbers (see _apply_camera_limits above); you have written by hand what the engine does for it.

steps.title: Whole pixels
steps.task: Round the player's position to whole numbers before the camera uses it, then clamp. Change nothing else.

tests.label: after one step of 7.5 the player is at 327.5 and the camera sits on 328
after seven steps the player is at 372.5 and the camera on 373
the camera is on a whole number

hints: In follow() make a target from roundf(player.x) and roundf(player.y) and clamp that instead.
var target := Vector2(roundf(player.x), roundf(player.y)), then clampf(target.x, half.x, ROOM.x - half.x).
steps.explain: The game does this on every frame: _camera.position = _player.position.round(). It is the same care as everywhere else in the file: nothing is placed between pixels, so the world does not shimmer as you walk. The player's own position stays fractional, so slow walking is still smooth; only the lens is snapped.

title: Build a phone that cannot be gamed
intro: A small phone with the same rules: numbers you have earned, two calls a day, a call that rings out the same way each time you try, texts that rotate through a list without repeating, and one incoming call a day. The hash is a simpler cousin of the game's, because this interpreter does its bit-twiddling in a smaller number size. Everything is printed or returned as plain text.

steps.title: Whose number you have
steps.task: Three functions. has_number(id) is true when the person is in heard and you have heard at least 1 of their story. calls_left() is CALLS_A_DAY when out_day is not today, otherwise what is left of it, never below 0. call_problem(id) returns the reason you cannot ring, in this order: "I do not have their number.", then "It is too late." if night, then "I have done enough ringing round for one day." if no calls are left, and otherwise "".

tests.label: someone whose story you have started has a number
heard 0 means no number
and a stranger has none
a new day starts with two calls
no number is the first problem
ringing Hal is fine

hints: A dictionary answers has(id), and heard[id] >= 1 is the threshold. Join them with and so an unknown name never gets looked up.
calls_left: if out_day != day return CALLS_A_DAY; otherwise maxi(0, CALLS_A_DAY - out).
steps.explain: The calls count carries the day it belongs to, so nothing has to reset it at midnight: a stale day simply reads as "a fresh two". The game's calls_left() is the same few lines, and its call_problem() returns text rather than a yes or no so that the phone can say why.

steps.title: A roll that stays rolled
steps.task: Add mix(n: int) -> int, a small hash: (n * 2654435761 % 4294967296) / 65536. Then add no_answer(id: String, d: int) -> bool: true when mix(code[id] * 31 + d) % 4 == 0. Notice that it takes the day as an argument, so it is a pure function: the same person and day always give the same answer.

tests.label: on day 5 Hal does not pick up
asking again gives the same answer
on day 7 he does
over a hundred days about one call in four rings out
different people have different bad days

hints: Two short functions. mix is one return; the / 65536 is whole-number division, because both sides are int.
return mix(code[id] * 31 + d) % 4 == 0
steps.explain: There is no random number anywhere. The "chance" is a fixed function of two inputs that behaves like chance across a hundred days, which is what misses() shows: about a quarter. The game's _mix() does the same job with a stronger shuffle, and for the reason you can see here: a weak hash on neighbouring numbers gives neighbouring answers, and the game once rang the same person every time.

steps.title: Place the call
steps.task: Write place_call(id: String) -> String. If call_problem(id) is not empty, return "" and change nothing. Otherwise: if out_day != day, set out_day = day and out = 0; add one to out whether or not they answer; and return "no answer" or "connected" according to no_answer(id, day).

tests.label: no number, no call
and nothing is spent
a call to Marisol is placed
so is one to Hal
two calls used, whether or not they answered
a third is refused

hints: Refuse first: if call_problem(id) != "": return "". Then the day check, then out += 1.
The result is two ifs or one: if no_answer(id, day): return "no answer", then return "connected".
steps.explain: Count out before you look at the outcome, as the game does: a call that rings out was still a call. Together with the seeded answer this closes the loophole. Ringing again is not allowed once you have used up the two, and if it were, you would hear the same silence.

steps.title: Texts that take turns
steps.task: Add var sent := {} (how many texts each person has sent you) and var threads := {} (id to an array of messages), and thread(id) -> Array, which makes an empty array on first use and returns it. Then receive_text(id: String) -> bool: false if you have no number; otherwise take the person's next line, which is texts[id][sent_so_far % size]; add one to their sent tally; push {"w": "them", "t": line, "d": day} on to their thread; and trim the front off so the thread never holds more than THREAD_KEEP. Return true.

tests.label: a stranger cannot text you
Hal texts twice
his first two texts are a then b, not a twice

tests.expr: receive_text("hal") and receive_text("hal") and receive_text("hal") and receive_text("hal")
tests.label: four more arrive
the thread holds THREAD_KEEP and no more
but the tally still says six were sent
and the sixth text wrapped round to b

hints: Read the tally with sent.get(id, 0), so a first text finds 0. The line is lines[n % lines.size()].
Trim with while msgs.size() > THREAD_KEEP: msgs.pop_front(). Write the new tally to sent, not to anything the trim touches.
steps.explain: Check the last two tests together: the thread shows four messages but sent["hal"] is 6. Had you worked out the next text from msgs.size() you would be stuck at 4 forever, which is the bug the game's comment describes. State that must survive trimming gets a variable of its own.

steps.title: Somebody rings you
steps.task: Add var ring_day := 0, var ring := "" and var ring_done := false, and incoming_call() -> String. If ring_day == day, the question was settled this morning: return "" if ring_done, otherwise ring. If fraction < 0.40 or it is night, return "" and settle nothing. Otherwise list everyone with a number (could); the caller is could[mix(day * 7919 + 13) % could.size()] but only when could is not empty and mix(day) % RING_ODDS == 0, else "". Store ring_day, ring and ring_done = (pick == ""), and return the pick. A helper at the bottom, on_day(d), jumps to day d and asks.

tests.label: day 5 is a quiet one
day 6 somebody with a number rings
asking again gives the same caller
over a hundred days about one day in four has a caller
and never somebody whose number you do not have

hints: Build could with a for id in heard loop and has_number(id). The early return comes first, so a settled day never re-asks.
After the two guards: var pick := "", then one if that sets it from could, then store all three variables and return pick.
steps.explain: You have now made a chance twice over: seeded in the hash, and settled in the three stored variables. Either alone would nearly do; together they mean the phone gives the same answer whenever, and however often, you look. That is what lets the game promise a person has "rung" on a given day. Try changing RING_ODDS to 2 and watch rings_in(100) climb.

title: Build the fishing bar
intro: The float, the green, the catch and the record book. The starter draws a bar and a float that does not move yet. Space is the reel button – click the view first so it has the keyboard, or use the A button under it.
starter:
extends Node2D

const TRACK := Rect2(20, 76, 280, 28)   # the bar the float slides along
const FISH := {   # the game's own table; you will need it at step 4
	"sardine": {"name": "Sardine", "min": 8, "max": 22},
	"bass": {"name": "Sea Bass", "min": 20, "max": 55},
	"salmon": {"name": "Salmon", "min": 35, "max": 90},
	"koi": {"name": "Golden Koi", "min": 40, "max": 110},
}

var _t := 0.0
var _speed := 0.62     # crossings a second; the game picks 0.55 to 0.80
var said := "Space to reel it in"

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	queue_redraw()

func marker() -> float:
	return 0.0

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#f3f7f9"))
	draw_rect(TRACK, Color("#dfe9ef"))
	draw_rect(TRACK, Color("#b6c9d4"), false, 2.0)
	var mx := TRACK.position.x + TRACK.size.x * marker()
	draw_rect(Rect2(mx - 3, TRACK.position.y - 8, 6, TRACK.size.y + 16), Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(20, 40), said, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))

steps.title: Bob the float
steps.task: Make the float move. In _process, add delta * _speed to _t. Then make marker() turn _t into a number that goes from 0 up to 1 and back down to 0, over and over: 0.5 at _t = 0.5, 1 at _t = 1, 0.75 at _t = 1.25, 0 again at _t = 2.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const TRACK := Rect2(20, 76, 280, 28)   # the bar the float slides along
const FISH := {   # the game's own table; you will need it at step 4
	"sardine": {"name": "Sardine", "min": 8, "max": 22},
	"bass": {"name": "Sea Bass", "min": 20, "max": 55},
	"salmon": {"name": "Salmon", "min": 35, "max": 90},
	"koi": {"name": "Golden Koi", "min": 40, "max": 110},
}

var _t := 0.0
var _speed := 0.62     # crossings a second; the game picks 0.55 to 0.80
var said := "Space to reel it in"

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	_t += delta * _speed
	queue_redraw()

func marker() -> float:
	var f := fposmod(_t, 2.0)
	return f if f <= 1.0 else 2.0 - f

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#f3f7f9"))
	draw_rect(TRACK, Color("#dfe9ef"))
	draw_rect(TRACK, Color("#b6c9d4"), false, 2.0)
	var mx := TRACK.position.x + TRACK.size.x * marker()
	draw_rect(Rect2(mx - 3, TRACK.position.y - 8, 6, TRACK.size.y + 16), Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(20, 40), said, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))

tests.label: after one second the float is 0.62 of the way along
after two it has turned at the end and is coming back: 0.76
after three, 0.14
after four it has turned again and is going out: 0.48

hints: First the count: _t += delta * _speed in _process.
fposmod(_t, 2.0) is the remainder after dividing by 2: it climbs from 0 to 2, then starts again. The first half of that climb is already what you want.
Keep the remainder in a variable f. If it is no more than 1, return it; otherwise return 2.0 - f, which runs from 1 back down to 0.
steps.explain: Watch the ends. The float slows for nothing and jumps nowhere: it reaches the edge and comes back at the same pace. Replace the last line of marker() with return fposmod(_t, 1.0) to see the wrap the game's comment decided against, then put it back.

steps.title: Paint the green
steps.task: Give the bar its bite window. Add var _zone_start := 0.38 and var _zone_size := 0.24, both fractions of the bar. Write in_zone() -> bool, true while the marker is between the start of the zone and its end, and zone_rect() -> Rect2, the zone's rectangle on the TRACK. In _draw(), fill that rectangle with a see-through green before the float is drawn, and draw the float in Color("#7fae72") while it is in the zone.

tests.label: at the start the float is at 0, outside the green
the green starts 0.38 of the way along the bar
and is 0.24 of the bar wide
and as tall as the bar
three quarters of a second in, the float is in the green
at two seconds it is past it
and on the way back it crosses the green again
_draw() fills zone_rect()
tests.why: Draw the green with draw_rect(zone_rect(), …) so you can see where to aim.

hints: in_zone() is two comparisons joined by and. Ask for marker() once and keep it in a variable.
The bar is TRACK.size.x wide and starts at TRACK.position.x, so the zone's left edge is TRACK.position.x + TRACK.size.x * _zone_start and its width is TRACK.size.x * _zone_size.
In _draw(): draw_rect(zone_rect(), Color(0.49, 0.71, 0.45, 0.55)) before the float, and var col := Color("#7fae72") if in_zone() else Color("#e0808f") for the float itself.
steps.explain: The float turning green is the game being fair: it shows you the answer to in_zone() before you commit. Everything is in fractions of the bar, so the same two numbers work on a bar of any width – the game's is as wide as the card it sits in. Change _zone_size to 0.08 to find out how hard this could have been.

steps.title: Reel it in
steps.task: Add var caught := 0 and a function reel(). If the float is not in the zone, set said to "Splash. It got away." and stop there. If it is, add 1 to caught and set said to "Got one!". Call reel() from _process on the frame ui_accept is first pressed.

tests.label: Space with the float at the edge: it gets away
and nothing is caught
Space with the float in the green: one caught
holding nothing down catches nothing more

hints: Deal with the miss first and return, so the rest of the function can take the catch for granted.
if not in_zone(): then set said and return. After it: caught += 1 and the other message.
In _process: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"): reel(). Just pressed, or holding Space would reel sixty times a second.
steps.explain: This is the whole of the skill: one question, asked at the moment you press. The bar knows nothing about fish and reel() knows nothing about time; in_zone() is the only thing that passes between them. In the game they are even in different classes – the bar is a control, and the card that holds it does the reeling.

steps.title: See what bit
steps.task: Decide what was on the hook. The FISH table at the top has been waiting for this. Add a variable night_or_rain := false, and fish_pool(koi_bites: bool) -> Array: three "sardine", two "bass", one "salmon", and one "koi" as well when koi_bites is true. On a catch, reel() should pick one entry of fish_pool(night_or_rain) at random into last_fish, pick a whole length between that kind's min and max into last_cm, and say it: "A 31cm sea bass."

tests.label: by day and in the dry there are six tickets in the pool
three sardine, two bass, one salmon
and no koi
at night or in the rain, one koi ticket joins them
making seven
a catch names one of the four fish
with a length inside that fish's range
and says so, in the form: A 31cm sea bass.

hints: Build the pool as a list with repeats in it – ["sardine", "sardine", "sardine", "bass", "bass", "salmon"] – and append the koi inside an if.
One entry at random: pool[randi() % pool.size()]. A whole number in a range: randi_range(low, high).
Look the fish up once: var info: Dictionary = FISH[last_fish]. Then last_cm = randi_range(info["min"], info["max"]) and said = "A %dcm %s." % [last_cm, str(info["name"]).to_lower()].
steps.explain: Catch a dozen and count: about half are sardines. Nothing in the code says "50%" – the list has three sardines in six entries, and that is the whole of the weighting. Now set night_or_rain to true and fish for the koi; it is one ticket in seven, so it may take a while. Changing the odds means editing a list, which is the kind of change you can make without fear.

steps.title: Keep the best
steps.task: Remember the biggest of each kind. Add var records := {} and record_best(key: String, value: float) -> bool: if value is bigger than what is stored under key – or nothing is stored yet – store it and return true; otherwise change nothing and return false. In reel(), offer every catch to it, and when it is a record say "A 31cm sea bass! My biggest yet." instead.

tests.label: the first bass is a record
a smaller one is not
and does not replace it
equalling the record does not beat it
a bigger one is, and is stored
each kind has its own record
a catch from the bar goes in the book

hints: A dictionary can answer for a key it does not have: records.get(key, 0.0) gives 0.0 when nothing is stored, so the first fish always beats it.
var prev := float(records.get(key, 0.0)), then if value > prev: store it and return true. The last line is return false.
In reel(), after the ordinary message: if record_best(last_fish, float(last_cm)): and set the proud one. To see the book, draw records under the bar in _draw() with a for key in records.keys(): loop.
steps.explain: The function both changes something and answers a question, and the answer is what lets the caller celebrate without looking in the book itself. Compare it with the game's record_best above: the same lines, with a save at the end. report_score for the arcade is the same again. Once you have seen the shape – old value with a default, compare, store, say which – you will find it in every game that has a high score.

title: Build tap, walk, then act
intro: A room with one thing in it, a kettle, and somebody to walk to it. Your script is the room; she is a point called her. Click or touch the view to tap – the starter already turns that into a call to handle_tap() – and the pink dot shows where she has been sent.
starter:
extends Node2D

const SPEED := 80.0        # pixels a second; the game's is 280, in a far bigger room
const ARRIVE_EPS := 2.5    # closer than this counts as there
const KETTLE := Rect2(236, 40, 36, 36)   # the thing in the room
const KETTLE_ACT := Vector2(254, 96)     # where she stands to use it

var her := Vector2(50, 130)
var _target := Vector2(50, 130)
var said := ""
var cups := 0
var _was_down := false

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func walk_to(p: Vector2) -> void:
	pass

func handle_tap(p: Vector2) -> void:
	walk_to(p)

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	# a click or a touch in the view is a tap
	var down := Input.is_mouse_button_pressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT)
	if down and not _was_down:
		handle_tap(get_global_mouse_position())
	_was_down = down
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#e8d9c5"))
	draw_rect(KETTLE, Color("#7ea8c6"))
	draw_circle(KETTLE_ACT, 2, Color("#b9a58c"))
	draw_circle(_target, 3, Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_circle(her, 7, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 20), said, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 170), "cups: %d" % cups, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))

steps.title: Walk to a point
steps.task: Make her go where she is sent. walk_to(p) should remember p as the _target, and every frame _process should move her towards the target at SPEED pixels a second, stopping on it and never going past. Then click about in the view.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const SPEED := 80.0        # pixels a second; the game's is 280, in a far bigger room
const ARRIVE_EPS := 2.5    # closer than this counts as there
const KETTLE := Rect2(236, 40, 36, 36)   # the thing in the room
const KETTLE_ACT := Vector2(254, 96)     # where she stands to use it

var her := Vector2(50, 130)
var _target := Vector2(50, 130)
var said := ""
var cups := 0
var _was_down := false

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func walk_to(p: Vector2) -> void:
	_target = p

func handle_tap(p: Vector2) -> void:
	walk_to(p)

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	# a click or a touch in the view is a tap
	var down := Input.is_mouse_button_pressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT)
	if down and not _was_down:
		handle_tap(get_global_mouse_position())
	_was_down = down
	her = her.move_toward(_target, SPEED * delta)
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#e8d9c5"))
	draw_rect(KETTLE, Color("#7ea8c6"))
	draw_circle(KETTLE_ACT, 2, Color("#b9a58c"))
	draw_circle(_target, 3, Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_circle(her, 7, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 20), said, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 170), "cups: %d" % cups, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))

tests.label: walk_to(Vector2(210, 130)) sets the target
one second later she has gone 80 pixels
and she stops on the spot, not past it

hints: walk_to is one line: _target = p.
A Vector2 can step towards another without overshooting: a.move_toward(b, distance). The distance for one frame is SPEED * delta.
In _process, before queue_redraw(): her = her.move_toward(_target, SPEED * delta).
steps.explain: Click, and she goes; click again before she gets there and she turns, because there is only one target and the new one replaced the old. The game's walk has more in it – a route round the furniture, a ramp up to speed and down again – but it ends the same way, by closing the distance to one point.

steps.title: Know when she arrives
steps.task: Something has to notice the moment she gets there – once, not sixty times a second. Declare signal arrived. Give walk_to a second parameter, notify: bool = false, kept in a variable _pending_arrival. In _process, after moving her: if she is within ARRIVE_EPS of the target and an arrival is pending, clear the flag and emit the signal. Connect the signal in _ready() to a new function, _on_player_arrived(), which for now adds 1 to a variable arrivals.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

signal arrived

const SPEED := 80.0        # pixels a second; the game's is 280, in a far bigger room
const ARRIVE_EPS := 2.5    # closer than this counts as there
const KETTLE := Rect2(236, 40, 36, 36)   # the thing in the room
const KETTLE_ACT := Vector2(254, 96)     # where she stands to use it

var her := Vector2(50, 130)
var _target := Vector2(50, 130)
var _pending_arrival := false
var arrivals := 0
var said := ""
var cups := 0
var _was_down := false

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view
	arrived.connect(_on_player_arrived)

func walk_to(p: Vector2, notify: bool = false) -> void:
	_target = p
	_pending_arrival = notify

func _on_player_arrived() -> void:
	arrivals += 1

func handle_tap(p: Vector2) -> void:
	walk_to(p)

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	# a click or a touch in the view is a tap
	var down := Input.is_mouse_button_pressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT)
	if down and not _was_down:
		handle_tap(get_global_mouse_position())
	_was_down = down
	her = her.move_toward(_target, SPEED * delta)
	if _pending_arrival and her.distance_to(_target) <= ARRIVE_EPS:
		_pending_arrival = false
		arrived.emit()
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#e8d9c5"))
	draw_rect(KETTLE, Color("#7ea8c6"))
	draw_circle(KETTLE_ACT, 2, Color("#b9a58c"))
	draw_circle(_target, 3, Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_circle(her, 7, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 20), said, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 170), "cups: %d" % cups, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))

tests.label: sent 80 pixels away and asked to report: nothing yet
half-way there, still nothing
she arrives, and it is reported once – not once a frame
a walk that does not ask to be told…
…is not reported when it ends

hints: Four small pieces: signal arrived at the top, var _pending_arrival := false and var arrivals := 0, the new parameter on walk_to, and arrived.connect(_on_player_arrived) in _ready().
In walk_to: _pending_arrival = notify. The distance left is her.distance_to(_target).
After the line that moves her: if _pending_arrival and her.distance_to(_target) <= ARRIVE_EPS: then _pending_arrival = false and arrived.emit().
steps.explain: Nothing new shows yet, but the walk now has an end that the rest of the script can hear. The flag is what makes it happen once: without it, "is she at the target?" is true on every frame she stands there. This is Player.walk_to() and its arrived signal, with the same names.

steps.title: Queue the errand
steps.task:
Now the note. Add var _pending_action := "" and three functions:

  • _queue(action: String, walk_to_point: Vector2) – remembers the action and sends her to the point, asking to be told on arrival
  • _run(action: String) – does the thing. For "kettle": add 1 to cups and set said to "The kettle is on."
  • _on_player_arrived() – keeps counting arrivals; then, if there is a pending action, clears it and runs it

To watch it, call _queue("kettle", KETTLE_ACT) at the end of _ready().
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

signal arrived

const SPEED := 80.0        # pixels a second; the game's is 280, in a far bigger room
const ARRIVE_EPS := 2.5    # closer than this counts as there
const KETTLE := Rect2(236, 40, 36, 36)   # the thing in the room
const KETTLE_ACT := Vector2(254, 96)     # where she stands to use it

var her := Vector2(50, 130)
var _target := Vector2(50, 130)
var _pending_arrival := false
var _pending_action := ""
var arrivals := 0
var said := ""
var cups := 0
var _was_down := false

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view
	arrived.connect(_on_player_arrived)
	_queue("kettle", KETTLE_ACT)

func walk_to(p: Vector2, notify: bool = false) -> void:

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#e8d9c5"))
	draw_rect(KETTLE, Color("#7ea8c6"))
	draw_circle(KETTLE_ACT, 2, Color("#b9a58c"))
	draw_circle(_target, 3, Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_circle(her, 7, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 20), said, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 170), "cups: %d" % cups, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))

tests.label: _queue("kettle", KETTLE_ACT) leaves the note
and sends her to the spot in front of the kettle
a second into the walk, nothing has happened
when she gets there, the kettle goes on
once
and the note is used up

hints: _queue is two lines: store the action, then walk_to(walk_to_point, true).
_run is a match action: with one branch, "kettle":.
In _on_player_arrived, after counting: if _pending_action == "": return. Then copy the action into a local variable, set _pending_action = "", and only then call _run with the copy.
steps.explain: She sets off the moment the view starts and the words appear when she stops, not before. The kettle did not have to know anything about walking, and the walk knew nothing about kettles: the note joins them. Add a second branch to _run and queue that instead – nothing else needs to change.

steps.title: Read the tap
steps.task: Let the tap decide. Take the _queue call out of _ready(), and rewrite handle_tap(p) to ask what is under the point. First of all it forgets any errand she was already on – write that as its own function, _drop_pending(). Then: if p is on the KETTLE, queue "kettle" at KETTLE_ACT; anywhere else is bare floor, a plain walk to p that asks to be told on arrival.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

signal arrived

const SPEED := 80.0        # pixels a second; the game's is 280, in a far bigger room
const ARRIVE_EPS := 2.5    # closer than this counts as there
const KETTLE := Rect2(236, 40, 36, 36)   # the thing in the room
const KETTLE_ACT := Vector2(254, 96)     # where she stands to use it

var her := Vector2(50, 130)
var _target := Vector2(50, 130)
var _pending_arrival := false
var _pending_action := ""
var arrivals := 0
var said := ""
var cups := 0
var _was_down := false

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view
	arrived.connect(_on_player_arrived)

func walk_to(p: Vector2, notify: bool = false) -> void:
	_target = p
	_pending_arrival = notify

func _queue(action: String, walk_to_point: Vector2) -> void:
	_pending_action = action
	walk_to(walk_to_point, true)

func _drop_pending() -> void:
	_pending_action = ""

func _on_player_arrived() -> void:

		_queue("kettle", KETTLE_ACT)
		return

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	# a click or a touch in the view is a tap
	var down := Input.is_mouse_button_pressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT)
	if down and not _was_down:
		handle_tap(get_global_mouse_position())
	_was_down = down
