	if _pending_arrival and her.distance_to(_target) <= ARRIVE_EPS:
		_pending_arrival = false
		arrived.emit()
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#e8d9c5"))
	draw_rect(KETTLE, Color("#7ea8c6"))
	draw_circle(KETTLE_ACT, 2, Color("#b9a58c"))
	draw_circle(_target, 3, Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_circle(her, 7, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 20), said, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 170), "cups: %d" % cups, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))

tests.label: nothing is queued until something is tapped
tapping the kettle queues it
and sends her to the spot in front of it, not to where you tapped
tapping the floor on the way forgets the kettle
she walks to the floor you tapped
and no kettle goes on behind your back
tap the kettle again: nothing yet
she walks over, and then it goes on

hints: _drop_pending() is one line, _pending_action = "", and it is the first line of handle_tap.
A Rect2 can tell you whether a point is inside it: KETTLE.has_point(p).
After dropping: if KETTLE.has_point(p): queue the kettle and return. The last line, for everything else, is walk_to(p, true).
steps.explain: Tap the kettle and watch the pink dot: it lands in front of the kettle, not on it, and the words wait until she is there. Now tap the kettle and then the floor before she arrives – she turns, and the kettle stays off. Take _drop_pending() out and try that again: she walks to the floor and the kettle goes on from across the room, which is the bug the game's comment describes. The game's _handle_tap is this function with more questions in it, asked in a fixed order.

steps.title: Within arm's reach
steps.task: The keyboard's way in. Add const REACH := 30.0 and a function _interact_nearby(), called from _process when ui_accept (Space) has just been pressed. If she is within REACH of the kettle – inside its rectangle grown by that much – drop any errand and run "kettle" on the spot, with no walking. If she is not, set said to "Nothing within reach." and leave any errand she is on alone.
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

signal arrived

const SPEED := 80.0        # pixels a second; the game's is 280, in a far bigger room
const ARRIVE_EPS := 2.5    # closer than this counts as there
const REACH := 30.0        # how far her arms go; the game's is 60
const KETTLE := Rect2(236, 40, 36, 36)   # the thing in the room
const KETTLE_ACT := Vector2(254, 96)     # where she stands to use it

var her := Vector2(50, 130)
var _target := Vector2(50, 130)
var _pending_arrival := false
var _pending_action := ""
var arrivals := 0
var said := ""
var cups := 0
var _was_down := false

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view
	arrived.connect(_on_player_arrived)

func walk_to(p: Vector2, notify: bool = false) -> void:
	_target = p
	_pending_arrival = notify

func _queue(action: String, walk_to_point: Vector2) -> void:
	_pending_action = action
	walk_to(walk_to_point, true)

func _drop_pending() -> void:
	_pending_action = ""

func _on_player_arrived() -> void:
	arrivals += 1
	if _pending_action == "":
		return
	var action := _pending_action
	_pending_action = ""
	_run(action)

func _run(action: String) -> void:
	match action:
		"kettle":
			cups += 1
			said = "The kettle is on."

func handle_tap(p: Vector2) -> void:
	_drop_pending()
	if KETTLE.has_point(p):
		_queue("kettle", KETTLE_ACT)
		return
	walk_to(p, true)

func _interact_nearby() -> void:
	if not KETTLE.grow(REACH).has_point(her):
		said = "Nothing within reach."
		return
	_drop_pending()
	_run("kettle")

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	# a click or a touch in the view is a tap
	var down := Input.is_mouse_button_pressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT)
	if down and not _was_down:
		handle_tap(get_global_mouse_position())
	_was_down = down
	if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):
		_interact_nearby()
	her = her.move_toward(_target, SPEED * delta)
	if _pending_arrival and her.distance_to(_target) <= ARRIVE_EPS:
		_pending_arrival = false
		arrived.emit()
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#e8d9c5"))
	draw_rect(KETTLE, Color("#7ea8c6"))
	draw_circle(KETTLE_ACT, 2, Color("#b9a58c"))
	draw_circle(_target, 3, Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_circle(her, 7, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 20), said, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(10, 170), "cups: %d" % cups, 0, -1, 12, Color("#4c3438"))

tests.label: Space from across the room: nothing within reach
and no kettle
tap the kettle, so she sets off…
…and Space too early does not cancel the errand
she arrives and the kettle goes on
Space while standing beside it: on again, at once
without taking a step

hints: KETTLE.grow(REACH) is the kettle's rectangle made REACH bigger on every side. If her is inside that, she is close enough.
Deal with the far case first: if not KETTLE.grow(REACH).has_point(her): set said and return. Then _drop_pending() and _run("kettle").
In _process: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"): _interact_nearby(). Click the view first so it has the keyboard.
steps.explain: Two ways to the same kettle, and both end in _run("kettle"). Tapping brings her to it; Space only works once she is already there, so neither is a shortcut past the walk. Notice which branch drops the errand and which does not: pressing Space with nothing in reach did nothing, so it has no business cancelling a walk that was on its way to something. The game makes the same choice, and says so in a comment.

title: Build a save that cannot break the game
intro: A life of three values – a day, some coins, a room – saved, loaded, checked, kept in three slots and turned into a backup code. The book's interpreter has no files, so a dictionary called disk stands in for the phone's storage: a file's path is the key and the text in it is the value.

steps.title: Write it down
steps.task: Give each life a file. Make slot_path(n) return "user://tinyhome_save_slot1.json" for slot 1, and the same with 2 or 3 – and for any other number, the nearest of those. Add save_now() -> bool, which turns state into text with JSON.stringify, writes it to the current slot's path and returns true. Then make earn() save as its last act, and at the end of _ready() print the file so you can read it.

tests.label: slot_path(9) is clamped to slot 3
slot_path(0) is clamped to slot 1
after earn(5) the file already has the new total
_ready() prints the saved file

hints: The path is a format string: "user://tinyhome_save_slot%d.json" % n. Keep n in range first with clampi(n, 1, SLOTS).
save_now() is two lines: write_file(slot_path(slot), JSON.stringify(state)), then return true. Call it on the last line of earn().
To see the file: print(read_file(slot_path(slot))) at the end of _ready().
steps.explain: The line in the output is the whole save: a dictionary written as text. Nobody has to remember to save, because the function that changes the coins does it. In the game that last line is _changed(), and it also tells the screen to redraw. Add earn(12) under earn(30) and watch the file follow.

steps.title: Read it back
steps.task: Add load_save() -> Dictionary. If the current slot has no file, return default_state(). Otherwise read the text and give it to JSON.parse_string; if what comes back is not a dictionary, return default_state() again; if it is, return it. At the end of _ready(), set state from load_save() and print its coins.

tests.label: what was saved comes back: the same coins
a damaged file loads as a new life, day 1
so does a file that is JSON but not a dictionary
and no file at all is a new life too

hints: Three ways out, each with a return. The first is if not file_exists(slot_path(slot)):.
var parsed = JSON.parse_string(read_file(slot_path(slot))) gives null when the text is not JSON. Ask what you got with typeof(parsed) != TYPE_DICTIONARY.
Leave the type off parsed – write var parsed =, not := – because it may be a dictionary, an array or nothing.
steps.explain: Look closely at the second line of output: 30.0, not 30. JSON has one kind of number, and Godot reads every one of them back as a float. Nothing is broken yet, but a game that later writes "%d coins" or uses the day to pick from a list will care. The next step puts it right, along with everything else a file can get wrong.

steps.title: Trust nothing
steps.task:
Add sanitize(s: Dictionary) -> Dictionary. Start from default_state() and copy a value across only when it passes:

  • day – a number, at least 1, kept as an int
  • coins – a number, kept as an int and never below 0
  • room – a String that is one of ROOMS

Anything else in s is left behind. Then make load_save() return sanitize(parsed).

tests.label: a good save comes through whole
day 4.0 becomes the int 4
day 0 is refused: the default, 1, stays
a day that is not a number is refused
coins are never below 0
a room that does not exist is refused
a key the game does not know is left behind
load_save() uses it: the coins come back as an int

hints: Begin with var d := default_state() and end with return d. In between, one if per key, and nothing happens when it fails.

Each if asks three things in order: is the key there, is it the right type, is the value allowed. For the day: if s.has("day") and typeof(s["day"]) in [TYPE_INT, TYPE_FLOAT] and s["day"] >= 1: then d["day"] = int(s["day"]).
Coins: the same type check, then d["coins"] = maxi(0, int(s["coins"])). Room: typeof(s["room"]) == TYPE_STRING and ROOMS.has(s["room"]).
steps.explain: The output now ends in 30. Notice what the function never does: it never fixes the dictionary it was given. It builds a good one and lets values in. That is why the order inside each if matters – s["day"] >= 1 on a day that is a word would be an error, and the type check before it stops the line getting that far.

steps.title: Three lives
steps.task: Add switch_slot(n: int) -> bool. For a slot that does not exist, or the one you are already in, it does nothing and returns false. Otherwise it saves the life you are leaving, changes slot, loads the life that is there and returns true. In _ready(), visit slot 2 and come back, printing the slot and its coins each time.

tests.label: switch_slot(3) moves to slot 3
which is a new life: 0 coins
earn 7 there, then move to slot 2
slot 2 is its own life: 0 coins
earn 2 there and go back: slot 3 kept its 7
and slot 2 kept its 2
switching to the slot you are in does nothing
there is no slot 9
and a refused switch leaves you where you were
_ready() visits slot 2 and comes back

hints: Start with the guard: if n < 1 or n > SLOTS or n == slot: then return false.
After the guard, the order matters: save_now() while slot still names the old life, then slot = n, then state = load_save().
In _ready(): switch_slot(2), then print("slot ", slot, ": ", state["coins"], " coins"), and the same pair again for slot 1.
steps.explain: Nothing new was needed for a second life: save_now() and load_save() already ask slot_path(slot) where to look, so changing one number changes which file they mean. Slot 2 had no file, and the first way out of load_save() turned that into a fresh start. Swap the first two lines after the guard and see what happens to slot 2.

steps.title: A code to keep
steps.task:
Last, a life you can carry in an email. Add a constant CODE_HEADER := "TINYHOME-1" and three functions:

  • backup_code() -> String – the header, the length of the JSON, and the JSON, joined by colons
  • code_problem(text: String) -> String – a sentence saying what is wrong with a code, or "" if nothing is. It should refuse an empty paste, a code without the header, a code whose text is not as long as its number says, and one that does not hold a dictionary
  • restore_code(text: String) -> bool – if the code has a problem, change nothing and return false; otherwise sanitise what is inside, make it the state, save, and return true

Print backup_code() at the end of _ready().

tests.label: a code starts with TINYHOME-1:
a fresh code has no problem
an empty paste is refused
a code with another header is refused
a code with its end cut off is refused
a code with no dictionary inside is refused
a good code is restored, spaces round it or not
sanitised on the way in: day 9, 0 coins, the bedroom
and saved
restore_code() returns false for a bad code
and leaves the life alone: still day 9
_ready() prints the code

hints: The code is one format string: "%s:%d:%s" % [CODE_HEADER, json.length(), json], where json is JSON.stringify(state).

To take a code apart, find the first two colons: var a := clean.find(":") and var b := clean.find(":", a + 1). The header is clean.substr(0, a), the number int(clean.substr(a + 1, b - a - 1)), and the life is everything after: clean.substr(b + 1). Do not split on colons – the JSON is full of them.

code_problem() is a ladder of ifs that each return a sentence, with return "" at the bottom. restore_code() starts with if code_problem(text) != "": return false, then state = sanitize(JSON.parse_string(…)) and save_now().
steps.explain: The last line of output is your life as text. Copy it, change the 30 inside it to 300 by hand, and give it to code_problem(): the count in the middle no longer matches and the code is refused – which is exactly how a line clipped by a mail program gets caught. The game's code is the same three parts with the JSON gzipped and written in base64, so it is shorter and has no colons or spaces of its own. And because a restored life goes through sanitize() like any other, a code cannot put in anything a save file could not.

title: Build a talk box
intro: A box that types, rests, waits for you, offers answers and reports which was chosen. The drawing and the plumbing are in the starter; you write how the box behaves. Click the view so it has the keyboard: Space is the tap, the up arrow changes the speed, and left and right will choose an answer.
starter:
extends Node2D

const TEXT_SPEEDS := [26.0, 46.0, 0.0]   # characters a second
const TEXT_SPEED_NAMES := ["Calm", "Normal", "Instant"]
const BOX := Rect2(10, 104, 300, 66)
const LINES := [
	"Each letter arrives on its own.",
	"A full stop rests. A comma, less.",
	"Tap early, and the line is finished.",
]
const REPLIES := [
	{"id": "warm", "text": "Say thanks"},
	{"id": "wry", "text": "Make a joke"},
]
const ANSWERS := {
	"warm": "That came back as the id warm.",
	"wry": "That came back as the id wry.",
}

var text_speed := 0        # a position in TEXT_SPEEDS; the game starts on 1
var is_open := false
var _queue: Array = []     # lines still to come
var _full := ""            # the line on screen
var _shown := 0            # how many of its characters are showing
var _typing := false
var _budget := 0.0         # seconds of typing time not yet spent
var _hold := 0.0           # seconds still to rest on a full stop (step 3)
var _pending: Array = []   # answers waiting for the lines to be read (step 4)
var choices: Array = []    # answers on screen now (step 4)

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view
	say(LINES)

func cps() -> float:
	return TEXT_SPEEDS[text_speed]

func cycle_text_speed() -> String:
	text_speed = (text_speed + 1) % TEXT_SPEEDS.size()
	return TEXT_SPEED_NAMES[text_speed]

## Open the box on some lines.
func say(lines: Array) -> void:
	_queue = lines.duplicate()
	_pending = []
	choices = []
	is_open = true
	_show_next()

func close() -> void:
	is_open = false
	_typing = false
	_queue = []
	_pending = []
	choices = []

func _show_next() -> void:
	_full = _queue.pop_front()
	_shown = 0
	_budget = 0.0
	_hold = 0.0
	_typing = true
	if cps() <= 0.0:   # Instant: the whole line at once
		_finish_line()

func _finish_line() -> void:
	_typing = false
	_hold = 0.0
	_shown = _full.length()

func _type(delta: float) -> void:
	if not _typing:
		return
	if cps() <= 0.0:   # switched to Instant in the middle of a line
		_finish_line()
		return
	# step 1 goes here

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_up"):
		cycle_text_speed()
	_type(delta)
	queue_redraw()

func prompt() -> String:
	if not choices.is_empty():
		return "your turn"
	if _typing:
		return "…"
	if not _queue.is_empty():
		return "Space: next"
	if not _pending.is_empty():
		return "Space: answer"
	return "Space: finish"

func _draw() -> void:
	var font := ThemeDB.fallback_font
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#cfe3c8"))
	draw_string(font, Vector2(10, 16), "speed: " + TEXT_SPEED_NAMES[text_speed], 0, -1, 10, Color("#4c3438"))
	if not is_open:
		return
	draw_rect(BOX, Color("#fffafb"))
	draw_rect(BOX, Color("#f0c7d0"), false, 2.0)
	draw_string(font, BOX.position + Vector2(10, 16), "Somebody", 0, -1, 10, Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_string(font, BOX.position + Vector2(206, 16), prompt(), 0, -1, 10, Color("#8a6b73"))
	draw_string(font, BOX.position + Vector2(10, 33), _full.substr(0, _shown), 0, -1, 10, Color("#4c3438"))
	for i in choices.size():
		var r := Rect2(BOX.position.x + 10 + i * 142, BOX.position.y + 42, 136, 18)
		draw_rect(r, Color("#fbe4e8"))
		draw_rect(r, Color("#f0c7d0"), false, 1.0)
		draw_string(font, r.position + Vector2(6, 13), ("< " if i == 0 else "> ") + str(choices[i]["text"]), 0, -1, 10, Color("#4c3438"))

steps.title: Type it out
steps.task: Finish _type(delta), which runs every frame while a line is typing. One character costs 1.0 / cps() seconds. Add delta to _budget, then, for as long as the budget can pay for a character and there are characters left, pay for one and add 1 to _shown. When every character of _full is showing, call _finish_line().
steps.solution:
extends Node2D

const TEXT_SPEEDS := [26.0, 46.0, 0.0]   # characters a second
const TEXT_SPEED_NAMES := ["Calm", "Normal", "Instant"]
const BOX := Rect2(10, 104, 300, 66)
const LINES := [
	"Each letter arrives on its own.",
	"A full stop rests. A comma, less.",
	"Tap early, and the line is finished.",
]
const REPLIES := [
	{"id": "warm", "text": "Say thanks"},
	{"id": "wry", "text": "Make a joke"},
]
const ANSWERS := {
	"warm": "That came back as the id warm.",
	"wry": "That came back as the id wry.",
}

var text_speed := 0        # a position in TEXT_SPEEDS; the game starts on 1
var is_open := false
var _queue: Array = []     # lines still to come
var _full := ""            # the line on screen
var _shown := 0            # how many of its characters are showing
var _typing := false
var _budget := 0.0         # seconds of typing time not yet spent
var _hold := 0.0           # seconds still to rest on a full stop (step 3)
var _pending: Array = []   # answers waiting for the lines to be read (step 4)
var choices: Array = []    # answers on screen now (step 4)

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view
	say(LINES)

func cps() -> float:
	return TEXT_SPEEDS[text_speed]

func cycle_text_speed() -> String:
	text_speed = (text_speed + 1) % TEXT_SPEEDS.size()
	return TEXT_SPEED_NAMES[text_speed]

## Open the box on some lines.
func say(lines: Array) -> void:
	_queue = lines.duplicate()
	_pending = []
	choices = []
	is_open = true
	_show_next()

func close() -> void:
	is_open = false
	_typing = false
	_queue = []
	_pending = []
	choices = []

func _show_next() -> void:
	_full = _queue.pop_front()
	_shown = 0
	_budget = 0.0
	_hold = 0.0
	_typing = true
	if cps() <= 0.0:   # Instant: the whole line at once
		_finish_line()

func _finish_line() -> void:
	_typing = false
	_hold = 0.0
	_shown = _full.length()

func _type(delta: float) -> void:
	if not _typing:
		return
	if cps() <= 0.0:   # switched to Instant in the middle of a line
		_finish_line()
		return
	var per := 1.0 / cps()
	_budget += delta
	while _budget >= per and _shown < _full.length():
		_budget -= per
		_shown += 1
	if _shown >= _full.length():
		_finish_line()

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_up"):
		cycle_text_speed()
	_type(delta)
	queue_redraw()

func prompt() -> String:
	if not choices.is_empty():
		return "your turn"
	if _typing:
		return "…"
	if not _queue.is_empty():
		return "Space: next"
	if not _pending.is_empty():
		return "Space: answer"
	return "Space: finish"

func _draw() -> void:
	var font := ThemeDB.fallback_font
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#cfe3c8"))
	draw_string(font, Vector2(10, 16), "speed: " + TEXT_SPEED_NAMES[text_speed], 0, -1, 10, Color("#4c3438"))
	if not is_open:
		return
	draw_rect(BOX, Color("#fffafb"))
	draw_rect(BOX, Color("#f0c7d0"), false, 2.0)
	draw_string(font, BOX.position + Vector2(10, 16), "Somebody", 0, -1, 10, Color("#e0808f"))
	draw_string(font, BOX.position + Vector2(206, 16), prompt(), 0, -1, 10, Color("#8a6b73"))
	draw_string(font, BOX.position + Vector2(10, 33), _full.substr(0, _shown), 0, -1, 10, Color("#4c3438"))
	for i in choices.size():
		var r := Rect2(BOX.position.x + 10 + i * 142, BOX.position.y + 42, 136, 18)
		draw_rect(r, Color("#fbe4e8"))
		draw_rect(r, Color("#f0c7d0"), false, 1.0)
		draw_string(font, r.position + Vector2(6, 13), ("< " if i == 0 else "> ") + str(choices[i]["text"]), 0, -1, 10, Color("#4c3438"))

tests.label: a new line starts with nothing showing
half a second at 26 a second: 13 letters
and still typing
a second later all 31 are showing, and no more
and the typing has stopped

hints: Start with var per := 1.0 / cps() and _budget += delta.
The spending is a while loop with two conditions: while _budget >= per and _shown < _full.length():. Inside it, take per off the budget and add 1 to _shown.
After the loop: if _shown >= _full.length(): _finish_line().
steps.explain: The first line types itself and stops. Press the up arrow to hear the other two speeds described – Normal is nearly twice as quick, and Instant does not type at all – then edit a line to see the new speed. A loop, and not a plain _shown += 1, is what keeps the pace honest: a frame that took twice as long pays for twice as many letters.

steps.title: Let a tap decide
steps.task: Only one line ever appears, because nothing moves the box on. Write advance() and call it from _process when ui_accept has just been pressed. It does one of three things: if a line is still typing, finish that line and nothing more; otherwise, if lines are left in _queue, show the next; otherwise close() the box. If the box is not open it does nothing at all.

tests.expr: [say(["One two three four five six seven", "Next"]), _typing][1]
tests.label: two lines are said, and the first begins to type

tests.expect: [false, 33, "One two three four five six seven"]
tests.label: a tap while it types finishes that line – and stays on it
the next tap moves on to the second line
a tap finishes that one too, and the box stays open
with nothing left to say, a tap closes the box
and a tap on a closed box does nothing

hints: Four cases, each ending in return except the last. Put them in the order the task gives them, with if not is_open: return first.
Typing: if _typing: then _finish_line() and return. Nothing left: if _queue.is_empty(): then close() and return. Last line of the function: _show_next().
In _process: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"): advance().
steps.explain: Press Space early and the sentence completes; press it again and the next begins. The word in the corner of the box changes with the state, because prompt() in the starter asks the same questions advance() does. Swap the first two cases – move on before checking _typing – and tap twice quickly: half a line goes missing. The order is the whole of the manners.

steps.title: Rest on the full stops
steps.task: Give the typing some breath. Add const PAUSE_STOP := 0.24 and const PAUSE_SOFT := 0.12, and a function pause_after(text: String, i: int) -> float that says how long to rest after character i: PAUSE_STOP after . ! or ?, PAUSE_SOFT after , ; or :, and 0 for anything else. A mark only counts when the character after it is a space; if it is the very last character, treat it as if a space followed. Then use it in _type: after showing a character that earns a rest, with more of the line still to come, put the rest in _hold and stop the loop. While _hold is above zero, _type counts it down and types nothing.

tests.label: a full stop at the end of a word rests 0.24
a comma rests 0.12
an ordinary letter does not rest
the full stop inside 4.50 does not rest
a mark that is the last character counts as the end of a word
a line with a full stop four letters in is said
a quarter of a second later it is resting on that full stop
and it still gets to the end

hints: In pause_after, work out the next character first: var nxt := text[i + 1] if i + 1 < text.length() else " ". If it is not a space, return 0.0 straight away.
In the loop, straight after _shown += 1: var pause := pause_after(_full, _shown - 1), then if pause > 0.0 and _shown < _full.length(): set _hold = pause and break.
Above var per: if _hold > 0.0: then _hold = maxf(0.0, _hold - delta), and if it is still above zero, return.
steps.explain: Tap through to the second line and watch it: a beat after "rests.", half a beat after "comma,". Nothing about the speed changed – the same budget and the same loop – but now it reads like somebody talking. The condition _shown < _full.length() is why there is no rest after the last full stop of a line: there is nothing left to wait for, and the reader is already waiting for you.

steps.title: Offer the answers
steps.task: Now a question. Add ask(lines: Array, replies: Array): it says the lines exactly as say() does, and keeps a copy of the replies in _pending. Then give advance() two more cases. When the last line has been read and replies are pending, a tap moves them from _pending into choices – the box stays open. And while choices has anything in it, a tap does nothing. Change _ready() to ask(LINES, REPLIES).

tests.label: ask() holds its two replies back while the line is read
a tap finishes the line; still no buttons
the next tap puts the answers up and leaves the box open
in the order they were given
while they are up, a tap does nothing
say() still offers no answers

hints: ask is two lines: say(lines), then _pending = replies.duplicate(). In that order – say() empties _pending.
The do-nothing case goes near the top of advance(): if not choices.is_empty(): return.
Inside if _queue.is_empty():, before close(): if not _pending.is_empty(): then choices = _pending, _pending = [] and return.
steps.explain: Tap through the three lines and the buttons arrive only when you have had the chance to read what they answer. After that Space is dead, on purpose: a tap that closed the box now would be answering the question for you. The buttons do nothing yet. Each one is a small dictionary with an id and a text, and the last step is about which of those two matters.

steps.title: Answer by id
steps.task: Let the answers be chosen. Declare signal chose(reply_id: String). Write _pick(i: int): if there is no choice number i on screen it does nothing; otherwise it takes that choice's id, clears choices, and emits chose with the id. In _process, ui_left picks 0 and ui_right picks 1. Then the other side of the conversation: connect chose in _ready() to a function _on_reply(reply_id: String), which looks the id up in ANSWERS and says what it finds – or closes the box if there is nothing under that id.

tests.label: a question is asked
the arrows do nothing before the answers are up
tap: the line is finished
tap: the answers are up
the right arrow picks the second, and the buttons go
and what is said next is the answer kept under its id, wry
asked again, picking the first gives the answer for warm
an id with no answer under it closes the box
_pick() reports the choice by emitting chose
tests.why: The box should not call _on_reply itself: it emits the signal and whoever is listening decides what the id means.

hints: _pick starts with a guard, if i < 0 or i >= choices.size(): return. Then var id: String = choices[i]["id"], choices = [], chose.emit(id).
In _ready(), before asking: chose.connect(_on_reply). In _process: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_left"): _pick(0), and the same with ui_right and 1.
_on_reply: var back := str(ANSWERS.get(reply_id, "")). If it is empty, close() and return; otherwise say([back]).
steps.explain: Tap through, choose with an arrow, and the reply types itself in the same box. Now change the word "Say thanks" in REPLIES to anything you like and choose it again: the same reply comes back, because nothing ever looked at the wording. That is the reason the game gives for passing ids. Notice too where the line is drawn: _pick is the box and knows only that something was chosen; _on_reply is the game and knows what it means. In Little Hours they are in different files, and the signal is all that joins them.

title: Build a themed card and a toast
intro: One card, one button and a toast, drawn in whole pixels from a palette you can switch. The drawing and the pixel loop are written at the bottom of the script; the palette, the cache, the corners and the fade are yours. Click the view first, then press Right to change the look.

steps.title: Pick a palette
steps.task: The colours live in four variables, and THEMES holds three sets of values. Write apply_theme(id): use the id if THEMES has it, otherwise "pink"; copy that set's four colours into PANEL, BORDER, INK and ACCENT with Color(...); and return the id it used. Press Right in the view later to cycle the looks.

tests.expr: apply_theme("blue") == "blue" and ACCENT == Color("#6f9ec4") and PANEL == Color("#f8fbff")
tests.label: blue sets the blue accent and panel
an unknown theme falls back to pink

tests.expr: apply_theme("sand") == "sand" and BORDER == Color("#d8c39a") and INK == Color("#4a3f2c")
tests.label: sand sets all four

hints: Start with var key := id if THEMES.has(id) else "pink", then var t: Dictionary = THEMES[key].
Then PANEL = Color(t["PANEL"]) and the same for the other three, and return key.
The game's apply_theme does exactly this for nine colours. It assigns to static vars, which is why the palette can change at all: a const could not.
steps.explain: Nothing on screen changes yet, because the drawing asks theme() and that is not cached. The fallback is the point of line one: an id read from a save file can be anything, and a made-up one must not leave the palette half-set.

steps.title: Build it once, announce the change
steps.task: Right now theme() rebuilds its dictionary every time it is asked, which is every frame. Cache it: if _theme is not null return it, otherwise count a build, store the dictionary and return that. apply_theme must then set _theme = null so the next ask rebuilds. And change set_theme(id): ignore an id THEMES does not have; otherwise apply it and theme_changed.emit().

tests.label: after eight drawn frames the theme was built once

tests.expr: apply_theme("sand") == "sand" and theme()["button"] == Color("#c9a05f") and builds == 2
tests.label: a new palette throws the cache away and builds once more
an unknown theme announces nothing
a real one announces itself once
and the next theme() has the blue button

hints: Two edits in theme(): if _theme != null: return _theme at the top, and _theme = {...} instead of returning the dictionary directly.
In apply_theme add _theme = null before the return. In set_theme: if not THEMES.has(id): return, then apply_theme(id), then theme_changed.emit().
The counter rebuilt goes up in a function connected to the signal in _ready. That function is the HUD's job in the game.
steps.explain: Two ways of finding out about a change, and the game uses both: the cache is told by = null inside apply_theme, and everything that baked colours in at build time hears the signal. The HUD connects theme_changed to its own _build and is rebuilt from scratch. Note the order: apply first, announce second, or listeners would rebuild with the old colours.

steps.title: Round the corners
steps.task: The box in the view is a grid of whole pixels, each drawn as one PX-sized square. Write corner(r), how many pixels each of the first r rows is cut in: [] for 0, [2, 1] for 2, [4, 2, 1, 1] for 4, and otherwise from the circle: for row i, let y = r - i - 0.5 and the cut is int(r - sqrt(r*r - y*y) + 0.5). Then inside(x, y, w, h, r): false outside the w by h rectangle; otherwise find the pixel's distance from the nearest row edge cy and column edge cx (mini(y, h - 1 - y) and likewise for x), and it is outside only when cy is inside the profile and cx is less than profile[cy].

tests.label: the small corners are the hand-drawn ones
a bigger corner follows the circle

tests.expr: inside(0, 0, 10, 6, 2) == false and inside(2, 0, 10, 6, 2) == true and inside(1, 1, 10, 6, 2) == true and inside(0, 1, 10, 6, 2) == false
tests.label: the top-left corner is cut

tests.expr: inside(9, 5, 10, 6, 2) == false and inside(7, 0, 10, 6, 2) == true and inside(8, 0, 10, 6, 2) == false
tests.label: and so are the others, by symmetry
outside the rectangle is out, the middle is in
the border is the pixels beside an outside pixel

hints: corner is three ifs that return literals, then a loop that appends one number per row.
var out := [], for i in r:, var y := float(r) - float(i) - 0.5, out.append(int(float(r) - sqrt(float(r * r) - y * y) + 0.5)).
inside: var prof := corner(r), then return not (cy < prof.size() and cx < prof[cy]) after the bounds check.
steps.explain: Watch the view: a rectangle with stepped corners, outlined in one pixel all the way round, the way every card and button in the game is. The game hand-draws the sizes up to 5, as you did for 2 and 4, because a computed circle that small comes out as a notch or a bevel, and uses the formula from 6 up. The border costs no extra work: cell() calls any pixel with an outside neighbour an edge.

steps.title: A toast that fades
steps.task: The line at the bottom of the screen. show_toast(text) ignores an empty string; otherwise it stores the text and sets toast_t to 0.0. toast_alpha() turns the time since then into opacity: 0 before it starts (toast_t < 0), rising from 0 to 1 over TOAST_IN, holding 1 for TOAST_HOLD, then falling to 0 over TOAST_OUT and staying there. Click the view and press Space or Enter to raise one.

tests.label: an empty toast does not start the clock
just after the tap it is fading in
a second in it is fully there
four seconds in it has gone

hints: Four ifs in order, each returning: not started, still fading in, still holding, then the fade-out sum.
In: return toast_t / TOAST_IN. Hold: return 1.0 while toast_t < TOAST_IN + TOAST_HOLD.
Out: var gone := (toast_t - TOAST_IN - TOAST_HOLD) / TOAST_OUT then return maxf(0.0, 1.0 - gone).
steps.explain: The game's show_toast does the same with a Tween (0.18 up, 2.4 held, 0.5 down), after first killing any toast still running so a second message starts cleanly instead of fighting the first. Here restarting toast_t at 0 does that job. Change TOAST_HOLD to 0.5 and watch it come and go quickly. Press Right to change the look: every box redraws in the new palette.

title: Build a voice you can see
intro: You will make one speech blip the way the game does – a list of samples – and give it to four people. The page cannot play it, so it draws it: the view beside the editor plots your samples from left to right, which is exactly what an oscilloscope would show. The drawing code is written for you; the sound is yours.

steps.title: A plain tone
steps.task: Fill in tone(f, dur) so it returns dur seconds of a sine wave at f hertz. The number of samples is int(dur * RATE), and at least 1. Keep a running phase that starts at 0; for each sample, first move it on by TAU * f / RATE, then append sin(phase).

tests.label: 0.04 seconds at 8000 samples a second is 320 samples
sample 7 is on the way up
sample 15 is back at zero: half a cycle of 250 Hz
sample 23 is below the line
sample 31 completes one cycle

hints: Three variables before the loop: var n := maxi(1, int(dur * RATE)), the empty out that is already there, and var phase := 0.0.
Inside for i in range(n): two lines – phase += TAU * f / RATE, then out.append(sin(phase)).
steps.explain: Ten even waves: 250 cycles a second for a twenty-fifth of a second. Change the 250 in _ready to 500 and count again. This is a pure tone, and played aloud it would start and stop with a click, because the speaker is asked to jump straight to full swing and straight back to rest.

steps.title: Let it die away
steps.task: A sound needs a shape in time, called its envelope. Write envelope(t: float) -> float, where t is how far through the sound we are, from 0 to 1. It returns pow(1.0 - t, 2.2) – the game's own curve for a blip. In tone, work out t for each sample as float(i) / float(n) and multiply the sample by its envelope.

tests.label: a quarter of the way through, the envelope is about 0.53
half way, about 0.22
at the end, nothing
tone() multiplies each sample by its envelope
the last sample is all but silent

hints: func envelope(t: float) -> float: is one line: return pow(1.0 - t, 2.2).
In the loop, before the append: var t := float(i) / float(n). Then append sin(phase) * envelope(t).
steps.explain: The wave now shrinks to nothing, quickly at first and then slowly – the shape of something struck. float(i) / float(n) is written with both float()s for a reason: i / n with two whole numbers is whole-number division, and would be 0 for every sample but the last (Chapter D).

steps.title: No click at the start
steps.task: Look at the left edge: the wave still leaps to full height on the very first cycle. Add const ATTACK := 0.15 and make the envelope rise from 0 to 1 over that first share of the sound, by multiplying what you have by minf(1.0, t / ATTACK).

tests.label: the envelope starts at nothing
half way through the attack it is half open
after the attack it is the same curve as before
the first sample is silent

hints: t / ATTACK climbs from 0 and reaches 1 when t is 0.15. minf(1.0, …) stops it climbing further.
return minf(1.0, t / ATTACK) * pow(1.0 - t, 2.2)
steps.explain: A quick swell, then the fall. The game's comment gives the reason and the arithmetic: a wave that starts at full height clicks, a line of talk has forty blips in it, and fifteen per cent of a blip is about six thousandths of a second – short enough to still sound like a consonant, long enough not to click.

steps.title: A different shape
steps.task:
Pitch is how fast the wave repeats; timbre is the shape of one repeat. Write shape(wave: String, phase: float) -> float with a match:

  • "square" – 1.0 for the first half of the cycle (phase < PI), −1.0 for the second
  • "tri" – asin(sin(phase)) * (2.0 / PI), a straight-sided zigzag
  • anything else – sin(phase)

Give tone a third parameter, wave: String = "sine", and use shape(wave, phase) where it used sin(phase). A square needs to know which half of the cycle it is in, so keep phase between 0 and TAU with fmod. Then ask for a "square" in _ready.

tests.label: a sine is at its top a quarter of the way round
a square is 1.0 in the first half of the cycle
and -1.0 in the second
a triangle is half way up an eighth of the way round
an unknown shape falls back to a sine
tone() with "square": sample 100 is on the top edge
and sample 150 on the bottom edge
tone() with two arguments is still a sine

hints: A match on wave with two branches that each return, and return sin(phase) after it for everything else.
The square: return 1.0 if phase < PI else -1.0.
In the loop: phase = fmod(phase + TAU * f / RATE, TAU), then out.append(shape(wave, phase) * envelope(t)).
steps.explain: Same pitch, same envelope, and a different sound: a square is hollow and buzzy, a sine is round, a triangle sits between. Try "tri". The game has three more – a narrow pulse, a saw, and one with noise mixed in for a breathy voice – and passes the harsher ones through a small filter (soft) so they do not fizz.

steps.title: A voice each
steps.task:
Now the people. Add a DEFAULT profile – {"f": 330.0, "wave": "tri", "dur": 0.045} – and a table BY_ID with four of the game's own: "marisol" at 392 Hz for 0.042 s (her wave is the default, so leave it out), "tobias" a square at 233 for 0.052, "nan" a sine at 208 for 0.072, and "bea" a square at 415 for 0.030.

Write voice_of(id: String) -> Dictionary: a copy of DEFAULT with that person's entries laid over it. Write blip(v: Dictionary) -> Array, which is tone called with the profile's three values. Add var speaker := "nan" and have _ready draw that speaker's blip.

tests.label: Nan's pitch is 208
Tobias is a square wave
Marisol's wave is filled in from DEFAULT
somebody with no entry gets DEFAULT, unchanged by the lookups before
Bea's blip is 0.030 seconds: 240 samples
Nan's is 0.072 seconds: 576 samples
_ready() draws the speaker's blip

hints: Start voice_of with var v: Dictionary = DEFAULT.duplicate(). Without duplicate() you would be changing DEFAULT itself (Chapter G).
Then var found: Dictionary = BY_ID.get(id, {}) and a loop: for k in found: v[k] = found[k]. Return v.
blip is one line: return tone(v["f"], v["dur"], v["wave"]). In _ready: samples = blip(voice_of(speaker)).
steps.explain: Change speaker to each name in turn and to "a stranger". Nan's blip is long, low and round; Bea's is less than half the length, twice the pitch and square. You can tell them apart with the sound off, which is the test of a table like this. voice_of is the game's Voices.of() line for line. What you have left out is small: the four pitch variants, the filter, and step – how many letters go by before the next one.

title: Build a rainy day
intro: A calendar that knows its season and its weather from the day number, and rain that falls when the calendar says so. Your script is one Node2D in a view 320 wide and 180 tall; it restarts each time you stop typing.

steps.title: Which season
steps.task: The caption says day 8 is spring, and it is not. Make season_index(d) return the right index into SEASONS for day d: days 1 to 5 are 0, days 6 to 10 are 1, and after winter it goes round to 0 again on day 21.

tests.label: day 1 is spring (index 0)
so is day 5
day 6 is the first of summer
season_key(8) is "Summer"
day 20 is the last of winter
day 21 is spring again

hints: Take one off the day so that counting starts at 0, divide by DAYS_PER_SEASON and round down, then wrap with %.
Rounding down: floor(float(d - 1) / float(DAYS_PER_SEASON)). It gives a float, so wrap it in int(…) before the %.
return int(floor(float(d - 1) / float(DAYS_PER_SEASON))) % SEASONS.size()
steps.explain: The caption now reads Summer. Change day at the top to 16, then 21, and watch it follow. Using SEASONS.size() in place of a bare 4 means a fifth season would need no change here.

steps.title: Roll the same dice
steps.task: Write weather(d: int) -> String, the game's own. First the dice: x is sin(float(d) * 127.1 + 311.7) * 43758.5453, and r is what follows its decimal point, x - floor(x). Then the season decides what r means. In winter (index 3): "Snowy" below 0.5, "Rainy" below 0.62, otherwise "Clear". In the other three: "Rainy" if r is below that season's chance – 0.35, 0.15 and 0.4 for spring, summer and autumn – otherwise "Clear". Add the weather to label(), so it reads Day 8, Summer, Clear.

tests.label: day 1 is rainy
day 2 is clear
day 12, in autumn, is rainy
day 16, the first of winter, is snowy
day 18 is a clear winter day
day 60 is the rare thing, winter rain
the caption shows the day, the season and the weather

hints: Two lines make the dice: var x: float = sin(float(d) * 127.1 + 311.7) * 43758.5453 and var r: float = x - floor(x).
Winter first: if s == 3: then if r < 0.5: return "Snowy" and return "Rainy" if r < 0.62 else "Clear".
The rest: var rain_chance: float = [0.35, 0.15, 0.4][s], then return "Rainy" if r < rain_chance else "Clear". In label(), a third %s and weather(day).
steps.explain: Try a few days. However often the view restarts, day 12 is rainy and day 16 is snowy – for you and for everybody who plays the game, because these are its real numbers. Nothing is stored, so nothing can be loaded wrongly. If you wanted a different climate you would change the three chances, not the dice.

steps.title: Make some rain
steps.task: Now something to look at. Add const COUNT := 40 and var drops: Array = []. Write make_drops(): empty the list, then append COUNT dictionaries, each with an "x" somewhere across the 320 of the view, a "y" somewhere down its 180, and "v", the drop's own speed factor, between 0.6 and 1.4. Call it from _ready. In _draw, make the sky a rainy Color("#7c8fa8") and draw every drop as a pale rectangle 2 wide and 12 tall.

tests.label: make_drops() makes COUNT drops
called again, it starts afresh and does not double them

tests.expr: drops.all(func(d): return d["x"] >= 0.0 and d["x"] <= 320.0 and d["y"] >= 0.0 and d["y"] <= 180.0)
tests.label: every drop starts inside the view
every drop has a v between 0.6 and 1.4
_ready() makes the drops
tests.why: Call make_drops() from _ready, or there is nothing to draw.

tests.label: _draw() goes through the drops
tests.why: Loop over drops inside _draw() and draw a rectangle for each.

hints: randf() is a random number from 0 to 1, so randf() * 320.0 is a random place across. randf_range(0.6, 1.4) picks between two limits.
In make_drops(): drops.clear(), then for i in range(COUNT): drops.append({"x": randf() * 320.0, "y": randf() * 180.0, "v": randf_range(0.6, 1.4)}).
In _draw(), after the sky and before the caption: for d in drops: draw_rect(Rect2(d["x"], d["y"], 2.0, 12.0), Color(0.86, 0.92, 1.0, 0.8)).
steps.explain: Forty streaks, hanging still – a photograph of rain. (It rains whatever the caption says for now; the last step puts that right.) Each drop is a dictionary and not a node. Forty nodes would be forty things for the engine to keep track of; forty dictionaries are a list you walk once a frame.

steps.title: Let it fall
steps.task: Add const RAIN_SPEED := 240.0 and a function speed() -> float that returns it. Write step_drop(d: Dictionary, delta: float) -> Dictionary: move the drop down by speed() times its own v times delta; if that takes it past the bottom of the view (a y above 180), put it back above the top at y = -20.0 with a new random x; return the drop. Then, in _process(delta), step every drop and ask for a new drawing.

tests.label: in a quarter of a second a drop falls a quarter of speed()
a drop with v 0.5 falls half as far
a drop that passes the bottom goes back to y = -20
and gets a new x inside the view
after seven seconds of frames, no drop has left the view
_process() steps the drops
tests.why: Call step_drop(d, delta) for every drop in _process.

tests.label: asks for a new drawing with queue_redraw()
tests.why: Without it _draw() runs once and the rain never moves.

hints: The fall is one line: d["y"] += speed() * d["v"] * delta.
The wrap: if d["y"] > 180.0: then d["y"] = -20.0 and d["x"] = randf() * 320.0. Finish with return d.
func _process(delta: float) -> void: – for d in drops: step_drop(d, delta), and after the loop queue_redraw().
steps.explain: Rain. Look closely and you can see why each drop has its own v: with one speed for all, the whole sheet would slide down like a picture; with forty, it has depth. The drops start above the view (−20) so that they slide in instead of popping into existence, and the same forty go round for ever. step_drop changes the dictionary it is given – a dictionary is passed by reference, so the one in the list is the one that moved (Chapter G).

steps.title: Only when it rains
steps.task:
Join the two halves. Add const SNOW_SPEED := 36.0, var kind := "Clear" and var active := false. Write the game's configure(weather_kind: String, outdoor: bool) -> void: remember the kind; active is true only outdoors, and only for "Rainy" or "Snowy"; empty the drops, and make new ones only when active; ask for a new drawing. Call configure(weather(day), true) from _ready in place of make_drops().

Then three small changes: speed() returns SNOW_SPEED when the kind is "Snowy"; _process does nothing when not active; and _draw uses a blue sky, Color("#a8d8f0"), when not active, and draws snow as white squares 4 by 4.

tests.label: _ready() sets up today's weather
a rainy day outdoors has COUNT drops
and the layer is active
rain falls at RAIN_SPEED
a clear day has no drops
indoors, rain is not active
and no drops are made
snow falls at SNOW_SPEED
and there are COUNT flakes

hints: active = outdoor and weather_kind in ["Rainy", "Snowy"] – in asks whether a value is in a list.
After that line: drops.clear(), then if active: make_drops(), then queue_redraw(). In speed(): return SNOW_SPEED if kind == "Snowy" else RAIN_SPEED.

First lines of _process: if not active: return. In _draw, the sky is Color("#7c8fa8") if active else Color("#a8d8f0"), and inside the loop if kind == "Rainy": draws the streak, else: a Rect2(d["x"], d["y"], 4.0, 4.0) in white.
steps.explain: Day 8 is clear, so the sky is blue and empty. Set day to 12 for autumn rain, 16 for snow, 18 for a bright winter day. That is the whole mechanic: a function of the day says what kind of sky it is, and configure – called by the game each time you walk into a room – turns that word into drops or into nothing. The game's snow also sways from side to side on a sine wave; adding d["x"] += sin(…) to step_drop is a good next thing to try.

title: Build a filter and a fallback
intro: Small talk from something unreliable, and a town that never has to notice. You will build the filter that cleans a line, the judge that refuses the wrong ones, the loop that tries twice and falls back to a written line, and a memory of how lines began. A stand-in called generate() plays the model, and try_it() tells it what to say. Everything is a plain call you can check.
starter:
extends Node

const TRIES := 2
const OPENINGS_KEPT := 3   # the game keeps 12
const REJECT := ["language model", "as an ai", "the player", "game", "<", ">", "*", "http"]
const STORY_WORDS := ["funeral", "married"]
const WINDOW := 12   # the game uses 30

var enabled := true
var outputs := []    # what the "model" will say next, one per try
var openings := []
var asked := 0       # how many times the model was used

func clean(text: String) -> String:
	return text

func acceptable(line: String, examples: Array) -> bool:
	return line != ""

func small_talk(written: String, examples: Array) -> String:
	return written

# ── Written for you. Your work is above this line. ──

# Stands in for the language model: it says whatever is next in `outputs`,
# or nothing at all, which is what a model that has failed looks like.
func generate() -> String:
	asked += 1
	if outputs.is_empty():
		return ""
	return outputs.pop_front()

func try_it(outs: Array, on: bool = true) -> String:
	asked = 0
	enabled = on
	outputs = outs
	return small_talk("WRITTEN", ["an example line to copy from here"])

func forget() -> bool:
	openings = []
	return true

steps.title: Clean what comes back
steps.task: Write clean(text). Turn \r and \n into spaces and strip the ends; replace every ! with .; squeeze double spaces down to one; return "" if the line contains anything in REJECT (compare against the lower-cased line with a space on each side); if the number of " marks is odd remove them all; and return "" if what is left is shorter than 8 characters.

tests.label: newlines, edges, the exclamation mark
runs of spaces become one

tests.expr: clean("As an AI, I cannot help with that.")
tests.label: a line that sounds like a machine is thrown out

tests.expr: clean("I like the game a lot today.")
tests.label: so is one that mentions the game
an unbalanced quote mark is removed
balanced quotes are left alone
a scrap is not a line

hints: Chain the replaces: text.replace("\r", " ").replace("\n", " ").strip_edges(). Collapse spaces with while t.contains(" "):.
For the reject list: var low := " " + t.to_lower() + " " then for bad in REJECT: if low.contains(bad): return "".
Count quotes with t.count("\"") % 2 == 1.
steps.explain: Nothing here asks whether the line is good. It asks whether it is the kind of thing the dialogue box can show. The game's version also swaps curly quotes for straight ones (the pixel font draws them as boxes), strips a block of the model's private reasoning, and cuts a line that is too long back to its last full sentence. The idea is the same: whatever comes back from something you do not control is cleaned at the door, and a line that cannot be cleaned is refused.

steps.title: Judge a line
steps.task: Write acceptable(line, examples). An empty line is not acceptable. Nor is one that contains a whole word from STORY_WORDS: lower-case it, turn ., , and " into spaces, put a space at each end and look for " " + word + " ". Nor is one that copies an example: slide a window of WINDOW characters along the lower-cased line, i going up by 6, and refuse if any window appears inside any lower-cased example.

tests.label: nothing is not a line

tests.expr: acceptable("There was a funeral last week.", [])
tests.label: a chapter's subject is refused
but only as a whole word

tests.expr: acceptable("Rain again, and the bins are out.", ["Rain again, and the bins are out, mind"])
tests.label: a copy of an example is refused

tests.expr: acceptable("Rain again, and the bins are out.", ["Something else entirely."])
tests.label: something new is accepted

hints: Whole words: put the line between spaces and look for the word between spaces, so "married" does not match "unmarried".
The copy test is a while i + WINDOW <= low.length(): loop that tests e.contains(low.substr(i, WINDOW)) and adds 6 to i.
Two loops: for w in STORY_WORDS and for ex in examples, each able to return false.
steps.explain: This is the filter's main idea: you cannot ask a model nicely never to spoil a story, so you check what it said. The game has a list of the subjects its chapters are made of (family, death and so on) and a list of unkind words, and a third check for a line that tells the player what they did. The copy test is the reverse worry: a small model shown three written lines hands one back about one time in four, and thirty characters in a row is more than two lines ever share by chance.

steps.title: Fall back, always
steps.task: Write small_talk(written, examples). If enabled is false, return written without ever asking the model. Otherwise have up to TRIES goes: get clean(generate()) and if it is acceptable, return it. If every try fails, return written. generate() stands in for the model and try_it() sets up what it will say.

tests.expr: try_it(["The tide is in, and so is the cat."])
tests.expect: "The tide is in, and so is the cat."
tests.label: a good line is used
a model that says nothing gives the written line

tests.expr: try_it(["As an AI I cannot help.", "Fine weather for it, isn't it!"])
tests.label: a second try can rescue the first

tests.expr: try_it(["There was a funeral last week.", "I hate the game, honestly."])
tests.label: two bad tries and the written line is used
switched off, the model is never asked
and it is asked no more than TRIES times

hints: Start with the switch: if not enabled: return written.
for _try in TRIES: then var line := clean(generate()) and an if acceptable(line, examples): return line.
The last line of the function, after the loop, is return written.
steps.explain: The last line is the whole safety design: the function cannot fail, because the thing it falls back to was written by a person and is always there. Nothing in the game is waiting on a model, so a neighbour never stands there with nothing to say, and TRIES keeps the cost of a bad answer small. The real function is async, because making a line takes seconds. The reader of this file only needs the shape.

steps.title: Do not repeat yourself
steps.task: The model has stock openings it reaches for whoever is talking. Add opening(line): the first five words, lower-cased, with " and , removed, joined by single spaces. Add fresh(line), true when openings does not already hold that opening, and remember(line), which appends it and drops the oldest while there are more than OPENINGS_KEPT. Make small_talk require fresh(line) too, and call remember(line) on the line it uses.

tests.expr: opening("\"Come on, you're not going to do that again.\"")
tests.label: the opening is five plain words

tests.expr: [forget(), try_it(["Come on, you're not going to stay."]), try_it(["Come on, you're not going to leave.", "Oh, the sea is flat as a plate."])]
tests.expect: [true, "Come on, you're not going to stay.", "Oh, the sea is flat as a plate."]
tests.label: a repeated opening is skipped for the next try

tests.expr: [forget(), try_it(["Alpha one two three four five."]), try_it(["Bravo one two three four five."]), try_it(["Charlie one two three four five."]), try_it(["Delta one two three four five."]), try_it(["Alpha one two three four five."])][5]
tests.label: after OPENINGS_KEPT others, an old opening is allowed again

hints: line.to_lower().replace("\"", "").replace(",", "").split(" ", false) gives the words; " ".join(words.slice(0, 5)) puts five back.
remember: append, then while openings.size() > OPENINGS_KEPT: openings.pop_front().
In small_talk: if acceptable(line, examples) and fresh(line): then remember(line) before returning.
steps.explain: A rule about the last dozen lines, not the whole history, which is why it forgets: the aim is that fifteen people do not share one turn of phrase this week, not that nobody ever says anything twice. The game remembers 12 openings across everyone. Try changing OPENINGS_KEPT to 1 and watch the last test's story change.

title: Build a calendar, a diary and a house that forgets
intro: A tiny life made of one number, day, and four lists that remember in different ways: a calendar worked out from the day, a diary and a record of what the town has said that keep the newest and let the oldest go, traces that expire, and a daily list that empties itself. The helpers on(d) (jump to a day) and fresh() (start a new life) are at the bottom, so every check starts clean.

steps.title: Count the years
steps.task: The calendar is only day, a number that goes up. Write four readings of it. year(): the year you are in, day 1 being the first day of year 1 (DAYS_PER_YEAR days a year, use maxi(1, day) so a bad value cannot go below the start). year_day(): which day of that year, counting from 1. years_here(): whole years, one fewer than year(). years_phrase(): "7 days" before a year is up, "a year" for one, and otherwise "two years" using WORDS (or the digits past its end).

tests.label: day 1 is the first day of year 1
day 20 is the last day of year 1
day 21 starts year 2
a nonsense day counts as day 1
before a year the phrase counts days
a year
two years

hints: Take one off the day before dividing and add it back after: (maxi(1, day) - 1) / DAYS_PER_YEAR + 1. Both sides are whole numbers, so / drops the remainder.
year_day is the same with % in place of /.
years_phrase: var y := years_here(), then an if for 0 and one for 1, then "%s years" % WORDS[y].
steps.explain: Nothing counts years. There is one number, day, and the year, the day of the year and the sentence are all worked out from it, like the clock in entry C. That is why a game with no ending can still say "your third spring": the same spring comes round every twenty days and the arithmetic knows which lap it is. The - 1 and + 1 are the usual price of counting from 1 instead of 0.

steps.title: Remember the latest, forget the rest
steps.task: Two lists that keep the newest first and let the old go. log_memory(text) is the diary: look at the entries from the front, and while they are from today return if one has the same text; then insert {"day": day, "text": text} at position 0 and trim to MEMORY_KEEP. note_fact(id) is what the town has remarked on lately: if recent already holds id remove it, push it on the front, and trim to RECENT.

tests.label: the same thing twice in one day is one memory
on another day it counts again
newest first

tests.expr: [fresh(), log_memory("1"), log_memory("2"), log_memory("3"), log_memory("4"), log_memory("5"), log_memory("6"), log_memory("7"), memories.size(), memories.back()["text"]][8]
tests.label: seven memories into a diary of five: it holds five

tests.expr: [fresh(), log_memory("1"), log_memory("2"), log_memory("3"), log_memory("4"), log_memory("5"), log_memory("6"), log_memory("7"), memories.size(), memories.back()["text"]][9]
tests.label: and the oldest two are the ones gone
a fact said again moves to the front, not twice
only the last RECENT are kept

hints: The duplicate check relies on order: for m in memories:, if m["day"] != day: break, if m["text"] == text: return.
memories.insert(0, {...}) puts it at the front; then while memories.size() > MEMORY_KEEP: memories.pop_back().
note_fact is the same trim, with recent.erase(id) first and recent.push_front(id).
steps.explain: The break is the clever line. Because the diary is newest first, the first entry from an earlier day means everything after it is older too, so the check looks at a handful of entries instead of all of them. The game's comment records the bug it prevents: the diary showed "Bought the house" five times over, one for each time the flow that logs it ran. Capping the list matters just as much, because the diary lives in the save file, and the save is a line of text you can mail to yourself.

steps.title: A house that forgets
steps.task: Traces are things your day leaves lying about. Write traces_in(room), the ones in a room. Then leave_trace(id): false for an unknown kind. A trace that grows is one thing getting bigger, not a second thing: if one of that kind is already there, add one to its "size" (never past stages - 1) and set its "day" to today, and return true. Otherwise, if the room already has MAX_PER_ROOM, remove the one with the smallest "day"; then append {"kind", "room", "day", "size": 0}. Finally age_traces(): keep only those where day - t["day"] is less than the kind's "life".

tests.label: there is no such trace

tests.expr: [fresh(), on(1), leave_trace("cards_out"), on(2), leave_trace("confetti"), on(3), leave_trace("flowers"), traces_in("living").size()][7]
tests.label: a room holds at most MAX_PER_ROOM

tests.expr: [fresh(), on(1), leave_trace("cards_out"), on(2), leave_trace("confetti"), on(3), leave_trace("flowers"), traces_in("living")[0]["kind"]][7]
tests.label: and it is the oldest that goes
laundry grows instead of piling up as two things

tests.expr: [fresh(), leave_trace("laundry"), leave_trace("laundry"), leave_trace("laundry"), leave_trace("laundry"), leave_trace("laundry"), traces_in("bedroom")[0]["size"]][6]
tests.label: but only as far as its last stage
a day later the washing up is still there
two days on it has gone by itself

tests.expr: [fresh(), on(1), leave_trace("laundry"), on(8), leave_trace("laundry"), on(9), age_traces(), traces_in("bedroom").size()][7]
tests.label: a pile you keep adding to does not expire under you

hints: var k: Dictionary = KINDS[id] and var here := traces_in(k["room"]) give you everything the rest of the function needs.
For the oldest: var oldest: Dictionary = here[0], then a loop that replaces it whenever it meets a smaller "day", then traces.erase(oldest).
age_traces builds a new array: if day - t["day"] < KINDS[t["kind"]]["life"]: keep.append(t), then traces = keep.
steps.explain: Three rules from the file's own comments: traces expire, so the game makes mess without making the player do the housework; there are few, because three traces read as a life and thirty as clutter; and each is specific. Two kinds change while they sit there, and in different ways. Flowers age, so their stage comes from the calendar; laundry grows, so its stage comes from how often you were busy, which is why it carries a size and restarts its clock. Try adding a kind to KINDS and leaving it.

steps.title: Today starts empty
steps.task: The day's list clears at midnight without anything clearing it. Keep today as {"day": …, "done": […]}. today_done() returns the done list, but an empty one when today belongs to another day. tick_today(id) starts a fresh record if the day differs, and adds id once. Then archive_notice(id, text): skip it if there is already a row with that id from today, otherwise insert {"day", "id", "text"} at the front and keep only ARCHIVE_KEEP.

tests.label: ticking the same thing twice is one tick
tomorrow it is empty again
and only tomorrow's ticks are on it
one filing per thing per day
the same thing on another day is filed again

tests.expr: [fresh(), archive_notice("a", "1"), archive_notice("b", "1"), archive_notice("c", "1"), archive_notice("d", "1"), archive_notice("e", "1"), archive.size(), archive[0]["id"]][6]
tests.label: the archive stops at ARCHIVE_KEEP

tests.expr: [fresh(), archive_notice("a", "1"), archive_notice("b", "1"), archive_notice("c", "1"), archive_notice("d", "1"), archive_notice("e", "1"), archive.size(), archive[0]["id"]][7]
tests.label: newest first

hints: The same test twice: today.get("day", -1) != day. In today_done it means "nothing yet"; in tick_today it means "start again".
today = {"day": day, "done": []}, then if today["done"].has(id): return and today["done"].append(id).
archive_notice is the diary again with a different check: row["id"] == id and row["day"] == day.
steps.explain: Nothing is reset at midnight. The record carries the day it belongs to, and a record from yesterday simply reads as empty: a missed day is gone instead of becoming a backlog. The game says so in its comments: the list is a reason to go out, not a chore list. The archive keeps swiped notifications for a different reason, the size of the save, which is why ARCHIVE_KEEP is 60 and not unlimited: a year of a chatty game would make the backup code unmailable.

title: Build the night's sleep
intro: What happens between the last evening and the next morning, in order. You write advance_day() a piece at a time: the clock restarting, the crops growing, the year turning and the world being told, and then a weather forecast that comes without being stored. The clock from entry C, the calendar from entry Y and some test helpers are at the bottom.
starter:
extends Node

signal day_changed(day: int)

const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0
const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5
const DAYS_PER_YEAR := DAYS_PER_SEASON * 4
const WORDS := ["", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five"]

var day := 1
var clock_t := 0.0
var night_held := false
var farm := []
var memories := []
var heard := []   # what a listener on day_changed saw

func _ready() -> void:
	day_changed.connect(func(d: int) -> void: heard.append([d, ripe()]))

func advance_day() -> void:
	pass

func season_index() -> int:
	return 0

func weather() -> String:
	return "Clear"

# ── Written for you. Your work is above this line. ──

func year() -> int:
	return (maxi(1, day) - 1) / DAYS_PER_YEAR + 1

func year_day() -> int:
	return (maxi(1, day) - 1) % DAYS_PER_YEAR + 1

func years_phrase() -> String:
	var y := year() - 1
	if y == 1:
		return "A year"
	return WORDS[y].capitalize() + " years"

func ripe() -> int:
	var n := 0
	for plot in farm:
		if plot["ready"]:
			n += 1
	return n

# The clock from entry C: it counts up and parks at nightfall.
func tick(delta: float) -> void:
	if night_held:
		return
	clock_t += delta
	if clock_t >= DAY_LENGTH:
		clock_t = DAY_LENGTH
		night_held = true

func run_to_night() -> bool:
	tick(DAY_LENGTH * 2.0)
	return night_held

func on(d: int) -> int:
	day = d
	return d

func reset() -> bool:
	day = 1
	clock_t = 0.0
	night_held = false
	farm = [
		{"state": "planted", "watered": true, "ready": false},
		{"state": "planted", "watered": false, "ready": false},
		{"state": "empty", "watered": false, "ready": false},
	]
	memories = []
	heard = []
	return true

steps.title: A new morning
steps.task: Write advance_day(). It adds one to day, puts clock_t back to 0.0 and clears night_held, so the clock that parked at nightfall runs again. Helpers at the bottom play the clock to nightfall (run_to_night()) and start a fresh life (reset()).
steps.solution:
extends Node

signal day_changed(day: int)

const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0
const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5
const DAYS_PER_YEAR := DAYS_PER_SEASON * 4
const WORDS := ["", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five"]

var day := 1
var clock_t := 0.0
var night_held := false
var farm := []
var memories := []
var heard := []   # what a listener on day_changed saw

func _ready() -> void:
	day_changed.connect(func(d: int) -> void: heard.append([d, ripe()]))

func advance_day() -> void:
	day += 1
	clock_t = 0.0
	night_held = false

func season_index() -> int:
	return 0

func weather() -> String:
	return "Clear"

# ── Written for you. Your work is above this line. ──

func year() -> int:
	return (maxi(1, day) - 1) / DAYS_PER_YEAR + 1

func year_day() -> int:
	return (maxi(1, day) - 1) % DAYS_PER_YEAR + 1

func years_phrase() -> String:
	var y := year() - 1
	if y == 1:
		return "A year"
	return WORDS[y].capitalize() + " years"

func ripe() -> int:
	var n := 0
	for plot in farm:
		if plot["ready"]:
			n += 1
	return n

# The clock from entry C: it counts up and parks at nightfall.
func tick(delta: float) -> void:
	if night_held:
		return
	clock_t += delta
	if clock_t >= DAY_LENGTH:
		clock_t = DAY_LENGTH
		night_held = true

func run_to_night() -> bool:
	tick(DAY_LENGTH * 2.0)
	return night_held

func on(d: int) -> int:
	day = d
	return d

func reset() -> bool:
	day = 1
	clock_t = 0.0
	night_held = false
	farm = [
		{"state": "planted", "watered": true, "ready": false},
		{"state": "planted", "watered": false, "ready": false},
		{"state": "empty", "watered": false, "ready": false},
	]
	memories = []
	heard = []
	return true

tests.label: before sleeping, the day is parked at nightfall
a night's sleep is one more day
the clock is back at the start
and the night is no longer held
so time passes again

hints: Three lines: day += 1, then set the other two back.
clock_t = 0.0 and night_held = false.
The order of these lines will matter in step 3, so keep them first.
steps.explain: The clock from entry C stops when the day is used up and waits for exactly this call. night_held is not a timer. It is a state that only sleeping can end, which is why nothing in the game is ever missed by being slow.

steps.task: Add the overnight growth to advance_day(). Every plot in farm that is "planted" and "watered" becomes "ready". A plot that is empty, or planted but not watered, is left exactly as it was.

the unwatered one is not
nor is an empty bed

steps.title: The year turns, then tell everyone
steps.task: Two more things, in this order. If year_day() is 1 and year() is above 1, add years_phrase() + " in this house." to memories. Then, last of all, day_changed.emit(day). A listener was connected in _ready; it records the day it was told about and how many plots were ripe at that moment.
steps.solution:
extends Node

signal day_changed(day: int)

const DAY_LENGTH := 480.0
const DAYS_PER_SEASON := 5
const DAYS_PER_YEAR := DAYS_PER_SEASON * 4
const WORDS := ["", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five"]

var day := 1
var clock_t := 0.0
var night_held := false
var farm := []

var heard := []   # what a listener on day_changed saw

func _ready() -> void:
	day_changed.connect(func(d: int) -> void: heard.append([d, ripe()]))

func advance_day() -> void:
	day += 1
	clock_t = 0.0
	night_held = false
	# Overnight: every watered plot finishes growing.
	for plot in farm:
		if plot["state"] == "planted" and plot["watered"]:
			plot["ready"] = true
	# A year turning is worth saying out loud.
	if year_day() == 1 and year() > 1:
		memories.append(years_phrase() + " in this house.")
	# Last, so whoever is listening sees the new morning, not half of it.
	day_changed.emit(day)

	return 0

	day = 1

		{"state": "planted", "watered": true, "ready": false},

tests.label: the listener hears about day 2, and sees the ripe crop already there
day 21 is a year
day 22 is just a day
and day 41 is two years
every morning announces itself once

hints: The year check reads two helpers already written: if year_day() == 1 and year() > 1:.
memories.append(years_phrase() + " in this house."), then the signal.
day_changed.emit(day) goes on the last line of the function.
steps.explain: The listener's record, [2, 1], is the proof of the order: when it was told, the crop was already ripe. Emit the signal before the growth loop and it would see [2, 0], a morning half made. In the game the listener is the main scene, which rebuilds the room for the new day, and it needs the finished world to rebuild from. The year memory is the calendar admitting how long you have been here.

steps.title: The sky comes free
steps.task: Nothing in advance_day() touches the weather, and yet it changes. Write season_index(), (day - 1) / DAYS_PER_SEASON rounded down, wrapped round four seasons with % 4. Then weather(): x = sin(day * 127.1 + 311.7) * 43758.5453 and r = x - floor(x). In winter (season 3): Snowy below 0.5, Rainy below 0.62, else Clear. In the other seasons it is Rainy when r is below 0.35 (spring), 0.15 (summer) or 0.4 (autumn), otherwise Clear.

tests.expr: [reset(), season_index(), on(5), season_index(), on(6), season_index(), on(16), season_index(), on(21), season_index()]
tests.label: five days to a season, four seasons to a year

tests.expr: [reset(), on(1), weather(), on(2), weather(), on(12), weather()]
tests.label: days 1, 2 and 12
deep winter snows
the same day always has the same sky

hints: int(floor(float(day - 1) / float(DAYS_PER_SEASON))) % 4 keeps the division from rounding the wrong way.
Pick the chance with var rain_chance: float = [0.35, 0.15, 0.4][s] once you know it is not winter.
return "Rainy" if r < rain_chance else "Clear".
steps.explain: There is no weather variable to update, and so nothing to forget to update. The number that goes up is the day, and the sky is a function of it, like the phase in entry C and the year in entry Y. sin of a big number, scaled and cut down to its fractional part, is a cheap deterministic dice: the same day, on any phone, any time, rolls the same. That is also why the game needs no weather in its save.
